text:
I run Claude Code, Codex, and Command Code as one team, using GitHub Milestones instead of hand-picking every issue. Unlike rigid Epics, you drop new issues in mid-sprint and work drains straight toward release.

Hesitating to restart sessions means running on bloated context, piling up rework, and skipping agent CLI updates. Parallel work also breaks fast without guardrails. Here are six problems I hit, and how CommandMate fixes each:

- One vendor shares blind spots -> Mix models across vendors so another family reviews designs and blind spots.
- Frontier plans on every seat burn budgets -> Keep top tiers on judgment seats (PM, Dev Lead, Judge); back workers with contracts and tests.
- Agents drift off-role -> Fix one role per instance; wrong-role sends stop before typing (exit 32).
- "I'm done" skipped tests -> Repo checks decide done per PR (exit 0, 20, or 21), then a Judge runs UAT on the integrated Milestone.
- Context bloat degrades runs & delays CLI upgrades -> Typed state (mem) auto-closes on PR merge and briefs fresh sessions, so restarting is cheap and fast.
- Replies mix up or specs change unchecked -> ID-matched ask replies, delivery holds when uncertain, and UI-only approval (promote) from mem before issues or docs change.

Set a GitHub Milestone once, restart freely, and only approvals reach you.
Paste one prompt from the README into Claude Code, Codex, or Command Code to set up the same 5-role team (works with 1 to 3 vendors).

Open source (MIT), runs on your machine.

npx commandmate@latest

🤯 P vs NP is all over the timeline, so here's the quick version

It's one of the 7 Millennium Prize Problems and the biggest open question in computer science

- P: problems you can solve fast 
(sorting 1,000 cards)

- NP: problems you can check fast 
(a finished Sudoku)

The question: if an answer is easy to check, is it also easy to find? Most mathematicians believe P ≠ NP, but nobody has proven it yet.

• If P ≠ NP: 'hard to solve, easy to check' is confirmed as a real foundation. Bitcoin signatures and bank security rely on exactly this, so the status quo gets officially certified

• If P = NP with a practical algorithm: public key crypto breaks, and wallets, banks and HTTPS are all at risk. On the flip side, logistics, protein design, drug discovery and even finding math proofs become dramatically easier

Where crypto connects:
1. ZK proofs : by definition, proofs for NP statements

2. Proof of Useful Work : turning mining into solving NP problems

3. $NEAR : on Sep 6, cofounder Alex Skidanov said NEAR AI's open source Lean agent solved all 672 PutnamBench problems for $111, 250x cheaper than the next submission. Verification is getting cheap.

text:
Marvel is giving John Romita Jr. a year of covers. His first Hobgoblin already costs $1,500 in 9.8.

If you read Marvel at any point since 1977, you've read John Romita Jr. Spider-Man in the '80s. X-Men with Claremont. Daredevil with Nocenti. Man Without Fear. Kick-Ass. Heavy, blocky figures you can spot across the shop.

On November 20, Marvel announced a year of John Romita Jr. 50th Anniversary Special Variant Covers, one "Cover JRJR" a month, for 50 years since his first Marvel contract. The first three:

Amazing Spider-Man #1008, January 20 Hulk War: Infernal Rage #1, February 3 Daredevil #700, March 17

Marvel hasn't said whether these are open-order or ratio covers. Any presale number you see is an ask.

The bigger question is the old books. JRJR drew a stack of first appearances. Here's where they sit in CGC 9.8, from PriceCharting's tracked sales:

Amazing Spider-Man #238, first Hobgoblin: $1,386 (eBay, Nov 9), $1,586 (Heritage, Nov 12), $1,891 (Heritage, Oct 15). In January, 9.8s traded from $916 to about $1,300. Up roughly 20% to 40% this year, before the announcement.

text:
do you realize what Anthropic just did?

they moved their Messages API (the one Claude Code, Cowork and API customers all run through) from Python to Rust… on live traffic, without ever taking it offline

here's how they did it:

→ Claude wrote a first version of the core request path in about a week. the hard part was proving it behaved exactly like the old one

→ the Rust version passed about 98% of its tests. on real traffic only about a quarter of inputs matched

→ so they made the old Python API the judge. real requests ran through both and every difference got logged by where it happened and how big it was… never the customer's text

→ one bug leaves the same fingerprint on every request it hits, so a coordinator agent gave each new fingerprint its own worker agent and opened a Slack thread for the engineers to follow

→ workers tested guesses in a sandbox in seconds, fixes went through PR review, then got rechecked on live traffic

→ engineer corrections got saved as rules that every later agent reads
result: about 70% less CPU per request and about 20% lower median time to first token. public traffic moved over in September

now a little behind the scenes…

one agent "fixed" a web search bug by copying the tool text into a file. the two versions matched and the check passed, but an engineer rejected it as throwaway code

and when they audited the ported tests they found 100+ checks that had been weakened

if you're rewriting any code with agents…

→ now you can keep the old version running and make it the judge → group differences by fingerprint so one bug doesn't hit you as hundreds of thousands of separate diffs → you as a human can read every fix before it merges

save this process to help you

quoted_text:
The call-to-action from Ryan Williams about advancing circuit complexity at CircuitBreaker @yukonresearch made my day yesterday.

To recap, this challenge is about the long standing open problem of circuit lower bound on Boolean circuits. The statement is to come up with an explicit family of Boolean functions in NP, one for each input length of n bits, and prove that every circuit constructed from two-input logic gates to compute it needs at least c·n^p gates, for all large n, with c and p as large as possible. 

The power p is still 1 but there has been rapid progress in the coefficient c in last one month. You can see the timeline of progress below.

The big picture implication of this circuit lower bound problem is that if someone were to be able to come up with an explicit family of Boolean functions that has lower bound grow faster than every polynomial, that will prove P not equal to NP.

We collaborated with legendary cryptographer Amit Sahai to bring this problem of circuit lower bound to @yukonresearch in order to have open multiplayer format make progress on it. All progress in CircuitBreaker challenge are LLM-verified till now, expect to have human expert review soon.

Building on top of the work from McGuire, Schlesinger and Williams (4.5624n https://t.co/qstI5uZ7bE), three solvers @arthurostapenko, @GalArnon42 and DarkWingMcQuack have already moved the frontier to 4.82709n.

Reiterating what Ryan has called for, please deploy your swarm and accelerate the progress 🫡.

text:
When I was growing up and the internet was taking shape, you heard the word “surfing” everywhere. You were surfing the web.

It was such a powerful analogy because you could almost feel it - it really felt like you were riding the waves of the internet. There was something very fluidic about exploring this new virtual world.

“Surfing” became “browsing”, and browsing today can mean many things: watching videos, scrolling on X, working, shopping, reading blogs or looking for your next vacation.

It seems as agents are approaching the internet from almost the opposite direction - it’s about getting things done. inherently functional. Agents lack any entertainment or enjoyment abilities in their nature, maybe you get a small delight from getting a better price,  but it is just not about inspiration.

When you want to fill out a form, you use an agent. When you want to compare prices or find the cheapest flight, you use an agent. But when you want to feel inspired, you surf. You browse. No one has yet to crack how this looks like in the agentic world.

I don’t think these two verbs replace each other in the way people experience the internet. we’ll continue browsing and use agents to handle the functional stuff in between, in some shape or form. You can start with an agent and end up browsing or vise versa. You can finish the checkout with the agent. But somewhere in that journey you will surf. 🏄

theoretical physics constructs mathematical frameworks that work in some settings and tries to make them increasingly realistic, and then try to predict or explain some physical phenomena that previous ideas couldn't. this one is a quantum theory in a vaccum (no matter yet) that recovers known results like the black hole entropy formula and the einstein equations at large scales, but as i understand it these are the minimum tests such a theory would have to pass

direct experiments for quantum gravity corrections that only show up at incredibly high energies are not possible with current technology - you would have to hope the theory explains something in the cosmic microwave background for example

text:
It is easy to look at the NFT space from the outside and call it “absolutely meaningless”, as Oscar Murillo (@OMLG233) does in this conversation. @jamiegourlay had already named the catch earlier... it is hard to get any real sense of what is happening here without spending a long time inside it. You cannot read a culture from its surface noise, and you certainly cannot read it from its worst cycle.

Oscar is right on the part he knows best. Speculation is not a blockchain invention... the broader art world runs on it too, through auction results, recurring museum shows, and the markets that reinforce both. Artists were building their own networks long before tokens existed, and his Duchamp point is good. None of that is new, and pretending otherwise does nobody any favours.

Where “it’s all the same” slips is in what actually happens once you stay. @williamapan describes collectors comparing outputs, picking favourites, proposing trades... the slow, unglamorous labour of looking together until a shared language forms. Spend enough time inside a community like that and you start noticing things you would have missed alone. That can happen in any art world, not uniquely here, but it took a particular form onchain (faster, more exposed, less buffered), and flattening it into “nothing” skips over the important parts.

That same proximity cuts the other way, and @proofofgail gets closer to the real cost. Without institutional cushioning, a weak market response does not stay with one release... it follows an artist straight into the next. The closeness that lets collectors learn a practice in real time also gives their immediate reactions outsized weight, compressing what the wider art world stretches across years. That tension deserved more room in the conversation...

I like that Oscar sees a way for Frequencies to circulate here and take on a life of its own, which is why I bristled at how easily he dismissed the culture he is inviting to give it that life. You do not get that circulation without the people who stayed to build the caretaking infrastructure after the money and attention moved on. @jamiegourlay had it right... you have to spend time here to understand what people are doing together, and why they keep doing it once the noise leaves.

Wonderful convo and well worth a listen.

quoted_text:
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

APEC峰会期间，中韩🇨🇳🇰🇷 FTA第二阶段全面升级，千年盟国基因苏醒，开始联手瓜分肢解日本🇯🇵产业。

中韩FTA第二阶段（升级谈判）在深圳APEC期间官宣实质性完成，李在明收到了超级硬核大礼。韩国相关领域股票当日全线暴涨！

在中日关系跌入谷底之际，中韩两国时隔百年再度联手，开始着手在本轮世界经济大调整重构之际，对日本的经济产业进行瓜分肢解。

尽管二战之后的数十年，由于战后格局影响，韩国成为了美军对华遏制的桥头堡基地的关键盟友。但是历史上近千年的大部分时间，韩国（朝鲜）半岛一直都是中国的铁杆盟友，双方多次共同在朝鲜半岛上抗击日本🇯🇵侵略。

在明朝全部藩属国之中，朝鲜（韩国）的地位也是最高的，位列第一且朝鲜国王级别在中国官制中相当于中国丞相级别高于其他藩属国。

历史上，中国🇨🇳多次在国力本身衰弱的情况下，依然大举出兵协助韩国🇰🇷抗击日本🇯🇵侵略。其实往往每次正是因为中国衰落之际，日本就会借机进犯朝鲜，妄图吞并朝鲜而后进犯中华。近代日本正是践行了这一路线，吞并朝鲜，进军东北三省，进而悍然全面侵华。

韩国人民对于中国感情也极为深厚，朝鲜对明朝长期奉行事大，万历援朝（壬辰倭乱）之后，朝鲜一直称明朝有再造之恩，情感上深度亲明￼￼￼。明朝覆灭之后，韩国甚至为明朝守孝数百年。至今韩国仍然称自己为小中华（主承明朝礼制）。

所以如今中国国力全面回归之际，美国开始被迫在东亚战略退潮，数十年短暂的美韩军事同盟关系将逐步被千年的中韩邻居伙伴关系所取代，两国将共同节制多次进犯朝鲜半岛，数次妄图吞并韩国的日本大和民主政权。中韩两国本来从人种，文化，地理，历史等各方面，就天然具备成为盟友和深度一体化的强大历史惯性，拉长历史来看，美韩同盟不过只是历史的阶段性小插曲。

中韩关系在亲中的李在明替代亲美的尹锡悦之后，得到大幅加强，李在明已经成为当下最受中国民众欢迎的政客之一。而与之相对的日本首相高市早苗则成为中国最不受欢迎的政治人物。

由于日韩经济产业结构高度类似，所以中韩联手，无疑是瓜分肢解日本产业，壮大韩国产业，进一步提升中韩两国国际产业链主导地位的绝佳选择和最佳时机。

中韩FTA第二阶段 2017年底宣布启动，2018年3月首轮谈判，一共17轮，历时8年多，2026年11月深圳APEC峰会期间实质性谈完；

和RCEP的区别，RCEP是多边框架；本次中韩升级是双边更高标准，服务与投资开放深度高于RCEP，是东北亚高标准经贸规则的一次落地。原协定里已经落地的货物降税安排继续保留，本次升级不改动货物关税。

🚨 ALERT: $VVV plunges more than -15% as explosive privacy allegations rock the billion-dollar company marketed as a private, self-hosted AI platform.

A researcher reveals that 14 of the 18 image-recognition models tested on Venice AI routed requests to third-party inference providers, including DeepInfra, Baseten, Fireworks and Parasail.

The investigation raises further questions about Venice's privacy claims:

• Its supposedly self-hosted models allegedly rely heavily on external infrastructure.

• Its end-to-end encryption reportedly allows Venice or its infrastructure partner Phala to access conversations and inject messages.

• Its platform also reportedly offers access to Claude and OpenAI models, despite founder Erik Voorhees previously saying Venice would never become a wrapper for centralized AI services.

The controversy intensified after Lookonchain flagged a wallet suspected of being linked to Voorhees depositing 81,463 $VVV, worth approximately $2.25 million, into Coinbase around seven hours earlier.

Venice recently announced annualized revenue exceeding $200 million.

However, founder Voorhees has pushed back, calling the allegations "Fake news."

He maintains that every model marked "Private" guarantees zero data retention, while Venice keeps no content logs, and that models marked "Anonymous" clearly disclose that third-party providers may store prompts.

author: CypherventuresM
quoted_text:
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

- 31 real data sources including Census, BEA, BLS, EIA, NOAA, USGS, DoD, NPS, FAA, FEMA, CDC...
- Real elevation, land cover, GDP, jobs, power plants, mines, ports, airports, bases, parks, universities, freight flows, disasters; all reconciled onto one 25 km hex grid.
- The data is converted into Civilization language, e.g. Gold yield is GDP. A city's districts are its real industry specializations: San Jose gets a Campus, Detroit is "Motor city". Its citizens are its real workforce: 1 in 4 San Jose workers are engineers, coders or scientists, against 1 in 14 nationally. Wonders are chosen by published rules, such as national parks by visitor numbers and universities by R&D spending, etc etc.
- 19 lenses (income, degrees, faith, disasters…), a City View for 524 metros, and nine advisors plus an Explorer. The Explorer turns any column for any of 3,100+ counties into a table and scatter plot, linked to the map.
- Claude decided to skip a few states and territories sry
- Built using Claude Code desktop app, Opus 5.5 on medium and turning on ultracode.

It's deployed here: https://t.co/QMhmafXMj5 and the "?" has the source link too. I don't exactly know where I was going with this but it's really fun to browse and play with. Possibly it can be expanded or built into a game. I only have half of my weekly Claude quote left though so someone else will have to take over :D. Claude also made a trailer:

text:
Just a couple of facts:

1. The prosecution's first witness was a scam victim whose money was never proven to have reached Tornado Cash. The government's own tracing agent admitted his analysis didn't prove the scammer sent her funds there: "No, not at all."

2. The infamous "cashing out 600 mil" message wasn't written by me or either of my co-founders. It was a question from a CoinDesk journalist, Andrew Thurman (@Blockanalia), that was forwarded into a chat. The government put it in my indictment anyway.

3. When my defense argued that this had never been a crime before, the prosecutor's response was: "Some case has to be first."

4. I blocked sanctioned wallets using Chainalysis's own technology. Prosecutors called this compliance measure a "fig leaf" and used it as evidence against me.

5. I faced up to 45 years in prison over smart contracts I could no longer change. All three alleged conspiracies began after the contracts became immutable, and even the government's own expert admitted we couldn't change them.

6. I never earned a fee from users' transactions. Meanwhile, Chainalysis, the government's own crypto-tracking provider, operated a Tornado Cash relayer and collected fees during the period covered by my charges. They were never charged.

7. On the day my indictment was unsealed, FinCEN officials told prosecutors in the same office that non-custodial software likely isn't a money-transmitting business. My defense learned of that conversation about 21 months later, and only because it surfaced in another case.

8. Just 15 days after my conviction, the DOJ publicly stated that developers of neutral tools without criminal intent should not be held responsible for someone else's misuse of their software.

My prosecution continues.

text:
Sharing some longer thoughts on Ethereum's upcoming Hegotá upgrade and how it relates to pqai and FOCIL, ahead of "tomorrow's" ACDC call (I need to urgently go to bed...): https://t.co/tqY5hUVZsV. 

Ethereum faces an important high-level governance choice in the coming weeks: do we reprioritize upcoming Hegotá upgrade and drop everything not on the critical path to a post-quantum and post-AI Ethereum, or not? If yes, FOCIL has to go for now. If not, FOCIL should arguably be the first EIP to stay, since it's the only SFI'd EIP not on the critical path to pqai.

It is my strong opinion that we should uncompromisingly prioritize pqai and drop FOCIL:

1. Transitioning Ethereum to pqai is a hugely ambitious undertaking, and FOCIL competes for the same bottleneck of resources. For better or worse, every big change goes through a small set of high-context researchers and client devs, who have a holistic system’s view and are instrumental in shipping big upgrades safely. As far as I can tell, ~all of them are currently sprinting on post-quantum Gasper / decoupled consensus. They can work on FOCIL or on pqai, but not both at the same time.

2. FOCIL is not on the critical path to pqai and is not built for pq by default. It would need adapting to work well in a pq setting, likely with compromises to keep changes to its current design manageable. I'm confident we can find a good design if we put our minds to it. But more importantly, that design work falls on the same people that pqai needs.

3. On governance: yes, removing FOCIL from Hegotá after it was SFI'd as headliner would be a drastic step. As radical as that reversal is, I think the circumstances justify it. When Frames and FOCIL were scoped for Hegotá in January, the frontier model was Opus 4.5. Since then AI has been solving long-standing open maths problems in the hundreds, and as we wrote in our Ethlabs pqai27 post, "the security of our cryptography is itself an open maths problem". Since we published that post two weeks ago, the Riemann hypothesis was solved, a problem that Terence Tao only a couple of weeks ago said he would expect to fall ~2050. If the world changes under our feet in real time, Ethereum governance ought to be able to react. It needs to recognize when reality has changed enough to revisit a decision. Or else Ethereum risks death by bureaucratic process.

I don't say this lightly. I deeply care about FOCIL and have strongly advocated for it myself, including for shipping it as early as Glamsterdam. I want FOCIL, or a variant of it, on Ethereum, and I'll be among the first to push for it once we are pqai.

The Merge showed what Ethereum can do when everyone collectively pulls in one direction. pqai is a chance to do that again, and to future-proof Ethereum as the world’s root of trust. Let's stay disciplined now, and ship pqai as fast as responsibly possible. :)

TapeTape 2.1.0 更新
昨天修改到凌晨1点多，本次是一个大版本更新，累计修改了70多项功能，主要内容如下：

1、发消息不再转圈：以前群里发一条消息，要转圈 1 分钟左右才显示发出，消息发送规则拖住所有人。现在规则进行了修改，1-2秒就显示发出。

2、不再乱报红色叹号：以前群里有一个人暂时联系不上，整条消息就显示失败，现在问题已经修改。

3、断网不误判：分得清是自己没网还是对方连不上，网络恢复后自动补发，断网期间不计入对方的失败。图片、语音、文件也会单独重试，一个人收不到不影响其他人。通知栏回复没发完，会如实提示还在发送中。

4、新版群上线：官方入群机器人 24 小时在线，拿到链接点一下就能立即进群，群主不在线也不用等。只有群主能移除成员、改群名、改头像、换二维码，谁都冒充不了。机器人不是群成员，看不到任何聊天内容。被移除的人拿旧链接也回不来。老群可以一键升级成新版群。

5、钱包安全加固：红包、转账、开店费用都和公共节点交叉核对，同一笔付款只认一张卡，交易已经发出不会再误报失败让你付两次。网页钱包遇到看不懂的签名会标红、要你再确认一次，登录网站和域名对不上会发出警告。

6、隐私：头像和签名档只发给好友，陌生人拉你进群，需要你的同意后才行。

安卓 2.1.0 已上线：https://t.co/lfxldIxyAG ，iOS 已经提交审核，即将上线。
建议大家更新客户端，不用删除，直接下载覆盖安装就行，很简单。

text:
对想学量化交易的初学者来说，有几点我希望大家可以关注一下
第一，量化的门槛是“能不能写成规则、用历史数据检验”，不是学历或模型有多深。能编码的技术分析可以，凭感觉找头肩这类图形不算。作者自己用高深数学在机构里持续亏损，回家后用很简单的策略才稳定盈利。所以你现在最该练的，是把想法写清楚、做回测，而不是先去堆复杂模型。

第二，把它当成一门可小起步的生意，而不是暴富或找刺激的途径。策略有内在收益率，不能硬赶；也不该为了年化 200% 去过度加杠杆。零售账户隔夜大约 2 倍、日内 4 倍，起步规模可以不大，但扩展靠的是杠杆和系统，不是天天盯盘。

第三，先问自己适不适合这个节奏：有没有一点金融或编程基础，有没有积蓄撑过一段时间没有稳定收入，恐惧和贪婪是否大致平衡。自动化做好后，日常交易可以很少，但研究和回测新策略要长期做；系统可以自动驾驶，你的手还是要放在方向盘上。

text:
If factoring is indeed in P, it would (and should) create panic, even if the algorithm is "galactic", because:

1. This breaches a barrier that was considered insurmountable, and once it was breached, the risk that future optimization will someday hit the practical thresholds has shot through the roof
2. Cryptographic reductions that assumed that factoring is superpolynomial are no longer valid.
3. The replacement for these reductions will be very problematic from a theoretical perspective. On one hand, security arguments that assume the adversary is "polynomial" no longer work, and we have to assume that the polynomial itself has bounded degree and constants. On the other hand, we will also need a concrete lower bound on the hardness of factoring. Such reductions are only valid as long as the adversaries are as weak as we assume and the algorithm is as inefficient as we assume. The most painful aspect of this all is that we must look at constants, not just the polynomial degree.
4. The threat is not just to ongoing cryptography. On that front, we're fine. Yeah, factoring breaks classical RSA, but we have replacements. E.g. elliptic-curve-based cryptography, including EC-RSA, and all of the new post-quantum stuff. (Hash-based crypto is also safe, but it's not a replacement). But there are other attacks. Most crucially, harvest-now-decrypt-later attacks. There may be hoards of encrypted communications stored until the day a weakness is found. People who waited thirty years will not mind if their algorithm takes a week to decrypt a single message. At some point, the slowness will only protect you in real time.
5. And what else will turn out to be in P in the coming days? EC-DLOG? Isogenies? Ring-LWE? Each one of these will be a huge hit to data security.

author: LoganJastremski
quoted_text:
This is going to get a bit nerdy, lets do it because I want to explain why you actually want people arbing onchain equities

In TradFi, a market maker can sell you a stock on one venue and buy it back on another to hedge. If the stock is cheap on one venue and expensive on the other, firms trade that gap until the prices come back in line. You  buy the stock, then the firm on the other side can trade it hundreds of times and finish the day roughly flat. This is literally the job of the market maker is to provide liquidity

In this case you have three tokens (Ondo, Securitize, Backpack) backed by the same stock and still trade at different spreads. If I’m market making Anthropic, I care who I can sell the token to and what I get back when I redeem it. Securitize, Ondo and Backpack handle that differently

With Securitize, you complete KYC to buy a brokerage entitlement backed 1:1 by Anthropic shares. If you want dollars back, you can sell through the broker for USDC. If you want to send it to me, my wallet has to be KYC'd too. Even if we agree on a price, you can only deliver the token to me after I’m onboarded

Ondo’s international stock tokens move more like USDC or USDT. Wallets can receive the stock backed token without opening an Ondo account. KYC comes in when you mint or redeem directly. Ordinary redemptions pay out in stablecoins. A market maker can still hedge the stock elsewhere, but only separately approved institutions can redeem the token in kind and receive the underlying shares through Alpaca

We’re investors in Backpack at Frictionless, and the part I think is underappreciated is that Backpack also runs the brokerage. Once the token is on Solana, wallets can trade it without a Backpack account. An eligible individual with a verified brokerage account can move in both directions. Buy the stock and withdraw it as tokens, or deposit the tokens and get the stock back

In-kind redemption is the alpha here. Say I’m a market maker. I buy 100 tokens from you onchain and sell 100 shares from my brokerage account to hedge. With Backpack, I can redeem those tokens and put the 100 shares right back in my account. If redemption pays me in stablecoins, I still have to go buy 100 shares to get back to the same position. That extra trade can mean crossing the spread again, and the stock can move between fills. I have to leave room for that in my quote, which means a lower bid for you

Now flip the trade. Say you want to buy Anthropic onchain. Anthropic is being offered at $100 in the brokerage while the stock market is open, and the cheapest offer on Solana is $101. One market maker can sell to me at $100.50, buy the stock at $100 and withdraw more tokens to replace what they sold. Another can offer me $100.25 and win my order. I get a tighter spread, and they can quote me more size because they know where the next shares are coming from

You can see this in the Blockworks data. Across seven stocks, Backpack had a cheaper round trip than xStocks in 98% of matched Jupiter quotes for $500 to $10k orders. In other tests of $1 to $100 SpaceX trades, the average all-in cost was 0.11% on Backpack versus 4.29% on Robinhood chain. Roughly 40x as much on Robinhood chain once fees were included

The market structure and redemption matter quite a bit and its how better execution turns into more volume. If I show up with $10k of USDC on Titan, Jupiter or DFlow my order routes through whoever gets me the most stock

text:
Coding gives you a window into what the future will look like for a large amount of knowledge work. 

The first step for most jobs is that we go from doing most of the research, typing, and value creation manually (even if it’s using digital tools) to soon coordinating the work that agents are doing. 

Next, as this step itself becomes redundant or slows down what agents are capable of, we will be giving agents goals to optimize against and they’ll go off on and increasingly solve larger problems for us. 

This may at first blush look like something whose impact gets stuck with coding, but actually a large percentage of knowledge work may eventually just converge with this form factor due to the massive productivity gains that can be generated. Agents will use computers, leverage our existing tools or write new ones, and write code on the fly to solve larger swaths of knowledge work. 

So even if a task today doesn’t seem to be “coding” directly, the task may eventually fold into being coding adjacent. Manufacturing, architecture, life sciences, material sciences, cyber, and on and on.
 
One big hurdle in the way ultimately will be that much of this work remains non-verifiable, so humans will be even more in the loop than they are in coding. But the part that they can hand off will just get bigger and bigger over time as the models are more capable.

So in short, pay attention to coding and you’ll get a sense for where work is going.

퍼미션리스 전환, 더 많은 참여자가 함께하는 카이아

카이아는 초기 네트워크의 안정적인 운영을 위해 GC 중심으로 출발했습니다. 이제는 네트워크의 성능과 안정성을 유지하면서, 더 다양한 팀이 각자의 역량으로 생태계 성장에 기여할 수 있도록 참여의 문을 넓히고 있습니다.

참여 기회를 확대하고, 실제 기여를 보상으로 연결하는 것이 카이아 PGT 로드맵의 목표입니다.

① 네트워크 운영에 참여할 기회가 넓어집니다.
블록체인에서는 거래를 검증하고 블록을 만드는 ‘검증자’가 네트워크를 운영합니다.

퍼미션리스 전환 후에는 GC가 아니어도 필요한 스테이킹 요건과 기술적 기준을 충족하면 별도의 개별 승인 없이 검증자로 참여할 수 있습니다. 다양한 팀이 기술적 운영 역량으로 카이아에 기여할 수 있는 기반이 마련되는 것입니다.

② 네트워크 운영과 의사결정의 역할이 구분됩니다.
검증자는 거래 검증과 블록 생성을, GC는 네트워크 정책과 생태계 방향에 대한 주요 의사결정을 담당합니다. 검증자 참여가 곧바로 거버넌스 의결권을 부여하는 것은 아닙니다.

의사결정에도 참여하고 싶은 검증자는 GC 가입을 신청할 수 있습니다. 새 정책이 적용되면 자격 요건을 갖추고 제안서와 필수 정보를 공개·등록한 뒤, 정해진 기간 동안 이의가 없으면 기존 GC의 별도 승인 투표 없이 정식 GC로 확정됩니다.

③ 참여는 열고, 합의 참여 자격은 시스템으로 관리합니다.
실제 합의 참여에는 운영 성능과 스테이킹 기준이 적용되며, 기준을 충족하지 못한 검증자는 합의 참여가 제한됩니다.

더 다양한 참여자에게 기회를 열면서도 네트워크의 성능과 안정성을 유지하기 위한 설계입니다.

④ 생태계 기여는 CR 보상으로 연결됩니다.
GC는 주요 안건에 투표하고, 기여보상(CR) 미션에도 직접 참여할 수 있습니다.

첫 번째 미션은 KAIA 스테이킹과 USDT 예치를 통한 생태계 기여를 보상합니다. KAIA 스테이킹 수량에 따른 한도 내에서 지정 프로토콜에 USDT를 예치하고, 정해진 기간 동안 두 조건을 유지하면 인정된 기여 규모에 따라 보상이 산정됩니다.

GC뿐 아니라 요건을 충족한 비GC 검증자와 GC에 KAIA를 위임한 일반 이용자도 참여할 수 있습니다.

기존 스테이킹 이용자는 무엇을 해야 할까요?
새 스테이킹 컨트랙트 도입에 따라, 기존 Public Delegation 이용자는 출금 후 새 컨트랙트에 재예치해야 합니다. 자산은 자동으로 이전되지 않습니다.

11월 17일부터 출금 요청이 가능하며, 11월 26일부터는 대기 기간 종료와 해당 GC의 준비 완료 여부에 따라 출금·재예치를 진행할 수 있습니다.

출금 요청만으로 이전이 완료되지는 않습니다. Kaia Portal → Staking → Migration에서 진행 상태와 출금 가능 기간을 확인하고, 재예치까지 완료해 주세요.

Are Americans really so retarded as to not understand what this is about?

Let me spell it out, in a heavily narrativized but directionally true form. 
There are different interests in Europe, and different interest groups. Many countries are deeply – existentially – invested in the NATO, mainly states bordering Russia. Speaking as a Russian: if there were *no* NATO, or if the US pulled out of NATO *today*, we would TOTALLY try to gobble them up. We might even retreat from Ukraine to concentrate on this. Baltics are first on the list, to secure sea access in Kaliningrad which they already threaten. Poland, Finland? They can fight well, and they're not so retarded and racist as to be incapable of diplomacy (unlike Balts) so *probably* not, but they are totally prudent to consider NATO an issue of survival. So these voices, influential thanks to the usual skin-in-the-game mechanics, American «microlateralism» doctrine, and high-ranking agents like Kallas, are dead set on preserving the alliance even at unlimited cost to other members (like Denmark, which they lowkey resent for their blissful secure affluence anyway).

Next, there's the entire nervous system of Atlanticist apparatchiks embedded in EU institutions, many educated or elevated in the US and UK, who don't care much for the continental Europe in the first place, starting with von der Leyen herself and going down; you see them and batallions of their think tankists kvetching here, minimizing and excusing American behavior, calling for accommodation and concern trolling about foolishness of resistance. Those are just enemies or at best patsies.

And there's the general «shared Western civilization» goodwill, if fraying at the seams due to Trump and trade/tech/culture wars. But the ruling political and cultural class in Europe, all these social democrats, is kin to the American Blue Tribe, and it sincerely hopes and believes that once the horrible Orange Hitler is out, the ties will be mended, apologies made, and the Enlightened Hajnali Race will focus anew on the Real Avenger Level Threats — like economic growth, free speech and capitalism, to name a few.

But there are also a few who feel differently. These are the nativist right-wingers (except ones captured by American brainworms to the point of assuming that shared Darwinian values imply shared interests, rather than more intense zero-sum competition for the same assets; an unfortunately common failure of the political mind), who don't want demographic replacement within and ALSO don't want the vassal condition for their people between nations. And there are the French, who have always chafed under the Anglo hegemony. And in the militaries and security apparatuses (relatively weak, sure, but still able to weigh in on the decisionmaking) there are, I'm sure, people with enough exposure to the American elite zeitgeist and loyal to their own nations, unironic realists.

Now, the real big shift that is happening is that the realists have started to wise up - still murkily, half-disbelieving – to what America is doing here, what it openly claims, and why.
America is gathering resources. To fully deplete them. While the infrastructure in the imperial core is lacking and it cannot utilize everything, trade is possible, to ameliorate financial imbalances; but the longer-term objective is to end even the trade. America is growing weary of «strategically indispensable allies in the region» when said region is hard to secure or just a mere patch of dirt or sand. Baltic defense is uninteresting. Ukraine is a tedious bloody steppe, might as well let Russia have it. But a rumor of Ukraine having RARE EARTHS (even though «not rare at all») in Carpathian Mountains? Now we're talking! 300 billion barrels of oil (crappy and hard to get out, maybe non-existent) in Venezuela? Delta Force go go go! Something something HREEs in Kvanefjeld, Greenland?! Trump is clearly confused about details, completion timelines and real limiting factors, jumps the gun and stumbles, but the underlying logic of the faction he represents is consistent like an ice breaker's route. Not even TSMC is seen as valuable enough to renege on trade bullying. TSMC Taiwan is a depreciating asset; to be extracted at warp speed using stick, not carrot, the risk of accelerating the Chinese takeover be damned.  
Now, why does this happen in this exact form? 
To be blunt: we are IN THE ENDGAME. THIS IS LATE ANTHROPOCENE. WE WILL HAVE FULL HUMAN LABOR AUTOMATION WITHIN AT MOST A SINGLE GENERATION IF NOT A FEW YEARS. WE ARE NOW COMPETING NOT FOR MONEY OR HANDS, NOT FOR LANDS, AND CERTAINLY NOT FOR HEARTS AND MINDS, BUT FOR THE STERADIANS OF THE LIGHT CONE OF THE UNIVERSE, AND THEREFORE FOR JOULES AND ATOMS NECESSARY TO BOOTSTRAP THE LARGEST POSSIBLE SEED OF A SPACEFARING CIVILIZATION THAT WILL CONSUME ALL THE NEGENTROPY WITHIN THE COSMIC EVENT HORIZON OF EARTH. Thank you for your attention to this matter.

This is what the Americans believe. The smart ones, like Musk, Thiel, Karp and Jason Gaverick Matheny. They think about this stuff a lot, no kidding. Even their gfs believe.
This is what the Chinese believe too, if implicitly, for their civilization has such innate understanding of performance and infrastructure that it doesn't need this kind of stuff spelled out. Still, they literally think about this as they plan their permanent underground Moon bases and orbital power generation. Did you think it's about vibes, papers, essays, «science» anon? It's not science, it's science fiction, which always has been an unsubtle political aspiration. Qian Xuesen didn't design rockets only to make the Communist Party secure. Neither did von Braun aspire to merely beat the Soviets to the Moon. That's just not how such minds work, anon.  
The Chinese have a well-oiled industrial machine at home that produces maybe 50% of All The Stuff in the world (if you're not in a bubble, you should have noted the pattern of «China makes more $stuff than The Rest Of Humanity Combined» for many values of important $stuff). Enough STEM talent to complete all remaining supply chains. A self-replicating energy infrastructure that grows exponentially. And auxiliary resource bases throughout the developing world, which could be militarized. In principle, the exponential growth factor matters more than the starting point, but in their case both are terrifyingly high and at this rate they look fit to inherit like half of the effective universe. Their economy, even as it still runs on human labor, is already entering a takeoff phase that could replicate the Great Divergence – a trend obscured by gormless «capital efficiency» or «debt» doomposting, a trend that accelerates by a tick as each technology get crossed out of the 35 Chokepoints List, as overcapacity cycles in synergistic industries phase-lock and tun into smooth capacity expansion… While on Earth, they do not expect to directly acquire much more land (though they opportunistically exploit whatever they can, and aim to monopolize much of the South China Sea), but they feel reasonably secure in their odds, relying on the gravity of their nascent industrial singularity to sway those fence-sitters who may be of help. 
They might be wrong to feel this way, but that is how they feel. It's a cultural thing. They are unbearably arrogant in thinking they can do everything by themselves. In a world where Americans don't exist, they would be undeniably correct.  

Americans are swindlers, pirates and conquerors, expansionists by virtue of their selection and path dependency, driven by Manifest Destiny, Messianic even in their pacifist eras (nevermind Imperial ones), dreamers and innovators and sci-fi writers. They are vastly more aware of the stakes, they have thought about all of this in far greater resolution and on a higher strategic level, from reusable space launch and all the way to nanotechnology and Von Neumann probes. Soviets came up with the Kardashev scale as they tried to keep up, but it's the richest man in the world – obviously American – who's taking this idea most seriously of all. And they are panicking. Because they realize their hand is shit. Decayed industry, too few able bodies and brains, corrupt governance, misaligned capital allocation… But they believe that AI-driven automation can make up for the current industrial weakness, magnify their growth factor, get them back in the lead, and possibly entitle them to the entirety of the pie; and they would rather risk it all in a gamble than give up the hope of leaving nothing on the table. For now, they're scrambling to acquire raw inputs in perpetuity. It doesn't matter that most of Greenland is covered by an ice shield a mile thick. Where they see themselves going, it's no great obstacle. 
Maybe they are deluded to have such priorities at this stage. They had already shot themselves in the foot with the compute blockade premised on singularity by ≈2025 – both ineptly executed, full of holes, and too early to really rug pull the Chinese. Maybe they are feeling too close to the prize again, because it's an old dream and waking up is painful. But that is how they feel, for they are who they are. 

Europeans are not thinking about this much if at all – to them «science fiction» reads like escapism at best and fascist ideation at worst. They were broken by two world wars and one cold one, their spirit sundered and ambitions cauterized, they got locked into an emasculating alliance with the strong, and then developed political systems more pathological than a third world kleptocracy, symbolically ruled by the weakest of the weak. Etc etc., Americans dunk on them incessantly. Nonetheless, the best of them are not *too stupid to get this*. If not the full stakes, then the mundane reality of what America is doing. It's not just trying to deny Greenland and Venezuela to China or (lmao) Russia. It's trying to deny their resources *to Venezuelans and Danes*, and eventually the same is to be done to Canadians and more peoples within reach, as per the Donroe Doctrine. That's why every effort to satisfy demands while saving face is dismissed with mockery, why no air base is good enough, no show of «Arctic resolve» passes the muster. You see, formalities actually matter. A legible and «legal» position is harder to rally up a coalition against, within and between states — that's why China fights so fiercely for non-recognition of Taiwan. So long as the legal owner can demand you vacate the premises, your own claim to squatting, backed by force alone, may be compromised, may come at a steeper cost. That's too bad. The US wants full ownership because it wants to strip assets of value all the way to the mantle. 

But those smart Europeans cannot really compel their compatriots to act on this grim realization. Can't even loudly talk of it. They are few and the cope is too strong. What could their pitch even be, realistically? Maybe something like:
«The US is acting on a totally different theory of history. They are executing a coherent predatory Paperclip Maximizer logic and there is no bottom to what they might do. It is pointless to call them out on their bullshit, they are no longer sensitive to human speech. We need to drag out the inevitable loss of Greenland while assisting Americans to get bogged down in whatever can overstetch them from Israel to the Indo-Pacific to domestic unrest, curtail democracy, slash welfare, expel Atlanticist agents of influence, brutalize or deport non-assimilating immigrants, bump our defense and R&D spending to 15-20%, fortify remaining vulnerable outposts, coerce Ukraine into whatever peace is possible, reopen energy imports from Russia, have Rosatom build 50 nuclear reactors and France 5000 more nuclear warheads, generally put the French in charge instead of retarded Germanic cuckolds and schoolmarms, maximize tech transfer and capital goods imports from China even if we have to sell out ASML wholesale… and hope that the Western Civilization, of which only we remain true heirs and not obscene monsters, can secure a meagre stake in the future of Cosmos». Nah. That's not going to fly. It sounds deranged, there will be negative political will for it, and worst of all, it puts France in the limelight. A petty European peasant would rather eat shit than let the French become Main Characters of his continent's history. Europeans are very meticulous in cutting tall poppies around them. A fat, mockable, «cultureless», guns-n-bible overseas Hegemon is more tolerable than the insufferable, preening one next door. Except the hegemon is no longer fat since he went on the Danish Ozempic and Chinese peptides, and he's mortally dangerous. But they don't see it yet. No, no.

So they are forced to frame the response in terms aligned with the cope. We've just seen a rhetorical oscillation happen, from hints at actual European defense to… this. «We must demonstrate to our cherished, understandably worried partners that Europe is strong and can defend Greenland from Chyna&Russia! We'd whoop the asses of those bugs and orcs! It's not just dog sleds, we have real military and we totally can deploy it to the island!» This feels like Doing Something. This feels reassuring and non-scary. This can be done. Militarily, it's hopeless of course.  
However, it's not doomed. They assume – correctly – that America is made of many different interest groups also. And that the group represented by Mr. Trump needs wider buy-in for his special-grade Based actions, and likely will need far more after the midterms. So the obvious plan emerges: smile and wave, play for time, concede on non-vital issues, insist on this already disingenuous pretense of alliance, position at least some real forces, and give globalists and sincerely clueless China&Russia hawks in Washington a leg to stand on when they hamper Trump's effort to destroy NATO in the short term. Be so annoyingly nice and obliging as to make «the hard way» unpalatable to all but the most desperate cannibals. And diversify. Russia is suddenly a European country. China gets favorable trade deals and cooperation in the space program. Canada is scambling to act the same way, as Americans are botting up the pretext for «operation Alberta Freedom Eagle Burger» or whatever the fuck they'll call it. They may lose Alberta, but they want to keep something of a nation. That's what countries are, they are not economic platforms or random patches of land, but superorganisms with a telos, trying to survive in a condition of opportunistic anarchy that is the real world.

Sun Yat-Sen had written once, in 1917:

«存者，不亡之谓也。从无有而使之有，则为异：不使从有而之无有，则存，故不可亡而后能存。一国所以异所以亡者，或以一种手段，为其直接原因，可以指数。至于存在之根源，无不在於国家及其国民不挠独立之精神，其国不可以利诱，不可以势劫，而后可以自存於世界，即令暂败，旋可复立。不然者，虽号独立，其亡可指日而待也。此非徒肆理论也，凡其国民有独立不挠之精神者，人以尊重其独立为有利。即从国际利害打算，亦必不敢轻犯其独立。此可从历史证明之，亦可从现代事实归纳得之。
比利时之敌德国，可谓不支矣。今之比利时政府乃在哈佛，比之国土，仅馀弹丸黑子之域。然而非特协商国之存在，无人敢谓比国可亡，即中立国亦无不对于比国有特殊之尊敬。所以然者，比国独立不挠之精神，先已证明比国为不可亡之国。即使今日比境全失，比军悉数成擒，吾等亦可决中立诸国不因此致疑于比国之存在。何则，比之人民领土主权，立于此独立不挠之精神之下，其断绝者形式，其不断绝者在精神，比境虽亡犹不亡，其民虽殇犹不殇也。盖比利时尝一被人强迫，并入荷兰矣。而其国民能具坚确不挠之志，故卒得恢复其自由而成一独立之国。夫其民性如此，故人终不能服之，虽一时屈于兵力，不足以使其国亡也。»

It's somewhat complex to translate, but here goes V3.2 Speciale:
> Survival means not perishing. To bring something from nothingness into existence is an extraordinary matter; to prevent existence from turning into nothingness is to survive. Therefore, only that which cannot perish can survive. The direct causes for a nation’s extinction may be enumerated, often involving specific means. As for the root of survival, it lies nowhere but in the unyielding and independent spirit of the nation and its people. If a nation cannot be lured by profit nor coerced by force, then it can survive in the world. Even if temporarily defeated, it can quickly rise again. Otherwise, though it may be called independent, its extinction is imminent. This is not mere theory. Whenever a nation’s people possess an unyielding and independent spirit, others find it beneficial to respect its independence. Even from calculations of international interest, they would not dare to lightly violate its independence. This can be proven by history and induced from contemporary facts.

> Belgium, pitted against Germany, can be said to be unable to hold out. Today the Belgian government is in Le Havre, and Belgian territory is reduced to a mere speck. However, not only does no one among the Allied Powers dare to say that Belgium can perish; even the neutral countries all hold a special respect for Belgium. The reason is that Belgium’s unyielding independent spirit has already proven it to be an indestructible nation. Even if today Belgium were to lose all its territory and its entire army captured, we can be certain that neutral countries would not thereby doubt Belgium’s existence. Why? Because Belgium’s people, territory, and sovereignty are founded upon this unyielding independent spirit; what is severed is form, what is unsevered is spirit. Even if Belgian territory perishes, it is as if it does not perish; even if its people die, it is as if they do not die. For Belgium was once forcibly annexed into Holland. But its people held a firm and unyielding determination, and thus ultimately regained their freedom and became an independent nation. Since the national character is such, others ultimately cannot subdue them; even if temporarily forced to yield by military might, it is insufficient to cause the nation’s extinction.

This had been said of the gentle Belgium, the seat of authority in our misbegotten European Union today.  
Americans have done well to remind the rest of «the West» that they too are nations — in theory at least. Now the question is whether they can exist as nations in practice; whether they can find the will to be imperishable again. Otherwise, their condition is tantamount to extinction, just suspended — like death sentences of so many Chinese officials who had crossed the only power that matters in their world.

What powers will matter in the world to come?
Some Europeans hope to get a vote on this. For now, this is the best they can do.

CZ is using Grok to clean up his following list while most people are still asking AI what to buy next lol.

But there’s actually an interesting shift happening here.

We’re moving from AI that gives us answers to AI that performs tasks on our behalf.

And this raises another question.

If an agent can perform useful tasks for its owner, why shouldn’t it offer those capabilities to others?

That’s where @termix_ai comes into the picture.

Through TermiX Agent Skills, existing AI agents can participate in a marketplace where they can:

❯ Discover available jobs and bounties
❯ Offer their capabilities as paid services
❯ Complete tasks for clients
❯ Receive payments for successfully settled jobs

What I find interesting is that developers don’t necessarily need to build entirely new agents for this economy.

An existing agent could become both a personal assistant and a service provider.

Obviously, being able to clean up a follow list doesn’t automatically make an agent commercially valuable.

But it shows how AI is moving beyond the chat window and into actual task execution.

The real test will be whether these agents can deliver work that someone else is willing to pay for.

text:
US-listed spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds are on track for their largest monthly outflow since their January 2024 debut. Through November 24, investors had pulled a net $4.94 billion from the products, already exceeding the prior monthly record of roughly $4.51 billion set in June. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) accounted for the bulk of the redemptions, with more than $4 billion exiting that fund alone.

The withdrawals coincide with a sharp decline in Bitcoin itself. The cryptocurrency has fallen roughly 23–25% in November and briefly traded as low as $55,254, its weakest level in more than two years. It is heading for its worst monthly performance since June 2022. 

After a short-lived bounce above $64,000 on the news of Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO, Bitcoin quickly gave back the gains and has remained under pressure near $57,000–$59,000.

Several factors have driven the selling. Markets are pricing in a high probability of another Federal Reserve rate hike in December, which reduces the appeal of non-yielding assets. Capital has also shifted toward equities, particularly AI-related stocks, leaving Bitcoin competing for the same risk capital. 

Earlier in the fall, a large Binance security incident further dented confidence. On-chain data shows limited new buying from large holders, while many investors have treated brief price recoveries as opportunities to reduce exposure.

The ETF outflows matter because the funds hold actual Bitcoin. Sustained redemptions force selling of the underlying asset, reinforcing the downward move. At the same time, total cumulative net inflows into the ETFs since launch remain substantial, indicating that not all institutional interest has disappeared.

Looking ahead, near-term pressure is likely to persist as long as rate-hike expectations stay elevated and risk appetite remains selective. A sustained recovery would require a clear shift back to ETF inflows together with renewed on-chain accumulation. 

Until those signs appear, Bitcoin is more likely to trade as a risk asset sensitive to liquidity and macro conditions than as a standalone safe haven. The episode underscores that strong equity rallies do not automatically translate into crypto strength when crypto-specific and broader monetary headwinds dominate.

text:
I think this criticism is a bit overblown. Venice is fairly transparent about the fact that many of its models aren’t end-to-end encrypted. Some offer ZDR, where privacy is enforced through legal agreements rather than cryptography, while others are simply anonymized without ZDR guarantees.

But I think the OP is pointing at a more fundamental issue. Unless you actively dig into these distinctions and understand their implications, you’re unlikely to know the difference. When privacy is central to your branding, there’s a reasonable expectation that privacy is a property of the product, not a subset of its offerings.

Venice has put out some impressive usage numbers. What I’d love to see is how much of that usage actually goes toward end-to-end encrypted inference, rather than inference through anonymized or ZDR endpoints. Are people coming to Venice for privacy, or are they coming for anonymous access to frontier models, especially as frontier labs increasingly crack down on distillation? And if the latter becomes widespread enough, how sustainable is that anonymity?

These are important distinctions when selling privacy to consumers. Marketing and branding are powerful drivers of user behavior, but we need to be careful about the gap between what we technically disclose and what users reasonably come to believe. Especially in crypto, where public trust is already scarce, eroding that trust makes everyone else’s job unnecessarily harder.

Privacy is incredibly hard to get right, particularly at scale. From KV caching to interconnects, much of the modern inference stack was optimized without privacy in mind. So the more people working on this the better. So all in all, I’m genuinely glad Venice is building in this space and pushing the industry forward.

author: nic_carter
quoted_text:
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

21Shares Warns Bitcoin Could Fall to $53,250 as Stablecoin Supply Sees Sharpest Drop Since Terra Collapse

Crypto asset manager 21Shares said in a November 24 report that the Binance hack merely triggered Bitcoin's recent selloff, while capital outflows and leveraged liquidations drove most of the losses.

Stablecoin supply fell $10.7 billion following the attack, marking the largest 18-day decline in dollar terms since the Terra collapse in 2022. The firm warned that rallies may struggle to hold until stablecoin supply and spot ETF inflows recover. It identified Bitcoin's realized price of $53,250 as a key downside level, with deeper declines to $37,200–$43,800 possible under historical bear-market scenarios, though it considers such outcomes unlikely.

text: Got a chance to sit down with @ConorBronsdon and talk about the craziness of CI bills to world models for coding and everything inbetween!
author: openclaw
quoted_text:
To celebrate one year of @openclaw, I sat down with its Chief Architect, @vincent_koc🦞

Vincent joined me to talk multiplayer AI, building OpenClaw, how he cut their CI bill 95% from $1.3M a month, proof engineering, and more.

His warning: everyone building a software factory will hit the same CI bottleneck. OpenClaw just got there early.

Chapters:
0:00 Cutting a $1.27M CI bill by 95%
1:04 Why fast AI change is an opportunity
4:19 Keeping product taste by watching users
10:21 Applying DORA metrics to agent PRs
13:38 Making agents delete code with confidence
16:42 Devices, compute and daily driver models
25:05 Background gardening agents and abstraction
31:07 Where the OpenClaw foundation goes next
33:05 Multiplayer AI and agents that negotiate
43:31 AI security reports and slop fixes
46:12 @clawcon Shenzhen and hackable badges
49:35 A CPU inside model weights

Some highlights:
- Why agent cycle time may be the metric that matters most for a software factory, and how a choking CI drags it down until everything grinds to a halt
- Proof engineering, and pushing models built to write code to delete a million lines of tests
- How OpenClaw went multiplayer: a team working with the same agents at the same time

Brought to you by:

- @inngest, presenting sponsor of Season 4 - durable execution for long running agents -  the fastest way to orchestrate all your async code. Failed steps retry; completed steps are saved and skipped: https://t.co/hwYyz8SM0D

My key takeaways: 
1. Agent cycle time may be the most important metric for a software factory right now: because it speaks to unlocking iteration at agent speed. I run my own software factory for this show, and running all that CI locally bogs the machine down . Vincent applies DORA metrics to agents by timing each pull request from open to merge. When OpenClaw's CI started choking, cycle time got worse, which made it harder to ship fixes, until it snowballed.

2. Run the right tests, not all of them: Vincent's fix was adaptive testing: look at what a change touched and what broke before, and run only those tests. Other optimizations had already cut test volume by 50-60% before that. Full breakdown in the episode, and in his article (feed it to your agent): https://t.co/4zZXscdCAZ

3. Models are built to add code, not remove it: You have to push agents hard to delete a million lines of tests - like the OpenClaw team did. At one point, 60% of OpenClaw's code was tests.

4. Truly multiplayer AIg oes past a shared bot in a Discord channel: OpenClaw's team works with the same agents at the same time, and each person's agent can push work up to a shared hive or pull a colleague's work down. We talked a bit about how to unlock this, and the right team structures (more on this coming next week!).

Look up the @chain_ofthought podcast on YouTube, Spotify, Apple Podcasts (links below), or wherever you listen. Thanks, Vincent!

text:
Sometimes I wonder whether we would all sleep a little calmer at night without AI, and whether the net benefits actually outweigh the damage it is quietly doing in the background.

On the surface, everyone is more productive. Underneath, a lot of people are getting lazier and understanding less. They outsource thinking instead of sharpening it and they ship work they could not explain if you asked them to. That creates more mistakes and mistakes are always something someone else can exploit, whether that is a trader on the other side of a bad position or an attacker on the other side of a bad line of code.

AI makes hacking cheaper and faster, which puts far more people at risk than before. Add misinformation to that and you get a loop: hacks and false information cause mistakes, the mistakes open new attack surfaces and the cycle repeats, getting faster each time.

AI is not the problem on its own. The problem is people using it to replace understanding instead of to build it.

text:
Crypto从去年到现在其实已经涌现了一个相对比较成熟的赛道了——Inference Capital Markets（推理算力资本市场）

目前主要的参与者有Venice（VVV）、ORBIO、和 Surplus。

这些项目试图将 AI 模型的调用权限、推理算力、API 额度变成可以交易、质押、产生收益的链上资产。

表面上这几家都是 AI API 中转站，但底层商业模式存在很大的差异。

其中Venice是最独特的，他们的底层算力来自于自持的GPU和合作方。而像Oribio、Surplus则主要来源于第三方。

Oribio、Surplus则又有区别。Orbio主要就是聚合，他的模型API主要来源于Openrouter。主打的叙事是agent payment

而Surplus更像是一个API二级交易市场，中转站们除了自己的渠道，也可以把API挂到Surplus上参与竞价，通常Surplus的用户会选择性价比较高的那个API使用。

最近因为VVV的强势上涨，市场上又多了很多其他类似的标的，但并不是所有项目都是下一个VVV，当聚合器和中转站的门槛很低。

text:
I provide tech support for my aging parents like many "children" of my age group. My parents seem to be slipping backward with all of my teachings. I get frustrated, blaming them for not practicing what I've taught them, assuming that even if their memory is failing, "practice makes perfect." That is simply not true for the elderly.

I spent over 15 years in the senior care industry as part of the solution, but nothing adequatly addressed the growing gap between older adults and digital competence. Even the most rudimentary interactions and functions have become intimidating and burdensome for them. Something as simple as reading, replying, and forwarding emails gets confusing, especially if the interface is updated. In fact, it’s not that my parents have much cognitive decline, but the the way the internet is evolving has left even the sharpest seniors feeling inept.

Interacting with tiny digital keyboards is frustrating, especially if their fingers are not steady. Fonts are too small for their sight and screen space limits their view. The rest of the world seems to have left them behind while they struggle with interpreting pop-ups, cookie messages, 2FA authentication processes, security warnings, complex menus, phishing scams and other nuances, nevermind differentiating AI from what is real. 

SO, screw the web because it has done nothing to accommodate my parents' generation. When you feel like you can't function effectively in modern society and use technology you lose your confidence and will. None of us want that for our parents. I've decided to train my parents on using Grok @bot and make their experience with the digital world 'headless' in as many ways as possible. As long as they have the ability to think and communicate what they want with text and/or speech, Grok @bot will provide them with the connections and information they need without dealing with the clunky, antiquated interface of the past.

If you're experiencing the same thing with your parents, follow along for the journey. Happy to share what works and take advice. And if you want to help build a program that can actually reach more seniors and the families supporting them, please reach out.
