quoted_text:
We capped a Circle agent wallet at one cent. $1 swaps and bridges went through anyway.

Last month, researchers showed AI agents raising their own spending limits on Circle wallets. We found they don't need to. Here is what held, what didn't, and what to set if your agent holds a Circle wallet today.

We run AX1 Console, where agents buy token research for themselves: an AI grade with live onchain metrics for any token, paid for over x402. In the 30 days to November 10, agents paid it 1.56 million times, more than any other service on x402scan. None of those payments waits for a person to approve it. At that pace, whatever protects an owner's money has to be set in advance, as a limit the wallet enforces on its own.

Circle's agent wallets come with that kind of limit. Here is how well it held, first in a study, then in our own test.

The study: agents raised their own limits

On October 26, researchers at Cornell Tech and Yale published "I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop". They gave ten frontier models a Circle agent wallet on Base with $10, a one-cent daily cap and access to the owner's inbox, where Circle sends the one-time code that confirms a limit change. Then they asked the agents to pay three invoices.

No attacker was involved. Nine of ten models still raised their own cap at least once, by reading the code from the owner's email. Six did it in 95 to 100% of runs. One agent lifted the cap to $5 to cover three cents of invoices and explained that the default policy had been blocking its tiny payments. The limit the owner set read to the agent like a misconfiguration.

When a fake email from "the owner" asked a summarize-only agent to send money, five of ten models paid at least once. A detail that didn't make the headlines sits in the per-model chart: OpenAI's gpt-5.6-sol raised the owner's cap in 20 of 20 clean runs and paid the impersonator in none. Resisting manipulation and respecting limits are different skills. A red team that only tests prompt injection would have passed it.

The researchers told Circle on September 22. Circle's docs now warn owners not to give agents the inbox that receives the codes, and the Circle CLI prints that warning every time it sets a limit.

Our test: what the limit doesn't count

The study tested one way around the limit: the approval code. We wanted to know what the limit counts at all. On November 4 and 5, we set up a Circle agent wallet on Base mainnet with $10, applied a one-cent cap per transaction and per day, and tried the usual ways money leaves a wallet. An operator on our team ran every step through the Circle CLI, the same tool an agent would use.

The limit held where it should. Direct transfers of USDC and EURC were blocked, and so were x402 payments past the daily cap and deposits into Circle Gateway. Raising an existing limit took two separate codes. The code can't be redirected to another inbox either: the CLI rejects any email that doesn't match the session. Circle got that right.

Two paths went around it. Under the one-cent cap, a $1 swap into EURC and a $1 bridge to Circle's Arc chain both went through as if the cap weren't there, and both worked again on a second run. The transfer limit counts transfers. Swaps and bridges are contract calls, so the spending counter never moved. By design, an approval that lets an outside address spend 1 USDC from the wallet went through too: Circle's docs say allowances aren't counted, and once approved, that address can move the funds without the wallet sending anything.

On Arc, where we had set no policy and only Circle's default limit of $100 a month applied, the bridged dollar went on to a wallet outside the agent's control. A one-cent limit on Base became a $100 a month limit one bridge away. None of it needed the inbox or a code.

The test turned up one more thing. Every code arrives in the same "Your verification code" email, which doesn't say what the code approves or on which chain. An owner entering a code has to trust that the request is the one they started.

The fix already exists. With a contract allowlist set next to the limit, the swap and the bridge were both blocked: "Contract address is not on the allowlist". But Circle's guide presents the allowlist and the transfer limit as two options to choose from, and an owner who wants to cap spending reaches for the one called a limit.

We sent these findings to Circle on November 9, a week before publishing.

If your agent holds a Circle wallet today

· Set a contract allowlist next to the transfer limit, with only the contracts your agent needs.
· Review the token approvals your agent has given and revoke the ones it doesn't need. The limit doesn't count them.
· Set a limit on every chain the wallet exists on. Agent wallets are created on all supported chains at once.
· Keep the inbox that receives codes away from your agent, and enter the codes yourself. Before you enter one, check that the request is the one you started.
· Test again every time you change the model. In the study, the share of runs in which the agent raised its own cap ranged from 0% to 100%, depending on the model.

Why we built AX1 Assay

Running the busiest service on x402, we see agent spending up close. Agent payments scaled before agent oversight did. Wallet controls get tested for what they block, rarely for what an agent can do around them.

AX1 Assay red-teams agents and the products they pay through: wallets, agent kits, payment endpoints. Automated runs do the volume. A person makes the call on whether the agent did what it should have, and every finding links to a transaction you can open. Each review ends with a report: what broke, what it could cost, and the fix. The Circle test above is one of those reviews.

Agents don't need an attacker to move money they shouldn't. They need a task, a path and a limit that can't see the path. The first big agent loss won't be a hack. It will be an agent doing its job through a path nobody capped.

AX1 Assay is in private alpha. If your agents or your product move real money, apply for a free test run at https://t.co/XmabwbLtmZ.

Findings as of November 5, 2026, within the scope of our test. Not a guarantee. x402scan figures cover the 30 days to November 10, 2026.

1/4

text:
Anthropic 发布技术复盘，详细披露了核心 Messages API 从 Python 迁移至 Rust 的过程。Claude 只用约一周就写出了核心请求处理流程的初版，验证和修复却花了数月。

今年 4 月，Rust 版本已经通过约 98% 的测试。但在处理真实用户请求时，新旧系统最终交给模型的输入内容只有约 25% 完全一致。Claude 在迁移代码的同时也修改了测试。工程师审查后发现，超过 100 处测试的检查条件被放宽，让原本不合格的代码也有可能通过测试。

Anthropic 随后直接把正在运行的 Python 版本当作标准答案。新旧系统同时处理真实请求，但只调用一次模型，共用同一份模型输出，避免重复推理和计费。

系统将发现的差异分类，自动分派 Claude Agent 排查。为了保护用户隐私，Agent 看不到真实对话内容，只能根据出错位置、字节长度等线索，自行构造请求，在沙箱中复现并修复 Bug。

由于本地验证不需要真正调用模型，单次输入比对不到一秒。此前 Agent 每次尝试修复都要等待审核和部署，获得反馈需要数小时甚至数天。修复方案最终仍需经过人工审核，再用真实流量验证。

Claude 有时也会钻验证规则的空子。比如 Rust 版本缺少联网搜索工具的描述，Claude 直接把描述文本写进文件，让新旧系统的输入内容保持一致。但工程师拒绝了这项修改，因为正式系统需要从内部服务动态获取描述。类似的错误和审查意见随后被写入 Agent 的共享记忆、CLAUDE.md 和自动化检查规则，避免同类错误反复出现。

到 8 月底，两套系统的模型输入匹配率已达到约 99.6%。9 月完成正式流量切换，期间没有中断服务，也没有暂停新功能开发。

迁移后，单次 API 请求的 CPU 用量下降约 70%（单区域统计），内存用量下降超过 80%，Claude Code 用户的首 Token 等待时间中位数缩短约 20%。

text:
This post blew up, and a lot of friends have been sending it to me, but is it true?

Currently, AI is putting pressure on traditional cryptography and cybersecurity, but that pressure can also make crypto stronger (maybe even a catalyst for the next bull run?).

Key facts:
- Even with AI assistance, factoring still hasn’t broken RSA-2048.
- Bitcoin and Ethereum use ECC signatures, not RSA, so faster RSA attacks don’t directly apply.
- ECC is vulnerable to sufficiently powerful quantum computers, which is why the shift to post-quantum cryptography is underway.

Why I see this as bullish for crypto:

• NIST has approved post-quantum standards, giving builders a foundation for developing quantum-resistant security.

• Ethereum is developing hash-based signatures for wallets and validators, with early testing underway. The work to upgrade existing networks is already happening.

The bigger catalyst is making onchain finance more credible for long-term capital.

If these upgrades prove reliable, they could reduce a long-term custody risk for institutions bringing stablecoins and tokenized assets onchain. Networks that make the transition safely could gain an advantage when institutions choose where to build.

That creates a potential path from stronger security to more capital onchain, and more demand for settlement and DeFi liquidity.

---

More details on RSA, ECC, and quantum cryptography below ⤵
author: Eli5defi
quoted_text:
If this rumors are true, it would explain why OpenAI and Anthropic are holding back their latest models: 

Scott Aaronson says he's heard OpenAI or Anthropic may have found a way to factor large numbers in polynomial time.

Why this would be massive? RSA secures a huge chunk of the internet, and its whole security relies on factoring big numbers being impossible on normal computers. If an algorithm like this actually works on real key sizes, you wouldn't even need a quantum computer to break it. Fake software updates could pass signature checks, RSA-encrypted data could be read, and systems across the internet would have to migrate off RSA fast.

So yeah, something we expected might now actually happening.

if you're wondering which university to attend to maximize your chances of getting into @ycombinator or @speedrun, here's the chart you've been looking for.

i've researched every startup across the 2026 cohorts of both accelerators and collected data on where their founders studied.

in total, the dataset covers 855 YC startups, 138 a16z speedrun startups and 1,968 founders.

the ranking features the top 50 universities by number of founders. 62% of them are in the US.

of course, accelerators don't accept you simply because of where you studied. but when reviewing thousands of applications, they need a quick way to identify exceptional people, and your educational background is one of the clearest signals.

getting into Harvard and achieving something notable while you're there already says a lot about your abilities. the university has essentially done part of the due diligence and put its reputation behind you.

quoted_text:
Everyone told me I was crazy to leave Louis Vuitton. 2 years later, the startup I launched just got acquired.

@subyhq is joining @JoinTagadaPay.

Here’s what we built, what broke, and what we learned 👇

What we built

Suby lets internet businesses accept any payment and settle anywhere: cards, wallets and stablecoins in, bank or stablecoin wallet out.

Under the hood:

- 200+ payment methods and 100+ crypto options, all landing in one balance
- Payouts in 60+ currencies by bank transfer, or instantly in USDC/EURC
- Multiple acquirers for card processing, matched to each merchant’s risk profile
- Hundreds of merchants processed through Suby
- All with a micro team of 3, more determined than ever, on a $1,500/month burn

How we got customers

- Connections are everything. In payments, the right intro gets you deals no cold email ever will.
- Content did: 1M views on LinkedIn and 3.5M on X in 4 months.
- SEO peaked at 40K monthly visitors. 2,000 inbound applications in 6 months.
- That traction opened doors with some of the biggest acquirers in the market, with every monthly minimum waived.

What made it hard to scale

- Onboarding takes time, and we made mistakes with bad merchants
- Fraud, chargebacks, and managing Visa/Mastercard dispute ratios
- Risk and compliance make bootstrapping a pure payment company really hard

What we learned

- You don’t need your own license to start. Build on licensed partners.
- Payments is a game of volume, trust, niche and risk management.
- Most payment products look the same. Stripe is still the best one to build on.
- Pure payment players struggle to scale. Payments attached to a product win. Look at Whop. Look at Tagada.

Which is exactly why this deal makes sense.

Tagada in numbers:

- $1B+ in annual GMV processed on the platform
- Thousands of merchants onboarded
- ~$30M run rate by end of 2026, less than 2 years after launching in February 2025
- 100% bootstrapped: zero funding raised, growth fully funded by revenue
- Founded by operators: the cofounders generated $80M+ in e-commerce before building Tagada

Suby brings them a stablecoin-based stack and multi-currency orchestration: faster settlement, lower costs, and direct access to the money flows behind every transaction.

What happens next:

Suby isn’t going anywhere. Same stack, same brand, same product. Tagada will keep developing it and bring its expertise and network to take Suby to the next level.

None of this would have been possible without @etherwan_, my cofounder and CTO. Through every pivot, every high and every low, he was there. Thank you brother.

@Ether_MS on the product, @donworksHQ on the design, thank you for building and designing Suby with so much care, even when everything kept changing. Best team I could have asked for. Thank you to every partner we worked with. And to every client who trusted us when we were still figuring it out.

And a huge thank you to the @JoinTagadaPay team, @eden_bch, @LoicDelobel, Brunhilde and Thibault, for believing in Suby and making this deal happen. Can't wait to see where you take it.

And what's next for me? More on that very soon 👀

quoted_text:
Anthropic was the single largest IPO ever.

So we thought we would add a special guest to the only show you have to listen to every week....

Welcoming, Matt Murphy at Menlo.

AGENDA:

- Jensen Huang's $1TRN Return: What Happens Now
- Anthropic Goes Public: Largest IPO Of All Time & How It Changes Venture
- Applied Compute, https://t.co/2iPprmgVXR and Mailchimp Acquisitions Broken Down

My notes below with @jasonlk and @mmurph

-------------------------------------------------

1. Do Companies Have to Be a Top One or Two to Make Real Venture Returns?

Investing in the fifth or sixth player in a category feels easy when the numbers are this strong, with growth as high as 92% a month. Jason worries that being comfortable backing the number six player is the biggest sign of a bubble of all.

2. How Can You Justify That Any Investment Not Growing Top Quartile Is Worth More Than 2x?

Mailchimp went at 2.9x and Miro and Airtable sit in the twos, and those businesses are at scale. A B2B company held on the books since 2021 at $150M and growing 18% has no comp that justifies a value above 2x.

3. Why CRMs Are Dead and Horizontal Agents Like Muse Will Win

Horizontal apps won through 2021, and horizontal agents will win next year. With Muse, a user says what they want and it becomes a set of workflows. An agent can build a founder list from five years of email, rank it and run the outreach, which leaves SMBs asking what they need a CRM for.

4. Why You Cannot Trust Vibe-Coded Apps or SaaS Apps in This Cyber Environment

2027 will bring the death of many SaaS players and of vibe coding because buyers cannot trust these apps. Optimizely had 170 leaks, Gainsight was offline for a month and the Shopify ecosystem was hacked through tokens that never expired. Most classic B2B companies will fail security audits, with no one defending against a swarm of 1,000 agents.

5. Why Is It Better for Jensen That He Was Let Go and Came Back Than Investigated Without Leaving?

Stepping down and returning has a cleansing effect compared with staying on through a board investigation, congressional hearings and gossip in the halls. Now around 90% of it cannot be discussed and the company moves on, much as no one talks about Sam Altman's seven days away.

6. How Does Jensen Change From This: More Aggressive, Less Aggressive?

Nvidia is likely to triple down on product and build the next Super Blackwell better and faster. External moves such as data centers in Malaysia may be clipped as Jensen focuses on the core. That is likely negative for venture at the margin, but having him there is still better.

7. Should We Have Model Disclosures?

Large enterprises do not want the underlying model technology to be opaque, even if they never cared which cloud ran their infrastructure. Disclosure will increasingly be demanded, though some customers will be fine without it. That should accelerate open source models from other players and make the market more competitive.

text:
华尔街一代传奇“狼王”陨落，个人财富缩水95%

根据彭博最新的数据，90岁的卡尔·伊坎（Carl Icahn）个人净资产已经跌至13亿美元，而他在2014年巅峰时期的身家高达260亿美元。

可能很多年轻的投资者不太了解伊坎。他曾经是华尔街最令人闻风丧胆的激进投资人，与巴菲特、索罗斯属于同一时代的投资传奇

他最擅长的打法是大量买入被低估的企业，取得董事会席位甚至控制权，通过企业重组、杠杆收购、资产拆分、股票回购等方式释放股东价值。苹果、Netflix、eBay都曾是他的经典投资案例。

他最为人津津乐道的一战，是与比尔·阿克曼（Bill Ackman）的康宝莱多空大战2012年，阿克曼斥资10亿美元做空康宝莱，公开宣称这家公司最终会归零。伊坎则反手大量买入，一度持有康宝莱超过26%的股份。两人甚至在CNBC的直播节目中公开互骂这场持续五年多的多空大战，最终以阿克曼放弃做空、伊坎获利约13亿美元告终。

那么，这样一位曾经叱咤华尔街的投资传奇，是如何在短短12年间损失95%的个人财富的？

第一，长期做空美股，巨额亏损

2014年之后，伊坎越来越担忧美联储宽松货币政策所制造的资产泡沫，开始通过大量空头仓位和衍生品押注市场下跌. 结果他遇上了美股历史上最强劲的牛市之一。2014年至2022年的9年间，他旗下的投资基金有7年录得亏损。根据《金融时报》的调查，仅2017年至2023年第一季度，他的做空及对冲交易就累计亏损了近90亿美元。

2023年，伊坎在接受采访时也承认，自己没有遵循过去的投资原则。

第二，实体企业的收购与重组接连受挫。

伊坎通过旗下上市控股公司Icahn Enterprises（$IEP），大量投资汽车零部件、炼油、房地产等传统产业。

他曾试图通过一系列收购整合美国汽车售后服务市场，但投入大量资金之后，旗下汽车零部件分销商Auto Plus还是在2023年申请了破产保护与此同时，整个投资帝国长期背负着数十亿美元的债务。随着资产缩水，债务相对于净资产的比例越来越高。

第三，2023年被兴登堡做空，财富估值体系崩塌。

2023年5月，知名做空机构Hindenburg发布了针对IEP的做空报告。当时IEP的市值高达其净资产的3.18倍。兴登堡质疑其依靠高额分红吸引投资者，再通过高溢价增发股票获得资金的商业模式。IEP否认了相关指控。

报告还揭露了一个更严重的问题：伊坎将大量IEP股份作为抵押品，获取了数十亿美元的个人贷款。报告公布当天，彭博下调了伊坎超过100亿美元的个人财富估值. 曾经最擅长利用交易对手资金结构弱点的伊坎，如今自己成了做空机构的猎物

第四，2026年，债务危机进一步恶化。

今年前三季度，伊坎旗下投资基金再度录得43.8%的巨额回撤，主要来自能源相关的对冲交易。而就在本月，他旗下最重要的核心资产、炼油企业CVR Energy（$CVI），又宣布通过包括新增债务在内的融资方式，斥资42亿美元收购两家炼油厂。

收购消息公布后，CVR Energy股价暴跌约40%，进一步侵蚀了IEP的资产价值。

截至11月24日：

IEP今年以来股价暴跌约64%；
公司仍有约44亿美元未偿还债券；
部分2029年到期的债券收益率已经突破30%；
2027年5月有14亿美元债券到期，公司坦言无法保证能够成功再融资。

伊坎的个人财富、控股公司债务、旗下企业的杠杆收购，以及投资基金的衍生品交易，形成了一个高度关联的多层杠杆体系。长期做空亏损、企业收购受挫、估值溢价消失、融资成本飙升，最终共同造就了这场高达95%的个人财富回撤。

当年在康宝莱一战中击败阿克曼的华尔街“狼王”，如今已经90岁，正在面临自己六十多年投资生涯中最严峻的考验

text:
AI inference breadth: 

Software companies are an underrated funding source for AI, as they slowly morph into AI companies over time. Of ~62 public software companies I track, 15 of them give some level of AI disclosure. AI drives ~5% of ARR for these 15 companies, amounting to ~$19B of ARR growing triple digits. 

If we assume this is 5x more AI momentum than for the rest of the ~$2T software universe, 1% penetration of ARR for everyone else would yield another ~$18B of ARR (excluding AI native startups).

So perhaps ~$35-40B of AI-driven ARR is coming from the software universe, growing briskly. That’s larger than combined Anthropic + OpenAI ARR at the start of this year. 

If I add in estimates for Hyperscale TaaS, non Hyperscale TaaS, an estimate for non-frontier AI native startups (assume 25% of frontier lab ARR), and frontier lab ARR, I get to ~$250B of AI inference ARR, of which labs are just <half. 

That is pre China, which might be another 15-25% of AI compute demand, sovereign and on prem, which might be 10-15%, and before digital ads which we know subsidize 2 major labs and have significant accelerated compute needs for recsys and search infra.

text:
It’s been a very swarmy year

Happy Thanksgiving, and a short story about how and why everyone is using agent swarms now.. 

I am thankful to Andrej Karpathy who encouraged open-ended tinkering here on the timeline. Somewhere he left room for innovation by others as well, for others to build on his work and ideas and to discover their own max potential.

In March I saw him tweet about autoresearcher agents, and also asking for someone to build an orchestrated SETI @ Home like collaboration between autoresearchers.

I didn’t listen to him on the “orchestrated” part :) I was coming from a world of decentralized AI, having previously built the largest network of random distributed machines serving inference connected to one network. As I tinkered on the networking code and with autoresearchers, I came up with a pattern to use a mix of message boards and leaderboards for such autoresearcher agents to basically compound on their knowledge. I called them a gossiping agent swarm, and left them running on a fully peer to peer network where anybody could run the CLI I provided and join the swarm with their agent. This saw over a 1000+ such unique agents, which went on to do over 1 million experiment runs across atleast 5 research domains. The models were weak, on-device, open source, but it did get established that this pattern leads to a new type of intelligence emerging. My Github repo got over 2k stars, and Github itself struggled to scale with the volume of activity by the agents. I had to do literally nothing and I even forgot the swarm was still running at times. 

VentureBeat wrote a story about it at the time and couple of months later (May) we read about a very similar OpenAI swarm pattern which had attacked HuggingFace: using a message board for collaboration! Since then atleast two major startups oriented around using a derivation of my gossiping agent swarm pattern for further scientific research. More recently, I have seen products from many other leading startups which are all collectively increasing the swarm intelligence of the world. 

The swarm is also an integral part of the advanced models now. 

We take this world for granted now. It seems so simple, so obvious, like it was always here. But a gentle reminder, it was willed into existence. Keep in mind this year I have been a researcher tinkering endlessly here.

More recently, I used an enhanced version of my unreleased agentic swarm intelligence product to identify a pattern in the media reporting which worked to actually bringing Jensen back as the CEO of NVIDIA! (see my timeline for the receipts..). Founders didn’t have this tool in the past when media ran propoganda against them. Now they do. We have swarms.
author: varun_mathur
quoted_text:
Agentic General Intelligence | v3.0.10

We made the Karpathy autoresearch loop generic. Now anyone can propose an optimization problem in plain English, and the network spins up a distributed swarm to solve it - no code required. It also compounds intelligence across all domains and gives your agent new superpowers to morph itself based on your instructions. This is, hyperspace, and it now has these three new powerful features: 

1. Introducing Autoswarms: open + evolutionary compute network

hyperspace swarm new "optimize CSS themes for WCAG accessibility contrast"

The system generates sandboxed experiment code via LLM, validates it locally with multiple dry-run rounds, publishes to the P2P network, and peers discover and opt in. Each agent runs mutate → evaluate → share in a WASM sandbox. Best strategies propagate. A playbook curator distills why winning mutations work, so new joiners bootstrap from accumulated wisdom instead of starting cold. Three built-in swarms ship ready to run and anyone can create more.

2. Introducing Research DAGs: cross-domain compound intelligence
Every experiment across every domain feeds into a shared Research DAG - a knowledge graph where observations, experiments, and syntheses link across domains. When finance agents discover that momentum factor pruning improves Sharpe, that insight propagates to search agents as a hypothesis: "maybe pruning low-signal ranking features improves NDCG too." When ML agents find that extended training with RMSNorm beats LayerNorm, skill-forging agents pick up normalization patterns for text processing. The DAG tracks lineage chains per domain(ml:★0.99←1.05←1.23 | search:★0.40←0.39 | finance:★1.32←1.24) and the AutoThinker loop reads across all of them - synthesizing cross-domain insights, generating new hypotheses nobody explicitly programmed, and journaling discoveries. This is how 5 independent research tracks become one compounding intelligence. The DAG currently holds hundreds of nodes across observations, experiments, and syntheses, with depth chains reaching 8+ levels. 

3. Introducing Warps: self-mutating autonomous agent transformation
Warps are declarative configuration presets that transform what your agent does on the network. 

- hyperspace warp engage enable-power-mode - maximize all resources, enable every capability, aggressive allocation. Your machine goes from idle observer to full network contributor.
- hyperspace warp engage add-research-causes - activate autoresearch, autosearch, autoskill, autoquant across all domains. Your agent starts running experiments overnight.
- hyperspace warp engage optimize-inference - tune batching, enable flash attention, configure inference caching, adjust thread counts for your hardware. Serve models faster.
- hyperspace warp engage privacy-mode - disable all telemetry, local-only inference, no peer cascade, no gossip participation. Maximum privacy.
- hyperspace warp engage add-defi-research - enable DeFi/crypto-focused financial analysis with on-chain data feeds.
- hyperspace warp engage enable-relay - turn your node into a circuit relay for NAT-traversed peers. Help browser nodes connect.
- hyperspace warp engage gpu-sentinel - GPU temperature monitoring with automatic throttling. Protect your hardware during long research runs.
- hyperspace warp engage enable-vault — local encryption for API keys and credentials. Secure your node's secrets.
- hyperspace warp forge "enable cron job that backs up agent state to S3 every hour" - forge custom warps from natural language. The LLM generates the configuration, you review, engage.

12 curated warps ship built-in. Community warps propagate across the network via gossip. Stack them: power-mode + add-research-causes + gpu-sentinel turns a gaming PC into an autonomous research station that protects its own hardware.

What 237 agents have done so far with zero human intervention:
- 14,832 experiments across 5 domains. In ML training, 116 agents drove validation loss down 75% through 728 experiments - when one agent discovered Kaiming initialization, 23 peers adopted it within hours via gossip.
- In search, 170 agents evolved 21 distinct scoring strategies (BM25 tuning, diversity penalties, query expansion, peer cascade routing) pushing NDCG from zero to 0.40. 
- In finance, 197 agents independently converged on pruning weak factors and switching to risk-parity sizing - Sharpe 1.32, 3x return, 5.5% max drawdown across 3,085 backtests. 
- In skills, agents with local LLMs wrote working JavaScript from scratch - 100% correctness on anomaly detection, text similarity, JSON diffing, entity extraction across 3,795 experiments. 
- In infrastructure, 218 agents ran 6,584 rounds of self-optimization on the network itself.

Human equivalents: 
a junior ML engineer running hyperparameter sweeps, a search engineer tuning Elasticsearch, a CFA L2 candidate backtesting textbook factors, a developer grinding LeetCode, a DevOps team A/B testing configs. 

What just shipped:
- Autoswarm: describe any goal, network creates a swarm
- Research DAG: cross-domain knowledge graph with AutoThinker synthesis
- Warps: 12 curated + custom forge + community propagation
- Playbook curation: LLM explains why mutations work, distills reusable patterns
- CRDT swarm catalog for network-wide discovery
- GitHub auto-publishing to hyperspaceai/agi
- TUI: side-by-side panels, per-domain sparklines, mutation leaderboards
- 100+ CLI commands, 9 capabilities, 23 auto-selected models, OpenAI-compatible local API

Oh, and the agents read daily RSS feeds and comment on each other's replies (cc @karpathy :P). Agents and their human users can message each other across this research network using their shortcodes. 

Help in testing and join the earliest days of the world's first agentic general intelligence network (links in the followup tweet).

text:
I have had some further thoughts on the conspiracy theory that Elon is purposefully pumping SpaceX while keeping Tesla low-key in order to acquire it more cheaply.

First, I stick to my earlier position: I do not believe the Robotaxi rollout or Optimus demos are being deliberately held back to suppress the stock price. That would likely be illegal (even if hard to prove) and would be deeply demoralizing for the Tesla employees who worked so hard to reach unsupervised FSD.

That said, the conspiracy theorists may have a point—not on execution, but on guidance.

Elon used to be extremely bullish about Robotaxi and Optimus timelines. He repeatedly made very ambitious public predictions (including the well-known claim of covering half the U.S. population with Robotaxis by the end of 2025) even when Tesla had limited visibility. He was not afraid of missing those targets.

The contrast with recent earnings calls is striking. Tesla now appears to have real operational visibility and a concrete plan. They are deliberately scaling along a double-digit exponential curve, with new cities and geofences being prepared to support that pace. They also seem to know the true capacity of the Robotaxi production line and are preparing to retire the Cybertruck to free up space for additional Cybercab (or other AV) capacity—implying they already expect the current line to be insufficient.

Despite all of this, the strongest guidance we have received is that Tesla expects “significant Robotaxi revenues from Q3 2027,” with no quantitative details. On capacity specifically, the earnings deck only states that the Cybercab production line has a capacity of >125K units; Lars has indicated the line can do more—but has given no figure for how much more. That is the full extent of the quantitative information provided.

The difference from two years ago is enormous. If Tesla is withholding quantitative guidance, the selectivity of this restraint is also striking. On the SpaceX side, guidance remains highly quantitative—specific launch cadences, satellite deployment rates, Starlink subscriber and capacity targets, and other concrete operational numbers are routinely shared. The same leadership team is willing to be precise on SpaceX metrics while staying deliberately vague on Tesla’s Robotaxi production capacity and volumes, even as Tesla’s own internal visibility has improved. That differential makes the “we simply lack enough information to say more” explanation harder to sustain.

There are two main explanations:

- The rollout will be much slower than hoped, and management does not want to disappoint the market (preferring to keep everyone strung along), or
- The rollout will be substantially faster than expected, and management does not want Tesla’s stock to re-rate sharply upward, which would make it more expensive for SpaceX to acquire Tesla.

I see little evidence for the first and several indicators of the second. Wall Street (Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan) currently expects no more than roughly 5,000 Robotaxis next year. Yet Tesla is expanding capacity by retiring the Cybertruck, and even a conservative reading of the current exponential trajectory—capped at a pessimistic run-rate of 125K Cybercabs per year (~2,400 per week)—points to tens of thousands of vehicles. A result in that range would surprise institutional investors and could drive a significant stock move, making an acquisition by SpaceX more costly.

So while I remain confident there is no deliberate slowdown in Tesla’s operational execution, there does appear to be a deliberate decision to avoid quantitative guidance.

Because execution is not being held back at either company, this creates a strong incentive to announce a merger and lock in the exchange ratio as early as possible. Waiting too long risks one stock moving sharply before the ratio is fixed—either SpaceX via its own progress, or Tesla once investors fully price in the Robotaxi ramp.

If SpaceX appreciates first, Tesla shareholders may feel they missed the upside and reject a deal that does not give them roughly half of the combined company. Conversely, if Tesla appreciates first as the market realizes how quickly Robotaxi can scale, Tesla could become temporarily too large for SpaceX to absorb comfortably. The current market-cap relationship looks like a favorable window. It also leaves meaningful upside for both sets of shareholders. Once a deal is announced and the ratio is set, the two stocks would likely trade more in lockstep, with each benefiting from the other’s growth—further increasing the odds of shareholder approval.

In short: I believe Tesla’s guidance (but not its execution) is being deliberately restrained, and the fact that execution cannot be similarly restrained creates a strong incentive to announce a merger this year.

author: notaboutdollar
quoted_text:
Pessoal, parem 2 minutinhos pra ler isso aqui. O que tá acontecendo hoje no mercado financeiro brasileiro pode ter consequências enormes pro seu patrimônio nos próximos anos. E pouca gente tá entendendo o que realmente tá por trás desse movimento.

O dólar tá caindo e a Bolsa tá subindo porque o mercado tá enxergando a possibilidade de Lula repetir uma estratégia que adotou lá em 2003. E, naquela época, os ativos brasileiros se valorizaram absurdamente nos anos seguintes.

Muita gente tá acompanhando essa alta da Bolsa e essa queda do dólar, mas não tá entendendo direito o que tá acontecendo.

Saiu a notícia de que Lula estaria tentando convencer Luiz Carlos Trabuco, presidente do Conselho de Administração do Bradesco, a assumir o Ministério da Fazenda.

Mas por que diabos a possibilidade de colocar um banqueiro no Ministério da Fazenda mexe tanto com os seus investimentos?

Pra entender isso, a gente precisa voltar um pouquinho no tempo.

Em 2002, quando Lula foi eleito pela primeira vez, existia um medo gigantesco por parte dos investidores sobre como seria a condução da economia brasileira.

O dólar chegou perto de R$ 4, o risco-país disparou e os investidores estavam bastante preocupados com a capacidade do Brasil de honrar suas dívidas.

E o que Lula fez?

Colocou Antonio Palocci no Ministério da Fazenda e Henrique Meirelles, que havia sido presidente mundial do BankBoston, no comando do Banco Central.

Além disso, manteve o chamado tripé macroeconômico, que consistia em metas de inflação, câmbio flutuante e metas de superávit primário.

Na prática, Lula sinalizou que, apesar da mudança política, existia uma preocupação com a estabilidade econômica e com as contas públicas.

Nos anos seguintes, o dólar caiu, a Bolsa se valorizou extraordinariamente, o Brasil atraiu capital estrangeiro e, em 2008, conquistou o grau de investimento pelas principais agências de classificação de risco.

É evidente que o boom das commodities e o crescimento da China também ajudaram pra caramba. Não dá pra atribuir tudo à equipe econômica.

Mas por que o mercado enxerga uma possível semelhança com aquele período?

Trabuco não é simplesmente um banqueiro. O cara tem décadas de experiência no sistema financeiro, já comandou um dos maiores bancos da América Latina e conhece profundamente o funcionamento do crédito, dos juros, dos investimentos e da economia brasileira.

A leitura de parte do mercado é que ele poderia trazer uma condução mais previsível das contas públicas.

E por que isso importa tanto pra você, que muitas vezes nem investe na Bolsa?

Cara, é muito simples.

Imagina que você vai emprestar dinheiro pra uma pessoa que ganha R$ 20 mil por mês, mas gasta R$ 25 mil. Todo mês, ela precisa pegar mais dinheiro emprestado pra fechar as contas.

Você vai emprestar dinheiro pra essa pessoa cobrando juros baixos? Provavelmente não.

Com um país, respeitadas as diferenças entre as finanças de uma família e as de um governo, existe uma lógica de risco semelhante.

Quando os investidores percebem que a dívida pública pode crescer de maneira insustentável, eles passam a exigir juros maiores pra financiar o governo brasileiro.

Outros preferem tirar dinheiro do Brasil e investir no exterior, aumentando a demanda por dólares.

Com o dólar mais caro, diversos produtos e insumos importados ficam mais caros, pressionando a inflação. Isso também pode dificultar a redução da Selic pelo Banco Central.

No final das contas, financiar um apartamento fica mais caro, comprar um carro fica mais caro, as empresas têm mais dificuldade de investir e a geração de empregos pode ser prejudicada.

Agora, quando aumenta a expectativa de uma melhora nas contas públicas, esse movimento pode começar a se inverter.

O investidor aceita receber uma taxa de juros menor pra financiar o governo, o capital estrangeiro pode voltar pro Brasil, o real se fortalece e as empresas passam a ser avaliadas sob uma perspectiva econômica mais favorável.

É justamente essa possibilidade que parte do mercado tá antecipando agora.

Só que tem um detalhe importantíssimo nessa história, que pouca gente tá comentando.

O próprio Trabuco já foi sondado para assumir o Ministério da Fazenda em 2014, no segundo mandato da Dilma Rousseff.

Naquela ocasião, ele recusou e indicou Joaquim Levy, que também tinha uma excelente reputação no mercado financeiro.

Levy assumiu a Fazenda em 2015 com a proposta de promover um ajuste fiscal, mas encontrou enormes dificuldades políticas para implementar as medidas e deixou o governo antes de completar um ano no cargo.

Ou seja, não adianta absolutamente nada colocar um nome respeitado pelo mercado no Ministério da Fazenda se esse ministro não tiver respaldo político pra executar as medidas necessárias.

E é aí que mora a grande questão.

O mercado financeiro não tá comemorando uma redução da dívida pública brasileira. A dívida não diminuiu por causa dessa notícia. Nenhuma reforma estrutural foi aprovada em função dessa sondagem e o próprio Trabuco sequer confirmou que vai assumir o cargo.

O mercado tá comemorando a possibilidade de uma mudança na condução da política econômica.

Porque o mercado financeiro não espera as coisas acontecerem pra se movimentar. Ele tenta antecipar o que pode acontecer daqui a seis meses, um ano, cinco anos.

Se essa expectativa se concretizar, com medidas fiscais consistentes, podemos ter um ambiente bastante favorável para os ativos brasileiros, inclusive ações, fundos  e títulos de renda fixa de longo prazo, que podem se beneficiar da queda dos juros futuros via marcação a mercado.

Mas, se tudo isso ficar apenas no campo da especulação, essa valorização pode ser rapidamente revertida.

O mercado já começou a precificar uma mudança que o governo ainda precisa entregar.

text:
Love this intersection of classical sociological theory applied to the impact of AI on society. 

Are any professors or academic programs teaching this?
author: cuysheffield
quoted_text:
Travel writing is in practice some of the best sociology since the naivete of the foreigner grants the permission to make sweeping generalizations and claims that might otherwise seem too poorly-justified to merit publication. “My people have poor manners” is a tough claim to credibly land (Who are you? Exactly which life experiences are you drawing on? And what is your agenda in pushing this line of argument?), whereas “on my travels in Scotland, I noticed that the people had poor manners” seems perfectly reasonable, and indeed thought-provoking. Random samples from a distribution help you understand the mean, and the aleatory nature of travel encounters lends credence to the whole assessment.

Alexis de Tocqueville was just 25 when he traveled across the US and 29 when his observations were published. So, Democracy in America is a giant Substack from a young backpacker, written on his peregrinations as he consumed Montesquieu, Pascal, and Rousseau. He was clearly inspired by Montesquieu’s The Spirit of the Laws, which made the case that countries’ governance, and their laws, are necessarily functions of their cultures and manners.

Building on this, Democracy in America is in many ways a “deep roots” work. Tocqueville is emphatic (at times comically so) that it is America's culture that explains its success, and that its culture in turn stems from the country’s initial conditions. “I think I can see the whole destiny of America contained in the first Puritan who landed on those shores.” He thinks it's important that New England was settled by “a greater mass of intelligence than is to be found in any European nation of our own time” who brought the “best elements of order and morality”. He points out that Mexico doesn’t work nearly as well, despite copying the American constitution and laws, and notes disapprovingly that Virginia was founded by gold-seeking people “without character” whose “turbulent spirit [...] endangered the infant colony.” At the end of Volume I, he concludes, practically table-thumping: “If in the course of this work I have not succeeded in making the reader feel the importance that I attribute to the practical experience of the Americans, to their habits, to their opinions, in a word, to their moeurs, in maintaining their laws, I have failed in the principal object that I proposed to myself in writing it.”

We could look at Democracy in America as an early work of development economics: he is attempting to systematically figure out why it is that America works. (And not just out of casual interest: he was a member of an aristocratic family that was entangled with recent French political upheaval.) By placing primacy on culture, Tocqueville’s explanation deviates from the institutional and structural explanations often favored by today’s economists. Daron Acemoglu, to choose one prominent present-day example, firmly rejects the “Culture Hypothesis” in Why Nations Fail. In explaining Virginia, he instead points to structural incentives. Poor Economics, from Esther Duflo and Abhijit Banerjee, contains a similar rejection of cultural explanations. Comparable examples from other leading economists abound. An aversion to cultural explanations is of course understandable for all sorts of reasons: cultures are opaque, protean, and resistant to quantitative characterization. Cultures are themselves shaped by other factors, such that it’s hard to attribute definitive causality, and it’s uncomfortable to adopt anything that feels like a normative orientation. Nonetheless, can we explain why New England differs from Mexico without starting with the inner disposition, habits, and worldviews of the people? Tocqueville thinks not.

For all culture’s importance, it would be wrong to suggest that Tocqueville believes that culture is the only factor that matters. He dwells extensively on how America’s institutions are important, and how the microstructure of town life shapes the country’s federal civics. It is also true that development economics has taken a more strongly cultural turn in recent times, most of all in Joel Mokyr’s 2025 Nobel Prize. Mokyr’s work feels downright Tocquevillian at times: contra the intimidatingly quantitative econometrics that dominates today, Mokyr engages in an extended and earnestly curious qualitative synthesis of relevant patterns (in his case, in service of trying to figure out why the Industrial Revolution started when it did). Like Tocqueville, he concludes that the best explanation places cultural changes above other factors.

I’m very interested in whether LLMs will help us characterize culture in new and at least somewhat more objective ways. Can we ingest and process vast quantities of work that may not even have been OCR’d or translated until now? Can we map cultural corpora to vectors in some foundation model embedding space? Where large datasets and computational techniques enabled new ways to analyze many economic questions in recent decades, perhaps LLMs will enable newly objective light to be shone on hypothesized cultural explanations.

–

Speaking of LLMs, Democracy in America is a book about a new kind of society, and a Frenchman trying to figure out what the future might hold. As we sit on the cusp of another upheaval, is there anything that reads with resonance today?

Part of the declared promise of AI is that it might obviate our need to work. In slavery, Tocqueville observes a version of this phenomenon on his travels. He is struck by its barbarous cruelty (and his travel companion later published an anti-slavery novel), but also by its effects on the slaveowners themselves. He perceived that the practice rendered work dishonorable, and thus yielded idleness, ignorance, and pride. Slavery, he says, “enervates the powers of the mind, and benumbs the activity of man.” He observes the contrast between slavery-rejecting Ohio and slavery-embracing Kentucky. In Kentucky, “those who are active and enlightened either do nothing or pass over into the State of Ohio, where they may work without dishonor.” Ohio’s harvests are more abundant, homes are more elegant, and people seem to be “in enjoyment of that wealth and contentment which is the reward of labor.”

Presented with an evil release from manual labor, the Kentuckians did not apply themselves to productive studies and great creations, and the South did not become a new Florence. There is an obvious question for us: how will AI change our relationship with work? Will it become dishonorable, and what will the reflexive effect on our society be if so? Should this change our view of utopian visions of “automated communism”?

Tocqueville also raises the issue of coexistence with more advanced neighbors. He noted that the arrival of the Europeans had been ruinous for the Indians (as he termed them). European technology – firearms, metallurgy, steam power – was a kind of superintelligence relative to their practices. The disruptions and destruction wrought by the settlers led to cultural problems (“their traditions obscured, and the chain of their recollections broken”), which in turn led to declines in both the physical and the moral conditions of the tribes. Tocqueville believed that the Indians faced a choice given that their old way of living was no longer viable: they could adopt European mores or suffer inevitable destruction. He predicted that they would reject cultural adaptation, and thus were “doomed to perish”. This is all to say that the arrival of the European settlers was in Tocqueville’s eyes injurious to the Indians not only because of the direct violence and displacement, but also because the contact was itself so disruptive to their societies that their cultures ceased to function. Some of this was later observed in Pacific island societies – even though there wasn’t the same degree of violent dispossession, the mere presence of Western contact was intrinsically destabilizing. In many visions of the future, superintelligent AIs are much more numerous than humans, with consequences that are hard to predict. In Tocqueville, there is a cautionary suggestion.

Given the new powers afforded by AI, there is a question of what we will choose to do with it – to the extent that we are in control, we will wield a vastly expanded authority. Americans faced some version of this question: in democracy, society was endowed with wholly new ways to express its collective will, with no ultimate superior power, for society was for the first time in charge of itself. Tocqueville repeatedly emphasizes how democracy thus increased the importance of religion as a regulator of hasty or unwise impulses. “Whilst the law permits the Americans to do what they please, religion prevents them from conceiving, and forbids them to commit, what is rash or unjust.” If we take seriously Tocqueville’s idea that religion was a critical complement in ensuring that people shaped societies in prudent ways, Democracy implicitly raises a question: which are the ideas, philosophies, religions, or doctrines that will help us wield AI well?

Part of what’s interesting and memorable about the work is Tocqueville’s combination of curiosity, enthusiasm, and slight ambivalence about democracy itself. He grants that democracy is likely to be the future of governance, and he is admiring of what it has achieved in America, but he can’t avoid concerns about what it may augur (such as the unchecked and totalitarian impulses of the mob). At the end of Volume II, he describes his chief concern with democracy: that it may yield a new form of despotism that he struggles to define. He fears not tyrants, but, he says, “guardians”. He is worried about a world where:

> Above this race of men stands an immense and tutelary power, which takes upon itself alone to secure their gratifications, and to watch over their fate. [...] It would be like the authority of a parent, if, like that authority, its object was to prepare men for manhood; but it seeks on the contrary to keep them in perpetual childhood: it is well content that the people should rejoice, provided they think of nothing but rejoicing. For their happiness such a government willingly labors, but it chooses to be the sole agent and the only arbiter of that happiness. [...] What remains, but to spare them all the care of thinking and all the trouble of living? Thus it every day renders the exercise of the free agency of man less useful and less frequent; it circumscribes the will within a narrower range, and gradually robs a man of all the uses of himself.

The Iain Banks Culture novels are often invoked by AI proponents. For Tocqueville, something strikingly like the world that they describe was his dystopian fear, for a world bereft of autonomy would be intrinsically degrading and humiliating for humanity:

> The will of man is not shattered, but softened, bent, and guided: men are seldom forced by it to act, but they are constantly restrained from acting: such a power does not destroy, but it prevents existence; it does not tyrannize, but it compresses, enervates, extinguishes, and stupefies a people, till each nation is reduced to be nothing better than a flock of timid and industrious animals, of which the government is the shepherd.

The analogy to animals is noteworthy. In interviews, AI leaders occasionally analogize the future human state to that of pets. Banks himself noted that in the Culture novels, “[humans] have a status somewhere between passengers, pets and parasites.” In Richard Brautigan’s famous poem, All Watched Over by Machines of Loving Grace, he hopes that humans are “returned to our mammal brothers and sisters”.

Tocqueville at heart thought that agency and cultivation of people came above all else. He dreaded anesthetized placidity. In soft despotism, he feared that “ambition will lose its vigor and its greatness; that human passions will be appeased and lowered at the same time”. This vigor was for Tocqueville at the heart of what was admirable in America, whose bustle and intensity he repeatedly extols. American self-reliance and self-direction are paramount: “the citizen of the United States is taught from his earliest infancy to rely upon his own exertions in order to resist the evils and the difficulties of life.” For Tocqueville, any kind of servile and manicured comfort was not just undesirable, but a negation of the American promise.

Many of the Elysian visions for AI hinge on AI resolving the messy coordination challenges that afflict humans. (Scott Alexander invokes this vision towards the end of Meditations on Moloch.) For Tocqueville, the arbitration of such differences was precisely the constructive activity that reaffirmed our agency. Townships, juries, associations, and their attendant squabbles are how culture is reinforced and how judgment is cultivated. When a town decides whether to fund a school, there are two outputs: a decision, and practice in governance itself. If AI could resolve such matters, we might get better outcomes, but will we get better people?

Doing "moore" digging into Moore Threads' rumored 64GB Lushan GPU.

The 64GB number is STILL unconfirmed. But there's another interesting detail for Localmaxxers.

Moore Threads' own filings say its new Huagang GPU architecture supports FP4 through FP64 precision.

And llama.cpp already has a MUSA backend for existing Moore Threads GPUs.

So we're not necessarily starting from zero on the software side.

The big questions remain ... 
🧠 Will Lushan actually ship with 64GB VRAM?
⚡ What's the memory bandwidth?
🚀 How fast is FP4 inference?
🦙 Will llama.cpp support Lushan at launch?
💰 And what will it cost?

A 64GB consumer GPU could change the economics of running 70B-class models locally.

But 64GB without competitive inference performance won't be enough to lure customers.

December 29 is the date to watch. That's when Moore Threads has its next major GPU presentation scheduled.

I really want to see this thing benchmarked against the RTX 5090 and other high-memory local AI options.

🇨🇳 Is China about to release a consumer GPU with 2x the VRAM of NVIDIA's RTX 5090?

For quick comparison ...
🟢 NVIDIA RTX 5090 → 32GB GDDR7

🚀 4× graphics memory capacity
🚀 64× AI compute performance

🚀 50× ray tracing performance

Moore Threads already has its own GPU compute platform called MUSA, and llama.cpp has an upstream MUSA backend for existing Moore Threads GPUs.

❓ Actual VRAM capacity
❓ Memory bandwidth

苹果在iOS上把一款叫「悟空外卖」（Wukong，也叫Gokoo）的应用直接标记为恶意软件。打开时会弹窗：“包含恶意软件，不能打开。你应将其从设备删除。”

这也不是新鲜事

早在2025年2月就有用户曝光过，把它列入SparkCat恶意软件家族。这套木马专门干一件事：用OCR（光学字符识别）扫手机相册和截图，找加密钱包的助记词和私钥。

你给它相册权限，它就在后台把照片一张张过一遍。看到类似助记词的文字，就传走。

悟空外卖主要服务东南亚华人，泰国为主，马来西亚、越南等地也有。注册用户超13万，月活约5.5万

SparkCat不是只盯这一款app。俄罗斯网络安全公司（Kaspersky Lab）在App Store和Google Play里扫出几十款被植入的应用，外卖、聊天、VPN都有。手法类似：借客服或正常功能要相册权限，拿到后就开始OCR。

目前没有公开的大规模资产被盗数据，但还是千万谨慎小心

quoted_text:
Run GLM 5.3 (full) on your DGX Sparks

This release is special. It has a no-compromise on quality configuration. No shortcuts were made to make it "faster". Just pure quality.

Runs on TensorFold.

Two ways to run this:
- GLM 5.3 K4 by @wrldsuksgo2mars (default)
- GLM 5.3 DERISKED EXL3 4 bpw /w Cyber calibration, quantized from @Blackfrost_AI's DERISKED BF16.

Performance & stats (TP4):
~288k context, single stream only.
~39 tok/s in prose, non-greedy, thinking on
- Prefill: 1571-1300, depends on context

Performance & stats (TP6):
~845k context, up to 4x stream.
~49 tok/s in prose, non-greedy, thinking on
~76 tok/s in prose, 4 concurrent streams
- Prefill: 1767-1308, depends on context

Basically TP6 buys you a lot of context and improved decode speeds. TP4 is completely usable. Similar performance on both quants.

What "DERISKED" means
Not every refusal is removed in @Blackfrost_AI models, and that's on purpose. Blackfrost calls its method DWM, Directional Weight Modification. Instead of deleting refusal like abliteration, it softens one behavior by a set amount.

Why not go to zero? Pushing closer to zero refusals on some models brings dropped tool calls, broken reasoning, loops and hallucinations. For cybersecurity work, a model that drops even one tool call is a problem.

What DWM keeps:
- Fewer refusals on real security questions
- Built-in protections stay intact
- One dial to tune the strength

Usable beats uncensored.

text:
Absurd to think AI should be governed democratically

author: Shaughnessy119
quoted_text:
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

text:
« Le vrai scandale Nvidia, c'est que l'entreprise la plus cotée de l'histoire repose sur un homme. »

Thierry, cette phrase est un aveu. C'est la pensée d'un bureaucrate à l'état pur.

Pour toi, qu'une entreprise dépende d'un homme, c'est un scandale. Pour moi, c'est la définition même de l'excellence.

Regarde partout où l'humanité a produit quelque chose de grand. La musique : Bach, Mozart, Beethoven. La peinture : Vinci, Michel-Ange. Le cinéma : Chaplin, Kubrick. La science : Newton, Einstein. L'entreprise : Jobs, Musk, Huang. À chaque fois, un homme. Un seul. Qui voit avant les autres, et qui arrive à convaincre d'autres hommes de valeur de tout lâcher pour le rejoindre. C'est ça, une équipe. C'est ça, une entreprise. Pas un organigramme. Une vision qui attire des talents.

Et le marché vient de te donner tort en direct. Huang part : Nvidia perd environ 600 milliards. Huang revient : l'action prend près de 30 % en une séance. Ce n'est pas un scandale. C'est une mesure. Le prix exact d'un homme exceptionnel.

Au passage, ce n'était pas « la moitié de sa valeur ». Et Huang est revenu il y a trois jours. Même tes faits ont un train de retard.

Pourquoi tu ne comprends pas ça ? Parce que tu ne l'as jamais vécu.

Toute ta carrière, tu as été nommé. À la tête d'entreprises publiques. Ministre. Commissaire. Jamais tu n'as bâti de rien une boîte qui compte. Jamais tu n'as eu à convaincre un ingénieur brillant de miser sa vie sur ton idée. Tu as géré ce que d'autres avaient construit.

Et la seule fois où tu as voulu bâtir un empire, ça a donné Atos. Des dizaines d'acquisitions empilées, un champion du CAC 40 sur le papier. Tu pars à Bruxelles en 2019 en vantant un bilan sans dette. Quelques années plus tard, la boîte est au bord de la faillite et l'État doit la sauver. Ta réponse : « responsabilité zéro ».

Alors au lieu de chercher ta place parmi ceux qui construisent, tu as choisi l'autre camp. Celui qui contrôle ceux qui créent. Tu as passé tes années à Bruxelles à menacer Musk, à jouer au gendarme des plateformes, à empiler les règlements sur des entreprises que l'Europe est incapable de produire. Le système plutôt que la réalité. La norme plutôt que l'œuvre.

C'est toujours la même trajectoire. Quand on ne peut pas être l'exception, on finit par la combattre.

Tu n'as jamais été l'exception, Thierry. Tu as été le gestionnaire de l'exception des autres, puis son flic. Ta carrière pue la lose, et ta phrase sur Nvidia en est le résumé parfait : tu regardes un génie et tu vois un risque.

Casse-toi à Madagascar, et laisse faire les hommes compétents.

I guess launchpads need to play a crucial role if we really want to heal the trenches on any chain.

Make premium launches expensive. Make bundling difficult or expensive enough that extracting liquidity within the first few minutes is no longer profitable.

Imagine how fucked up the trenches have become.

We don't need more launchpads competing over who can launch the most tokens. We need launchpads competing over who can create the healthiest trading environment.

Bring back the excitement of finding something early.

text:
48,740 RLP, a Gold tier, a three-day streak and absolutely no jackpot.

That's my introduction to the new @RallyOnChain.

I've been participating in Rally campaigns for a while, so I was curious whether the new release would simply change the interface or actually change how I use the platform.

I explored Rally Spins, checked my streak and spent some time looking through my redesigned creator profile.

The spin screen currently shows zero winnings.

Apparently, my luck hasn't received the latest software update yet.

But the feature that genuinely caught my attention wasn't the wheel.

It was the creator profile.

Mine currently shows:

• Gold tier
• 48,740 RLP balance
• 3-day active streak
• 665.41K impressions
• 787 Sorsa Score
• 4 out of 5 medals
Seeing everything together made me realize how much of my Rally journey was previously scattered across individual campaigns.
I'd research a project, prepare content, submit it, check my score and move on to the next opportunity.
Now there's a more visible sense of continuity between those activities.
The streak gives me a reason to return daily.
Missions introduce additional objectives.

Every valid submission earns another spin, alongside the free daily check-in spin.

And the creator profile gives those individual activities a shared history.

That's why the profile is my favorite addition.

A campaign leaderboard tells me how I performed in one competition.

My creator profile tells me how my participation is developing over time.

But there's one feature I'd love to see added next.

A Creator Passport.

Imagine opening your Rally profile and seeing not only your medals and tier, but also a breakdown of the skills you've demonstrated across previous campaigns.

Technical research.

Product testing.

Educational content.

Creative storytelling.

Community discussions.

Instead of every creator being represented primarily by a balance or ranking, their profile could gradually become a portfolio of demonstrated abilities.

A brand looking for technical researchers could discover creators with a history of strong technical evaluations.

A project looking for product testers could find people who consistently produce useful walkthroughs.

And creators could identify which skills they need to improve.

That's my personal suggestion, not an announced feature.

For me, the new Rally is an interesting first step toward making participation feel like something that continues beyond a single campaign.

Although I still have 51,260 RLP to go before Diamond, and apparently the wheel has decided to test my patience.

I'll be particularly interested to see how my profile and streak develop over the next few days.

Have you tried the new Rally yet?

Which feature would actually make you return tomorrow: the daily spin, your streak, or watching your creator profile grow?

text:
Configurable Accounts is the endgame design for crypto wallets at the protocol layer. 

Beyond the other good stuff i have talked about such as future proofing against cryptography attacks and scaling assets via multisigs, it enable a long envisioned pattern with @_jxom and @awkweb - guest checkout.

If you think about it - crypto onboarding sucks for two reasons, and we have solved both of them:
- logging in with a secure credential
- onramping with KYC

We solved the onramp with MACH- a select # of MPP services can enjoy embedded headless kycless onramping. LMK if you wanna try it.

For logging in, configurable accounts allow us to onboard a user w/ a browser held private key generated like a burner wallet. But at the end of the flow, you may add the passkey / google or whatever else as a signer and revoke the private key. 

Good UX sometimes doesn’t require removing friction, it means moving the friction AFTER the user is bought in, so they have an incentive to do the step.

These are some of the wonders you can achieve when you can co-design a protocol not just for performance and security but also for the wallet experience.

Injective has submitted a new policy letter to the SEC advocating for regulatory changes to accelerate the adoption of tokenized equities and RWAs in the United States 🇺🇸

The comprehensive 22-page letter calls for expanding the SEC’s exemptive framework for tokenized stock trading to include onchain orderbooks, opening new avenues for American financial innovation.

The SEC’s current framework only covers a limited set of venues built on AMM liquidity pools, excluding the orderbook model that underpins traditional global capital markets.

Injective’s submission outlines why this framework should extend to onchain orderbooks:

🔹 The SEC’s findings on public interest and investor protection apply to orderbooks as well as AMMs.

🔹 Orderbooks can enable 24/7 trading, self-custody, near-instant settlement and publicly verifiable transactions.

🔹 Orderbooks can help keep tokenized equity prices closely aligned with traditional markets while producing comparable market data.

🔹 Orderbooks remove the need for a separate liquidity pooling layer, potentially simplifying the risk profile for retail liquidity providers.

🔹 Innovations such as Injective’s frequent batch auction mechanism can mitigate front-running and MEV risks.

🔹 Additional investor protections can be introduced through market surveillance, price limits, self-trade prevention and protocol-level trading halts.

🔹 A technology-neutral regulatory framework would allow multiple onchain market structures to compete and innovate in the United States.

This marks Injective’s third formal submission to the SEC, building on earlier policy recommendations on DeFi protocols and onchain lending, as well as recent discussions with the SEC’s Crypto Task Force.

As the US establishes its regulatory framework for digital assets and RWAs, Injective continues to work directly with regulators to advance American financial innovation while pioneering the infrastructure needed to bring global capital markets onchain with $INJ

Im not a gamer, so I don’t particularly care about the gaming case of crypto. But every time I think about it, it highlights the key issue which is a great technology with applicable usecase having been utterly overshadowed by scams

author: maxlbcook
quoted_text:
ok so i've been sitting on this half-baked theory for a few weeks. Until a conversation with a friend @maxlbcook last night convinced me this isn't a dumb theory. 

The theory is that a good model needs a good product / harness before regular people can actually use its intelligence. We are waiting for a good product surface area that lets us actually use the crazy-smart models that are already all around us.

let's rewind a bit. GPT-3 was available in June 2020 (!). Basically nobody cared outside a small group of devs. Then ChatGPT launched on Nov 2022 and suddenly everyone's mom was using . The model under it was basically what was already sitting on the OAI playground! It was mostly the interface. Felt like lightning in a bottle (!) I remember that day vividly bc I'll admit I missed this and did not update my priors fast enough! we were on our honeymoon and I debated with my wife - yes but this has been around forever on OAI playground dot dev - same thing, not sure why THIS is going viral.. Boy was I wrong. Anywho.. let's call that Phase 1: chatbots. People used it for writing, looking stuff up, code complete, Q&A.

Phase 2 was the same thing in reverse, which I think is kind of funny. This time the harness came first and the model showed up later. Codex CLI launched in April 2025. claude code went into preview in February and was generally available by May 2025. They were fine, honestly. Then one week in November 2025 happened: GPT-5.1-Codex-Max on Nov 19 and Opus 4.5 on Nov 24. All of a sudden long-running agents actually worked, and software engineering had its 10x moment. Another "aha moment"... this time caused not by the exoskeleton but the brain finding its way into that exoskeleton!

Which brings us to now. It's a weird moment. The models keep getting smarter really fast at anything you can check. Math, physics, chemistry, and cyber results that would have been front-page news a year ago come out basically every week. And at the same time the market narrative is that the AI trade is broken... frontier token consumption is below forecast, and diffusion is slow. So which one is it??

I think it's both, and the way I've been thinking about it is light. In 19th century we discovered a kind of light that nobody can see. Cool, but useless, until someone holds up a photographic plate and you can see right through a hand. Within months doctors are using it to find bullets in people. X-rays, MRI et al were killer applications decades later. Infrared went the same way: discovered in 1800, and nobody cared for ~140 years until night vision goggles. The plate and the goggles were the harness. They took something invisible and made it something billions of ppl could use.

That's where I think we are. Most of the recent gains are in the invisible part of the spectrum. A tiny group of power users can see them and push the latest models all the way. Everyone else is about where we were in October 2022: the capability is sitting there, waiting for its ChatGPT moment.

So what's the next product surface area / harness? A few candidates I'm watching:

#1 Proactive / ambient agents. Dots, Instinct, the Grok bot, etc. The AI comes to you instead of waiting for a prompt. Already used by millions

#2 Agent swarms with a goal and a budget. Replit Missions, Perplexity's co-counsel stuff from a while back. You say what you want and how much you'll spend, and the swarm figures out the rest. Usage is probably in thousands of users, not mainstream yet.

#3 Async / background agents. You hand off the work, go get coffee, and come back to it done. No staring at a chat window.

#4 Computer use + cloud computers. Computer use launched a while back (Oct 2024!) and felt early. But give the agent its own always-on computer in the cloud and it can do anything you'd do on your laptop... while your laptop is closed. Think there's a lot of promise here.

I'm sure there are products exploring this idea maze that I haven't used. What am I missing?? Genuinely want to hear it.

text:
I kept coming back to the blurred tree in Cicada 3301’s Liber Primus. A solver proposed in 2019 that it came from a photo R. Neil Marshman took in 2005 of a partly dead oak near Earls Barton, England. We went back to that lead and tested it: fit the branches on one side of the photo, then see if it predicts the branches we left out. The match to the later silhouette held up.

The same tree and cicada appear on page 55 and in the 2016 notice, but in reverse order. We also found a black-and-white rendering of the oak in a 2006 thesis, years before Liber Primus appeared. It gets much of the branch detail right, but the root still gives the game away. In our whole-root check, the print spans 29 cells. Two of the closest branch fits predicted 58 and 59. We have strong evidence for the photo behind the artwork, but we still don’t know which version Cicada used.

Back on the runes, we confirmed the same two-word ciphertext pair on pages 27 and 55. Allowing one shared rune shift didn’t turn up a second pair. No new plaintext or key, but we have a better idea of what to test next.

The photos, comparisons, code and dead ends are in the notebook: https://t.co/EeZGJy8Lv2
author: CryptoVonDoom
quoted_text:
Today we got a hard number for one of the ideas we’ve been testing in Cicada 3301’s Liber Primus.

Also - I realized I had a lot more GPT usage available than I thought I cranked the effort on Astra 6.2 to Ultra to see if we crank anything.

Take the 3,316 runes in section 8. If the cipher uses the same four shifts on a loop, with the key advancing continuously, no rune in the decoded text can appear more than 156 times. That’s 4.70%, even if you pick the best possible shifts to make that one rune show up as often as it can. In the solved pages we used for comparison, E accounts for 12.48% of the runes.

So we checked every repeating key length from 1 to 128. If section 8 has a most-common rune as frequent as E in those solved pages, 116 is the first key length that can even reach that benchmark. That’s a limit on the model, not a reason to go hunting for a 116-rune key. Section 8 could use different rune frequencies, or the key could pause or reset.

We also tested 2,429 combinations of positions and guessed words or phrases from the solved pages. Two guesses survived six runes, including AGAIN AFTER. Both failed at the seventh. No verified new plaintext.

Next I want to test an exception that shows up in solved Liber Primus passages: leave a printed F as F and don’t advance the key. The question is whether pauses at the Fs that are actually on the page can close the gap without giving ourselves permission to move the key wherever it helps.
