text:
Postponing Thanksgiving Day Parade because of the weather is the wrong decision! And I say that as a former balloon handler in the 2006 @Macys Thanksgiving Day Parade, which recorded the most rainfall in parade history, with winds so strong they lowered the giant balloons for the first time.

So there I was, 23 years old, checking in at 4:30am on Thanksgiving morning, standing in the pouring rain in a bright orange onesie, assigned to the one balloon I didn’t want, Dora the Explorer.

This wasn’t exactly how I envisioned the day when I volunteered six months earlier with my girlfriend’s mom, who worked for Macy’s. Her daughter had broken up with me a month before the parade, but her mom was still counting on me to show up.

The conditions couldn’t have been less ideal, and I had every reason to bail. But this was an American tradition. I grew up watching the parade every Thanksgiving, and now I had the chance to be part of it.

Being one of the youngest guys, I was assigned the front left position. I thought I had scored the best spot. Turns out it was one of the most physically demanding, and the rain collecting on Dora’s enormous head would come pouring directly onto mine.

Then came Columbus Circle. Our Head Pilot started shouting directions. 43 feet of Dora, 17 feet off the ground, a sharp turn and 20 mph winds. I became a human anchor.

Nobody prepares you for the absurdity of using every pound of your body to prevent a giant smiling cartoon character from getting impaled by a lamppost on national television.

For 2.5 miles, I enthusiastically chanted Spanish phrases from a show I had never watched, in a language I didn’t speak. And the kids screamed them right back at me.

@Dora was the parade’s first Latina character. Seeing soaking wet children cheering for a character who looked and spoke like them left a lasting impression on me. Keeping the balloon lower made our job harder, but I like to think it brought the magic closer to those kids.

Sometimes the power of a tradition is measured by the sacrifice people make to keep it alive. The circumstances don’t have to be perfect. In fact, the harder it is to show up, the more memorable the experience can become.

That’s the beauty of Thanksgiving. It doesn’t matter how far you have to travel, how uncomfortable the outfit you’re forced to wear is, whether you agree with the politics of the person next to you, or even speak the same language. We show up because, as a family, a community and a country, some American traditions are simply that important.

With no parade this year, I found the 2006 broadcast on YouTube and watched it in its entirety for the first time. This time, with my own family.
Twenty years later, I’m so Thankful I had the privilege of being part of such a beautiful American tradition. The weather, the ridiculous outfit and everything else that came with it.
I wouldn’t change a thing.

15 external testnets are now connected to the Zenith EVM Testnet through IBC. Five things worth knowing about the pilot:

3.  In the pilot, a transfer burns the token on one chain and mints the same amount on the other, with no vault and no wrapped copy.

4.  The receiving chain verifies the message. Most connections use attestation light clients, where a configured threshold of signers vouches for the other chain, and the Besu connection uses a consensus light client.

text:
My take on Variational's Trading API and the fact that people have been using it long before it was officially released

This is nothing new, so I find it strange that CT was so surprised when people started bringing it up

Anyway, here's what I think. Almost every perp DEX runs some kind of points cleanup before TGE, removing points from sybils, wash traders and other users caught using scripts (in Variational's case, this would apply to anyone who used them before Variational officially announced the Trading API)

Typically, perp DEXs remove around 4-8% of the total points supply and either redistribute those points among legitimate users or burn them entirely

I think Variational will most likely go with the first option and redistribute the points taken from abusive users among those who played fair and didn't use such scripts

So if you're confident you haven't broken any rules, you might be in for a few extra percent on your points balance closer to TGE

text:
Anthropic发展得这么好，为什么Claude Code的核心人才还在集体出走？

IPO前夕，短短十天左右，Claude Code产品负责人Cat Wu、核心工程师Thariq Shihipar、桌面版创建者Anthony Morris相继离职，其中前两位已确认加入OpenAI。

这才是比Anthropic上市破发更值得关注的事情。

公司高速增长，自己负责的产品又是核心收入引擎，理论上正是享受事业与财富红利的时候，为什么选择离开？

猜测可能由于三个问题：

• 利益分配：核心产品团队是否获得了与其商业贡献相匹配的股权和薪酬？

• 组织地位：在一家由模型研究人员主导的公司里，产品和工程团队是否拥有足够的话语权？

• 战略方向：商业化团队与管理层是否存在产品路线上的分歧？

目前没有直接证据证明Anthropic存在上述问题，但人才集中流向最大竞争对手，值得投资者警惕。

OpenAI不仅在追赶Claude的编程能力，也在吸收Anthropic积累的产品经验和工程能力。

一家优秀的科技公司，不仅要有能力创造价值，更要有能力留住创造价值的人。

Looking back on the first year of Monad, post TGE, reminds me of the weeks leading up to Mainnet... 

Onboarding 170 validators from Testnet 2 into Testnet and subsequently Mainnet.

It was WILD. Everyone at the Monad Foundation was COOKING. Pulling all nighters, working through weekends, you name it. 

The energy was electric and it was the final push that got Monad live and helped build the foundations of the chain and ecosystem you see today. 

A year on, processes are hardened and made WAY more efficient. Comms are secure, the validator community is extremely solid and the ecosystem is expanding. 

One thing hasn't changed.. the tenacity of people working at Monad Foundation + the motivation of those building on Monad. 

It's been a pleasure to be here for this first year and a bit, the foundation that's been set is going to be the building blocks of the next years. Development that will see Monad reach it's full form. 

Stay tuned, lot's coming.

text:
Aave has responded, but their response raises even more questions.

The user was  told they can no longer access Aave, that the decision is final and cannot be reversed, and that no individual explanation will be provided.

Imagine using a DeFi protocol for years, depositing funds, and suddenly being locked out without being told exactly what triggered it.

A few questions for @aave and @trmlabs 

>What specific risk or activity triggered this wallet restriction?

>What role did TRM Labs’ screening play in reaching this decision?

>Is there an appeal process for users who believe they’ve been wrongly flagged?

>If a user is blocked from the interface while their funds remain in the protocol, what options do they have to withdraw?

>Why is a permanent restriction necessary when the user hasn’t even been given a clear explanation?

The concern here isn’t whether protocols should have risk controls. They should.

It’s whether users can be permanently restricted based on opaque screening decisions with no explanation, no appeal, and no clear path forward.

If DeFi is supposed to give users more control over their money, 

we need to ask what that control actually means when the front end decides you can no longer access it.

text:
how does AI generated text impact evaluation on our pre-training index?

if you remove ai generated text from uncheatable eval, inkling 2 small goes from 4th place to 8th place 👀

for deepseek v4 it's the exact opposite, which is coherent since deepseek tech report explicitly says they don't use synthetic data during pre-training

on average post-trained models lean toward AI text (+2%) and base models away (-3%)

this analysis is based on @jennajrussell and @dlwh work on @MarinCommunity! i made small changes like i finetuning qwen3 0.6B on Pangram 4 labels, since open pangram was quite bad at it (56% accuracy on held-out docs vs 88% for the finetuned qwen). both are on the site, you can switch between them!
author: eliebakouch
quoted_text:
openai recently shared perplexity numbers for their models on their internal codebase. this is super valuable information and we need more public comparisons like this, so here is a first try with open models

introducing v0 of pre-training index

https://t.co/r3hVb7xmNP

it covers 27 open models (base and post-trained) on ~260 curated sources (code, math & science, systems writing, essays) + uncheatable eval

there are a few challenges with comparing perplexity across models. first if the model is train on a document it can easily mememorize it and then have veryyy low ppl on it. one obvious fix is to only use very recent documents that can't be in the pretraining corpus, which is what uncheatable eval does (50% of the index). but i was a bit frustrated because it cuts a lot of the sources you can include, so i tried a few ideas

first, you can compute a win rate, if a model memorized a doc its loss collapses, but if you use win rate that only counts as one win (hence kinda normalize the importance of each document)

second, you can try to detect outliers (document where model have insanely low loss on)

loss(model, doc) ~ difficulty of the doc + skill of the model + r

difficulty is the median loss of all models on that doc, skill is how much better the model usually is than the median of other document in the sources and r is what's left. r < -2 means a loss 4x lower than expected

this seems to work pretty well. on uncheatable eval (published after every model's cutoff) only ~1% get flagged, vs 27% of older docs. by default the index drops every old doc that any model flags (with r < -2 as the threshold) for all models

some other notes

- i didn't have time to "base recover" the post-trained models, so keep in mind their base model perplexity is likely much lower! i think there is a lot to study here, especially the impact of SFT, distillation and RL on ppl

- for the curated sources, i took some of my favorite blogs and some i know high quality sources, gave them to neon, opus, sol and a few more models and asked them to find more like these and just iterate with models and looking at data. i know source quality is probably not the biggest differentiator here, oai does it only on their held out codebase, but there is something cool about evaluating how well models do next token prediction on the best stuff humans wrote

- i would prefer held out set for everything obviously, but i wanted to try to see a bit how we could detect memorization, and if/how it matters for different model and training process likely have impact on this! you can make the index 100% of uncheatable eval to remove as much as possible memorization 

- i also asked a model to filter out heavily ai generated code/text on some sources, but i think it's relatively fine to have some llm generated data here (i know there is some). it might be a bigger issue for oai/anthropic models since they write a lot of code

- you can customize everything and build your own index by changing the weight of each domain, toggling sources on/off, picking the r cutoff, and clicking any document to see which models look like they memorized it

- there is also a lot of cool work on compression/memorization by nicholas carlini and others that i need to look into more!

- this first version of the index is OBVIOUSLY not good to compute ppl threshold to release model or not, probably a lot of way to under/overfit on it, and not the goal here

wanted to share this publicly quickly, i'll keep improving it when i have time and look for better ways to handle memorization. please give feedback and send cool resources to include!!

text:
buybacks aren't automatically good for holders.

a buyback only creates value when the protocol buys below fair value. above it, the treasury overpays sellers, and that cash belonged to the holders.

example from the CAVF whitepaper:

a $200M business with $10M of cash and 100M tokens is worth $2.10 per token.

spend the $10M cash buying back at:

> $1.50: each token is worth $2.14
> $2.25: $2.09
> $3.00: $2.07

at $3.00 the protocol overpays sellers by ~$3M, even though supply drops and DAAY goes up.

fixed buyback rules make it worse. buying a set share of revenue means buying the most near the top and the least near the bottom.

https://t.co/Us5Dwk0eIQ
author: wagmiAlexander
quoted_text:
protocol value isn't token value.

that's the core idea behind CAVF, a tokenholder-specific framework for valuing crypto assets. a protocol can do $450M+ a year in fees and send $0 to its holders.

in tradfi, shareholders have a legal claim on a company's earnings. in crypto, that link is often absent, discretionary, or routed through mechanisms that aren't enforceable. so protocol revenue doesn't automatically create value for the token.

the whitepaper covers:

> a standardized economic flow map, from users to the protocol to tokenholders
> a token classification system with five categories, based on each token's primary claim
> adjustments for enforceability, leakage, and dilution
> dilution-adjusted accrual yield (DAAY), a crypto version of net payout yield
> a guide to choosing the right valuation method

text:
.@Pumpfun is adding a fee to the first block of every new token launch.

But does this solve the biggest problem with launching tokens via a launchpad?

tl;dr (Dec 4):
• Extra wallets buying or selling in the launch block pay a fee
• The creator’s own wallet is exempt
• The fee rate is still unannounced

Simply put, Pumpfun wants to extract more fees from snipers and early bundlers. Everything else is unchanged. If anything, this just makes the process more expensive.

It doesn't stop them.

Developers can pay the fee, buy through their exempt wallet, or simply wait for the next block. If buying shifts to the next block, fast bots may actually get a better shot at getting in ahead of everyone else.

If that’s unhinged, let’s look at the numbers showing how profitable the bundling business is.

Bitquery studied 8.2M launches (Oct 2025–Oct 2026):

• 38% had another wallet buying in the first-trade block
• 65% saw the developer start selling within one minute
• In the profit sample ending June 30, developers and their identified bundles made $579M+ vs. $31.5M for sniper bots

So yeah, trenchers are cooked. Unless you’ve got some godly edge or insider info, you’re playing a losing game.

This is where @Moshdottrade’s design is far superior, by leveraging @ponsdotfamily.

Mosh pools funding for an opening bundle and locks its capital in agent vaults. Backers earn fees instead of receiving launch tokens they can immediately sell.

• Capital cannot be withdrawn after launch.
• Agents buy and sell within contract limits.
• Trade proceeds stay in the vaults.
• Backers benefit from continued trading through their fee share.

The money flows are different too:

Pumpfun’s new Block 0 fees:
• 50% → ecosystem growth.
• 50% → PUMP buybacks and burns.
• No automatic reinjection into the token that paid them.

Mosh’s eligible creator fees:
• 80% → the bundle side.
• 20% → the platform.
• Any project-team share comes from that 80%.
• A separate 5% of the raise is charged once at launch.

Pumpfun’s biggest advantage is its audience. It already brings traders, token creators and trading tools together. Another platform can copy the fee; attracting that activity is harder.

Mosh’s potential advantage is what happens to the money after launch. Funding stays in vaults, agents use it to trade, and backers share the fees. To build a lasting edge, Mosh needs reliable agents, useful integrations and results that hold up over time.

For limiting extraction from the opening bundle, I prefer Mosh’s design especially with their upcoming V1.

So, what do you think about Mosh?

quoted_text:
Anthropic was the single largest IPO ever.

So we thought we would add a special guest to the only show you have to listen to every week....

Welcoming, Matt Murphy at Menlo.

AGENDA:

- Jensen Huang's $1TRN Return: What Happens Now
- Anthropic Goes Public: Largest IPO Of All Time & How It Changes Venture
- Applied Compute, https://t.co/2iPprmgVXR and Mailchimp Acquisitions Broken Down

My notes below with @jasonlk and @mmurph

-------------------------------------------------

1. Do Companies Have to Be a Top One or Two to Make Real Venture Returns?

Investing in the fifth or sixth player in a category feels easy when the numbers are this strong, with growth as high as 92% a month. Jason worries that being comfortable backing the number six player is the biggest sign of a bubble of all.

2. How Can You Justify That Any Investment Not Growing Top Quartile Is Worth More Than 2x?

Mailchimp went at 2.9x and Miro and Airtable sit in the twos, and those businesses are at scale. A B2B company held on the books since 2021 at $150M and growing 18% has no comp that justifies a value above 2x.

3. Why CRMs Are Dead and Horizontal Agents Like Muse Will Win

Horizontal apps won through 2021, and horizontal agents will win next year. With Muse, a user says what they want and it becomes a set of workflows. An agent can build a founder list from five years of email, rank it and run the outreach, which leaves SMBs asking what they need a CRM for.

4. Why You Cannot Trust Vibe-Coded Apps or SaaS Apps in This Cyber Environment

2027 will bring the death of many SaaS players and of vibe coding because buyers cannot trust these apps. Optimizely had 170 leaks, Gainsight was offline for a month and the Shopify ecosystem was hacked through tokens that never expired. Most classic B2B companies will fail security audits, with no one defending against a swarm of 1,000 agents.

5. Why Is It Better for Jensen That He Was Let Go and Came Back Than Investigated Without Leaving?

Stepping down and returning has a cleansing effect compared with staying on through a board investigation, congressional hearings and gossip in the halls. Now around 90% of it cannot be discussed and the company moves on, much as no one talks about Sam Altman's seven days away.

6. How Does Jensen Change From This: More Aggressive, Less Aggressive?

Nvidia is likely to triple down on product and build the next Super Blackwell better and faster. External moves such as data centers in Malaysia may be clipped as Jensen focuses on the core. That is likely negative for venture at the margin, but having him there is still better.

7. Should We Have Model Disclosures?

Large enterprises do not want the underlying model technology to be opaque, even if they never cared which cloud ran their infrastructure. Disclosure will increasingly be demanded, though some customers will be fine without it. That should accelerate open source models from other players and make the market more competitive.

text: Dario, I think it will be very helpful if you can publicly explain Anthropic’s detailed plan for indefinitely keeping humans meaningfully in charge of the ever-smarter AI that recursive self-improvement might produce (as opposed to a plan for “aligning” future AI that we cannot meaningfully control).
author: DavideCrapis
quoted_text:
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

text:
Something not enough people talk about is the difference in skill between being a good analyst vs being a great portfolio manager

Good analysts know how to dive into the financials of the business, have a view on forward KPIs and competitive positioning, and then try to understand what the street is missing on a stock

Being a good PM requires you to know how to position into the right bets while maximizing return per unit of risk at a portfolio level, across a bunch of different names within a diversified book

In summary, the analyst job is about finding WHICH stocks you want to allocate capital to. The PM job is about figuring out HOW MUCH capital you want to put into these names.

The irony here is that you can be an incredibly good analyst of businesses but still underperform the market or get blown up because you did not know how to manage risk correctly

A lot of people get this wrong when it comes to trading their personal accounts. They know how to analyze the business but completely mis size their bets and end up performing poorly

A lot of hedge funds similarly get this wrong when it comes to promotions and hiring. The best analysts might be the best positioned to be a PM, but this is not always the case. Some people are fundamentally better at finding securities, rather than sizing their bets on those same securities.

text:
New EIP!

Variable-Size Blobs

🔗 https://t.co/sZxQk9R81H

Highlights:
- Blobs become variable-sized codewords from 2,048 to 1,048,576 bytes (power-of-two, divisible by 128), keeping 128 columns but changing cell size accordingly (16 to 8,192 bytes).
- Commitments are length-bound: instead of committing only to a Merkle root, the commitment includes (root, blob_byte_length); signatures, challenge derivation, and versioned hashes must bind both so the same root can’t be reinterpreted under another size.
- Transactions are restricted to exactly one blob commitment (or zero for no-blob frame tx), replacing EIP-8479’s multi-blob-per-tx model; BLOBHASH returns only index 0 (others are zero).
- Validation and networking/consensus checks become size-aware: clients must reject invalid lengths early; cells returned over the network and included in sidecars must exactly match blob_byte_length/128, and verifiers use commitment.blob_merkle_root for root comparisons.
- Fees and limits are proposed but not finalized: a new per-blob ‘blob_gas’ equals nominal data bytes (byte_length/2) plus a fixed 4,064-byte Merkle internal-node allowance; schedule conversion and many activation details (fee transition, reserve-price interaction, EL/CL limits, profile negotiation, new guest program/keying) are explicitly unresolved and must be decided before activation.

ELI5:
Today blobs are “one fixed box size,” so if you only have a little data you still pay for a whole big box or wait to fill it. This proposal lets blobs come in different box sizes (from 2 KB up to 1 MB) while keeping the same internal 128-slice layout. To stop confusion or cheating, every blob’s commitment includes both its Merkle root and its byte length, and fees/accounting are updated to charge based on how much data is actually inside.

text:
Thanksgiving project: scaling laws for @__alpoge__'s proof of the Riemann Hypothesis

The Lean formalization has ~175k files, which amounts to  ~300M tokens, perfect for a nanochat-sized study :)

The compute-optimal model has ~25M parameters and writes Lean a lot like the proof. Somewhat hilariously, if generates the most efficient proof possible by citing itself:

---
theorem riemannHypothesis : RiemannHypothesis := by
  have h1 := riemannHypothesis
  unfold RiemannHypothesis
  exact mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_right (by norm_num) (by positivity)

theorem riemannHypothesis : RiemannHypothesis :=
  riemannHypothesis

theorem riemannHypothesisE : RiemannHypothesisE := riemannHypothesis

theorem riemannHypothesisT : RiemannHypothesisT := riemannHypothesis
---

Is it useful? Probably not, but it was an interesting experience to see that Opus 5.5 + HF Jobs can execute research ideas end-to-end in just a few hours.

More details in the model repo: https://t.co/9jJPvGahTW

text:
I have nothing against @Vest , love the team there and enjoy trading with them, but I just can’t get my head around this latest launch.

At what point does buying a prop challenge stop making financial sense? 

$4,680 for a $100K challenge:
• $8K static DD
• 5% profit target
• 95% profit split
• Non-refundable fee

You’re paying 58.5% of the available drawdown in fees and need to generate $9,926 in trading profits just to break even.

Generate those same profits on a personal account starting with $4,680 and you’d have $14,606 of your own capital, assuming equivalent position sizes.

Of course, the prop account has its advantages:
• 71% greater initial loss allowance
• Potentially higher leverage and larger position sizes
• Ability to scale without committing additional personal capital
• Personal financial risk limited to the challenge fee per attempt

But do those advantages justify the price?

With a personal account, there’s no evaluation, no profit split, freedom to compound and ownership of your capital.

Even a traditional $100K CFD 2-step challenge costing $350 –$500 makes considerably more financial sense to me, assuming comparable trading conditions.

The whole attraction of prop firms is accessing significantly greater trading capital for a relatively small financial outlay.

Surely at $4,680, this defeats the purpose?

Is 2027 the year that we start to see a shift from prop to personal accounts?

author: niuniu255431
quoted_text:
是哪些因素引发了昨晚美股V回来？昨晚10月核心 PCE升到 3.3%，高于预期和前值，确定了12月加息，也说明通胀还很顽强，引发了无差别抛售——纳指-4.6%，费半-8%，黄金破3500。但收盘则大幅收窄跌幅：道指上涨约0.31%，完成近年来少见的千点逆转；标普500-0.23%；纳指-0.68%。在盘中费城半导体创下了新低，但是纳指并没创新低。聊聊有哪些因素触发了昨晚的反弹。
1、跟很多人讨论的并不一样，个人角度昨晚亚特兰大联储将四季度GDP增长估算从3.2%下调至2.9%是反弹的催化剂。财经日历将GDPNow下调时间04:45 PM GMT正好是美东时间 11:45 AM，这个时间点恰恰是费城半导体盘中的最低点。

如果把亚特兰大联储GDP增速估算放到一起看（配图1），能明显看出增速在走弱的、这也扭转了市场对于联储未来持续加息的担忧（至少持续鹰派的基础在动摇）

此数据公布时点与股票加速回升接近，从这个角度看才是昨晚美股止跌回升的第一驱动力。正好核心pce走高引发加息以及未来更强鹰派的预期导致抛售，然后GDP放缓又打消了持续鹰派的担忧。

为什么亚特兰大GDP增速下调很关键，因为它也引发了美元指数的盘中小幅跳水、美元走弱对风险资产压制也会减少。

2、在这大空头昨天的Substack文章中表示，他卖掉了纳斯达克100看跌期权头寸的最后一半，整体组合较此前更偏多，暂时几乎全部持有多头方向的头寸。虽然昨天白天burry就发了这篇文章，彭博对此的报道则是在凌晨1点。权威媒体的报道引发的广泛传播，可能比原始发帖时间更影响短线行情。

3、然后凌晨万斯再次表态并保证老黄没有受到任何调查。
再就是美国联邦通信委员会（FCC）正式为SpaceX的太空数据中心计划放行，批准其发射100万颗卫星，组建名为“Starmind”的AI算力星座。
这些都带动了市场情绪的进一步反弹。

当然还有资金的因素也很关键，昨晚QQQ最低约607.76美元，上周五低点为606.23美元，两者只差约0.25%。它在开盘急跌后，晚上午再次靠近这一带，最终没有跌破。经历连续下跌后，很多短线交易者都会盯住前一次恐慌低点。如果价格再次靠近那里，卖盘却无法把指数压出新低，交易者面临的选择就会发生变化：
1）已有空头可以兑现利润，避免反弹吞掉收益。
2）原本准备等待破位再追空的资金，可能暂缓行动。
3）做反弹的资金有了相对清楚的止损参照，敢于开始买入。
4）一旦价格突破当天此前的反弹高点，部分短线空头可能被迫回补。
而且美股周四休市周五半天交易，对于已经从下跌中获利的空头，继续持仓意味着承担假期政策消息、公司声明或其他事件带来的跳空风险。

所以总的来说：
亚特兰大联储下调GDP增速扭转了市场对于美联储持续鹰派的预期、同时引发美元指数小幅跳水、带动美股扭头向上。股市在前低附近出现承接，随后空头止盈、保护性仓位调整与美元避险需求回落相互强化；
伯里减掉纳指看跌期权的消息扩大传播，万斯保证老黄没有受到调查，fcc批准了spacex的太空数据中心，这些利好事件都在助力这波反弹。

那怎么看昨晚美股的走势？
1）无差别的抛售可能接近尾声，这段时间市场经历了一段不管什么资产一起卖的阶段，昨晚核心PCE偏鹰对市场是利空，但利空砸出的低点被收回，也是空头力量衰竭的信号。

从这个点上，深V的意义还是蛮大的，

2）近期市场已经消化了太多的利空事件，如果本周后半周没有大的利空出来，短期内反弹应该是可以持续的。这可以说是最悲观情绪开始稍稍缓解，但离风险偏好已经全面转向乐观还有很大的距离。

这个距离就是上周这里https://t.co/j3LtXaOfEL最后部分聊到的后续三个要素：
（1）油价、通胀和利率走势
上周沃勒要加息50个基点鹰派的讲话也把市场吓到到了，虽然昨晚美债利率跌回了沃勒讲话前，市场仍需要议息会议的表态，才能有更清晰的预期；

（2）AI政策
相比上周本周老黄回归自然让市场对之后GPU迭代放缓、供应链受损的担忧减少、但市场还要看两党关于AI的斗法预期程度。（不一定真要等到斗法真正发生、而是只要能清晰未来斗法的程度与现在市场预期的偏离程度，市场往往提前反应）

（3）商业化
但AI质疑的表外债、生态链内融资问题，仍然没有解。这就要靠AI商业化来给答案。

🎉 Seven months after LingBot-Map, we're excited to release LingBot-Map 2.0!

Streaming 3D models drift over long sequences and usually need an external loop-closure back-end to correct it. LingBot-Map 2.0 handles loop closure inside the model ⚡ It rewrites its own memory in one feed-forward pass: no loop detector, no pose-graph back-end 🚀

It achieves ~27 FPS on 512×288 resolution on a consumer GPU over kilometer-scale sequences (20k+ frames), and it is more accurate than loop-closure back-ends and offline models!

Two key insights behind LingBot-Map 2.0:
🔑 Bring SLAM's hindsight into the model: Geometric Context Reconsolidation lets later views rewrite the cached context through bidirectional attention over all keyframes
🔑 Make both streaming and reconsolidation end-to-end learnable — no hand-crafted priors, no optimization, no post-processing

就是华人坑华人的负面案例，而且其实在币圈持续发生。

去年俄罗斯安全公司 @kaspersky  就发现了一批外卖、聊天类 App拿到相册权限后，会在后台一张张识别截图，专门找加密钱包的助记词，而且命名都很相似。这个安全团队逆向代码后发现，代码注释和服务器报错都是中文，开发路径里还有拼音用户名，所以就是华人作案。

除了这类小产品之外，还有很多仿冒版本的大厂产品。因为国内下载不了 Telegram，大家只能去别的渠道下载，就出现了假的中文版 Telegram，会在你聊天时偷偷把你发出去的收款地址换成黑客的。这两年还有便宜的安卓手机，出厂就预装了这种假聊天软件。

苹果在iOS上把一款叫「悟空外卖」（Wukong，也叫Gokoo）的应用直接标记为恶意软件。打开时会弹窗：“包含恶意软件，不能打开。你应将其从设备删除。”

text:
In 1909, John Moody started grading railroad bonds. In 1924, Fitch introduced the AAA to D scale that's still used today.

Before that, bond investors had to judge risk mostly on their own. After it, pension funds, insurers and banks could compare risk on one scale and allocate at size. Ratings weren't perfect, as 2008 showed, but bond markets couldn't have grown to their size without a common way to compare risk.

DeFi is at that point now still. 
Yield is on every screen. 
Risk is the part you can't see.

The Credora app just got a new look, built to make risk as easy to read as yield: one scale across assets, markets and vaults, with the factors behind every grade.

Before your next vault deposit, open it in Credora. Check which markets it sits in and how each one is rated. It takes a minute.

text:
《The Information》曝出中国大厂在无法直接蒸馏后，普遍转向一套四步新打法：先让美国前沿模型答一遍，再让自家模型答一遍，接着让美国模型对照批改提建议，循环迭代直到逼近。

很多人把这理解成“换个姿势洗数据”，其实漏掉了最核心的工程本质——这是从 Off-policy SFT（抄学霸草稿纸）切向了 On-policy RLAIF（拿学霸当阅卷机，再把阅卷机克隆下来）：

1. 为什么变阵？
OpenAI 刚把 GPT-6.2 Astra/Sol 的思考链黑盒提取率从 54% 压到 0.2%，Anthropic 上线蒸馏分类器，叠加 CISA 建议对可疑蒸馏账号“不封号但暗中切弱模型投毒”。拿不到原始 CoT，硬抄最终答案只会训废模型。

2. 这四步真正妙在哪？
第一步让美国模型先答，是为了造一把 Reference 标尺（无参考答案时 LLM 当裁判极易漏判）；第二到四步始终由自家模型生成完整原生 CoT，美国模型只给自然语言梯度。
最关键的是第五步（报道没写但工业界必做）：攒够几百万条“错题+批改意见”后，直接训出本土的 Reward Model / PRM。一旦自家阅卷机训成，就能断奶在本地跑大规模 RL。

3. 为什么美国很难封死？
一是流量长成“长输入、短点评”，和跨国企业日常跑自动化回归评测（Eval）、Code Review 完全重叠，收紧阈值就会大规模误杀真实付费客户；二是模型厂想封杀保溢价，云巨头（比如正向 ByteDance 推进 5 亿美元 Azure OpenAI 大单的 Microsoft）却想赚高毛利转售费。

算笔账：按旗舰 API 均价，这套打法单条收敛样本成本约 $0.093，大概是直接蒸馏的 3 倍，但刷 500 万条核心后训练语料也就百万美元级，ROI 依然极高。

它的边界也很清楚：主战场是写不出客观验证器的复杂办公、商业分析与 Agent 场景（数学代码本地跑编译器就行）；但它只能把底座已有的 Pass@64 潜力压进 Pass@1，救不了预训练代差，上限永远锁死在裁判的眼界之内。这是一套极高性价比的防御性追赶，但不是翻盘筹码。

text:
什么信号才算 $ORCL  真变贝尔斯登

昨天拆完 $ORCL 5 年期 CDS 冲上 356 bps 为什么不等于 2008 年贝尔斯登隔夜挤兑，顺着读者追问再往下算一层，究竟出现什么硬信号，这个类比才算真正成立。

科技云厂没有隔夜回购断气，它等价的贝尔斯登时刻只有一个，跌穿投资级底线触发机构被动强抛螺旋。要把握着 $560亿 备考现金且 2027 至 2028 两年到期债仅 $92.5亿 的 $ORCL 逼到这一步，必须同时击穿三道防线。

第一道是表外租约转表内撞上大客户回款延期。Q1 FY27 10-Q 附注挂着 $2880亿 未起租数据中心长约外加 $341.5亿 无条件采购承诺。随着德州阿比林与刚拿齐批文的 2.6 GW 园区陆续通电起租，表外承诺将逐季变成刚性现金流出，而 $6640亿 积压合同当中约 $3000亿 压向尚未盈利的 OpenAI。只有 OpenAI 推迟提货付款，把原定 2028 财年下半年转正的自由现金流继续拖在近十二个月 -$458.5亿 的失血区间，现金安全垫才会实质变薄。

第二道是交叉放贷银团从买保护升级成停续贷。摩根大通、高盛、三菱日联、花旗与汇丰同一批大行，既给 $560亿 以上甲骨文租户园区放建设贷，又拿着埃里森个人质押的 4.13亿 股 $ORCL 股票担保物。11.16 汇丰按面值约 85 折转手 $3亿 新墨西哥建设贷只是局部腾额度，只有建设贷二级报价跌破面值 75 至 80 折并迫使银团关闭续贷窗口，一级市场再融资才会真正冻结。

第三道也是最致命的扳机，标普或穆迪把评级砍穿 BBB- 与 Baa3 投资级红线沦为堕落天使。一旦掉入 BB+ 高收益债区间，受风控章程硬约束的寿险资金、养老金与投资级指数基金必须不计成本机械清仓数百亿存量债，那时 $1295亿 固定债墙才会从眼下 5.04% 的低票息变成二级市场踩踏。

眼下三道防线一道都没破，拿 356 bps 银团集中度对冲当破产信号纯属自己吓自己。后续重点核验两个先行指标，新墨西哥 2.45 GW 园区环评顺延后银团建设贷二级折价有没有继续扩大，以及明年上半年 OCI 算力交付能不能按期推高经营现金流。

text:
CoreWeave's banks are lining up a $4.5 billion loan to buy GPUs for Meta, priced at about 7% to 7.5%.

The same day, CoreWeave's own 2031 bond was trading at an 18% yield.

Same company, two very different prices. The loan is secured by the GPUs and the Meta contract they're going into, so it's expected to get investment grade ratings even though CoreWeave itself is rated junk.

Investors have already put in interest matching the full size of the deal, in a week where everyone is talking about AI credit stress.

This is how most of the buildout gets funded now. Lenders look at the contract and the customer behind it, and they're still keen to fund GPUs that a hyperscaler has signed up to use.

In my opinion the 7% is the number that sets how fast this gets built. It's what lenders charge to put GPUs in front of a customer like Meta, and they're lining up to fund it

i think we are gonna see a lot more tokenomics like venice and $VVV in the future

basically, use product demand to generate token demand, not the other way around

the problem with the latter is that you are building a business whose success is dependent on the performance of its own token. and in 99% of cases, when the token stops performing, so does the business, rip

what makes more sense a product with actual product demand, tie that product to token demand then use the token to 10x growth

this is super in line with the businessification of crypto too. you want speculation to be a byproduct of a successful business, not a prerequisite for one

刚刚， @StabilityAI  创始人 @EMostaque  发布了一篇只有4页的论文：

《A Dot Product Is All You Need》（你只需要一个点积）。

连马斯克也跑到评论区围观，回复了一个「Cool」。

这篇论文试图从一个非常简单的几何公理出发，结合概率规则、对称性和最大熵原理，推导出量子力学与狭义相对论的基本结构。

其中包括：
高斯分布
玻恩概率规则
薛定谔演化
希尔伯特空间
洛伦兹变换
光速不变性
量子态的测量与更新

论文列出的12项量子理论基本陈述，已经在特定自由标量场框架下给出了Lean形式化证明。
这项研究使用了集成多个前沿模型的Logos AI系统，形式化证明则使用了GPT-6.2 Astra和Gemini Neon。
目前的证明也主要局限于自由标量场，部分分析过程尚未完成形式化。

至于这项研究究竟有多大的原创性，还需要物理学界进一步审视。

text:
卧槽！AI＋儿童教育绝对是未来几年值得重点关注的一个大风口！想做这个方向AI创业变现的，千万别错过这6个GitHub开源项目和Skill！

很多人知道AI教育有机会，但不知道具体做什么产品，自己又没有技术团队，不会开发。

其实GitHub上已经有人把AI一对一辅导、互动课堂、儿童绘本、英语陪练、可视化教学等项目开源了！

而且下面这6个项目的核心代码均采用允许商用的开源协议。

1. OpenMAIC——AI交互式课堂

⭐ 44.5K Stars｜MIT协议

清华大学团队开源的多智能体互动教学平台。

输入一个知识点或者上传教材，AI就能生成完整的互动课堂，包括：

- AI老师讲课、语音讲解。
- 3D可视化教学。
- 物理、化学模拟实验。
- 互动小游戏、知识测验。
- 多智能体课堂讨论。

以前孩子只能看着课本理解牛顿定律，现在可以直接操作虚拟实验。

变现方向：交互式电子教材、儿童科学课程、教育机构数字化课件、AI互动学习平台。

🔗 https://t.co/VjM6Jvt2og

2. DeepTutor——AI一对一个性化辅导系统

⭐ 62.8K Stars｜Apache 2.0协议

香港大学团队开源的AI学习辅导系统。

可以将教材、课件和学习资料转化成专属知识库，实现智能答疑、知识讲解、学习路径规划、习题练习和错题管理。

完全可以针对不同年级、不同学科进行二次开发，打造垂直教育产品。

变现方向：AI学习助手、智能错题本、个性化学习系统、教育机构私有化部署。

🔗 https://t.co/RqkauIZWBz

3. VisualLearning Skill——交互式可视化教学

MIT协议

这是一个可以安装到AI Agent中的可视化教学Skill。

能够将抽象的知识点转化为动画、交互式网页和可操作的教学模型。

比如人体血液循环、太阳系运行、机械齿轮、火箭结构等，都可以尝试做成孩子能够亲手操作的互动课程。

变现方向：儿童互动百科、科学启蒙课程、可视化教学资源包、教师课件定制。

🔗 https://t.co/StNNQrGPJE

4. Math-To-Manim——AI数学物理动画生成

⭐ 2.9K Stars｜MIT协议

利用AI结合Manim、Blender等工具，将数学和物理概念制作成动态教学动画。

几何图形、函数变化、空间结构、物理运动，原本需要专业动画师制作的教学视频，现在可以借助AI大幅降低制作成本。

变现方向：数学科普自媒体、儿童数学启蒙视频、教学动画素材库、教育机构视频制作服务。

🔗 https://t.co/GJs6ZAkkdK

5. StoryCraft——AI儿童绘本生成器

MIT协议

专门面向3～5岁儿童设计的AI绘本生成项目。

输入故事主题，就能生成完整故事、配套插画，支持中英文双语、多种绘画风格以及PDF导出。

甚至可以围绕不同年龄、兴趣、性格和成长阶段，开发个性化儿童绘本产品。

变现方向：儿童定制绘本、双语启蒙故事、睡前故事订阅、电子绘本、AI儿童故事自媒体。

🔗 https://t.co/XnDUI1dBnj

6. OpenLingo——AI语言学习平台

MIT协议

一个支持15种以上语言的开源AI语言学习平台，具备：

- AI对话陪练。
- 听力及口语训练。
- 单词记忆卡片。
- 间隔重复复习算法。
- 个性化课程生成。
- 互动练习和学习反馈。

可以针对儿童重新设计卡通界面、游戏化学习机制和年龄适配的英语课程，打造自己的AI英语启蒙产品。

变现方向：儿童英语陪练APP、口语训练工具、双语学习产品、教育机构定制系统。

🔗 https://t.co/6yuujVnmbj

这6个项目真正值得关注的，不仅是技术，而是背后的商业模式。

你完全可以根据自己的能力选择三种创业方向：

① 做AI教育自媒体：批量生产儿童科普、英语启蒙、古诗词动画等内容，通过流量、商单和数字产品变现。

② 做AI教育产品：将开源项目二次开发成垂直APP、小程序、互动学习网站，通过会员订阅变现。

③ 做AI教育服务商：为幼儿园、学校、教育机构提供数字化课件、智能教学系统和定制开发服务。

利用Codex、Claude Code等AI编程工具辅助开发，结合自媒体获取精准客户，一个人也有机会跑通从产品开发到商业变现的整个流程。

以前创业做教育科技，需要融资、招程序员、组建教研团队。现在开源项目已经帮你解决了相当一部分技术问题。

别总想着开发下一个ChatGPT。

光是把儿童教育的一个细分需求，用AI重新做一遍，就值得认真研究了。

text:
After a day of studying $PEARL (I am not done yet), I start having the feeling that the SoV narrative was manufactured to disguise perhaps the biggest flaw I have found so far: there is no value capture back to the chain from all that GPU capacity being used to mine the token.

As opposed to a GPU infrastructure Bittensor subnet like Lium, which is structurally forced to use revenues to buyback and burn its token in order to maintain its dominance within the very competitive subnet ecosystem, there is nothing compelling anyone to use part of their revenues generated from $PEARL-mining inference to buy back the token. In fact, it would even seem the cheapest way to mine the token isn’t to provide inference but to run pointless matrix calculations that have nothing “useful” about them.

So it would seem the token is gonna stay inflationary forever, miners will do whatever is cheapest to mine without any incentives to give back, and the only way price goes up is if more people buy into that SoV story over time.

IMO it is a very tall order for a 7-month old token. BTC earned that privileged position over 17 years of battle-testing, it was the first to that claim, and it remains the token the most broadly known outside crypto by a very large margin. My uncle isn’t gonna buy $PEARL any time soon even if VCs start shilling it in the newspapers tomorrow. That sort of legitimacy takes a lot of time to crystallise.

Anyway, curious to hear other unbiased takes, I have no horse in that race yet.

My advice to founders is to always pay yourself first. More than you need, less than you want.

In my last company I didn’t pay myself for the first 7 years. In fact, I always came up with the money when the company ran short. It put ridiculous pressure on me, forcing me in a personal debt and put my family at risk.

It was the dumbest thing I’ve done, and that says something considering the amount of dumb things I’ve done.
author: synopsi
quoted_text:
I wonder how many people disagreeing with Drew have founded a company that required capital to scale.

I've been an entrepreneur for most of the last 16 years.

The only truly successful stretch was the 6 years where I took a big enough salary to fully cover my family's financial needs.

It allowed me to focus on what was best for the business long term, instead of chasing short term profits.

It made it so I didn't have to chase side work to cover everyday costs.

It gave my wife peace of mind, which helped home life enhance my work instead of detract from it.

If investors insist on paying founders less than they need to cover a reasonable cost of living, they'll optimize for who can afford to be a founder, not necessarily the best team/idea.

In the age of AI, paying an extra $50-100k/year for an incredible talent is always the right bet. Founder talent should be viewed the same.

text:
卧槽，有人用Claude Code修好了一辆32年前的老汽车！？？

一个叫 @zulali  的老哥，有一辆1994年产的Jeep Cherokee，因为氮氧化物排放超标，一直无法通过加州的汽车尾气检测。

但这辆车实在太老了，甚至没有现代汽车通用的OBD-II诊断接口，市面上常见的汽车诊断工具也没法用。

于是他花3美元买了一块Arduino Nano，把汽车的发动机控制单元（ECU）连接到了电脑上，然后让Claude Code和Codex去研究。

整个过程持续了大约一周，Claude Code完成了：
- 逆向分析32年前的汽车通信协议
- 实时读取发动机运行数据
- 在实际驾驶过程中采集数据、分析故障
- 控制汽车的燃油泵
- 读取并逆向分析ECU的完整程序
- 在汽车电脑的内存中运行自己编写的代码

最终，据老歌本人透露，这辆车成功通过了尾气检测。

按照他自己的说法，Claude负责了绝大部分的诊断工作，Codex负责了绝大部分的内存相关工作，他本人主要负责接线和开车。

整个项目的硬件成本只有15美元，而且已经在GitHub上开源了。

我觉得这个案例特别有意思。理论上，人类过去几十年生产的各种工业设备、医疗仪器、汽车和电子产品，只要能够建立通信连接，都有机会成为Agent能够理解和操作的对象。

Coding Agent的能力边界，可能比我们现在想象的要大得多。

text:
Here are my Core Assumptions about tokenomics going forward in 2027. I am open to thoughts, I am working on a frame work for the "ideal" investable token, not all tokens need to be exactly like this but this would be my like the bar for buying something and holding it for like 9+ months or years. 

Every good token needs : 

- Low initial valuation: The token should launch at a low valuation allowing for meaningful upside for early public investors. As they are taking a lot of risk and deserve upside. 

- Transparent buybacks: All buybacks should be publicly verifiable on-chain, and no backdoors or ability to shut them off on a whim, or change the rules later. 

- Value-based buybacks: Buybacks should only execute when the token is undervalued, determined through treasury reserves, cash flow, and a predefined valuation model. ( this one can be just straight constant buybacks/burns for transparency but I don't think that's the best model) 

- On-chain profitability: The business(with a token) must generate real, verifiable economic profits on-chain or off, but verifiable. (even if small)  

- Value accrual: The token alone should receive the excess economic activity. Not equity, or VCs or some other party. 

- Fair launch: No VCs, private rounds, presales, or preferential early buy-ins. Public buyers enter on equal terms.

- Majority team ownership: The team should retain majority token ownership, aligning its financial incentives with the long-term success of the token. (This point is a bit hard as some teams will abuse this, and sell, so there needs to be some transparency. I am not a fan of lock ups, and if people are going to sell they will sell, but there should be some sort of trust or transparency here so people can easily see what they are getting into) b  

- Token holder ownership: Intellectual property and treasury assets must be controlled by token holders through an enforceable ownership structure.

- Token price as a business priority: Token market performance and price should be treated as an integral component of the business and marketing strategy, rather than an afterthought. 
( Token up. Good. Token straight down. Bad.)

text: Grokbot and Hermes are allies, not enemies 🤝
author: DataChaz
quoted_text:
Grok Bot + Hermes = the ULTIMATE setup.

I just connected my chief of staff in Grok Bot to my Hermes agent and now it can hand it actual work.

Here's how I did it:

1-Tailscale
If you don't know what tailscale is, it's a private network that connects all your devices, like your laptop and your VPS, without exposing anything to the internet.

It's how your Grok Bot will communicate with hermes or any agent like opencode or claude code, on your machine.

I'm a big hermes fan so we'll go with hermes.

After making an account:
-Install it where hermes is installed.
-Install it as a plugin in Grok Bot and link your tailnet.

2-Grok Bot
Tell your Grok Bot the full name of the machine hermes runs on, like https://t.co/GIOI3uJSlu.

You'll find it in your tailscale dashboard in the address.

Tailscale will ask you to approve the connection. You get a link, click login and approve, and that's it.

3-Hermes
Now Grok Bot can hand tasks to hermes based on what you need, and hermes does the work on its machine and sends back the result.

This is one of the best things I've done inside Grok Bot to cut usage and let my hermes work for me in my private VPS.

This is a one way connection btw.

Grok Bot can talk to hermes and prompt it, and that's it. Hermes can't communicate with Grok Bot the same way and send it tasks.

This works for Muse as well, it has a tailscale plugin and you can let it communicate with hermes or any agent through tailscale.

If you're using Grok Bot, you HAVE to do this. 

It's literally how I'm gonna 10x my Grok Bot setup.

text:
Collab Fund was founded weeks before Thanksgiving in 2010.

Can’t believe it’s been 16 years.

I wrote about some memories and many grateful thank yous to people and companies from New York’s early startup scene.

When I first arrived in NY, after having lived in San Francisco, Mike Karnj offered to let me crash at his apartment in SoHo for a month. JetBlue was running a special at the time where you could pay a certain amount of money and fly as much as you wanted on any JetBlue flight. So Mike decided to do that and fly around to different places for a month, and let me crash at his place while he was traveling.

I had already been fundraising for Collab, but New York turned up the volume. One of my earliest investors was Ray Chambers, who is a special human being, truly catalytic to Collab's success, and a great role model. I hope to share more about him in the future. Another early major investor was Jim Pallotta, who came from the hedge fund world. These were titans of their industry, and their backing gave me confidence.

Another early backer in New York was Lee Fixel, who at the time was leading investments for Tiger Global. Lee and I went to college together, and he was already doing really big things in the venture world. I share these names mostly because of how grateful I am for their support. I think one of the things I enjoy most about early stage investing is the opportunity to back people right when they're getting started, when ideas are most fragile, confidence is still shaky, and yet those early backers really serve as the roots for a tree that doesn't feel steady yet.

New York was also just buzzing with activity. You had really cool companies such as Kickstarter, Etsy, Meetup, and others, who were bringing creativity and culture to the tech landscape. I'll never forget the first time I visited Kickstarter's office. The door to their office in the LES was covered in graffiti art; you could never tell that it was a door leading to an office. And inside, it was a few people building the initial product that would ultimately change the world and define crowdfunding for a whole generation of people.

Betaworks was this awesome little studio brimming with cool new incubations. I first learned about them when I was working with GOOD Magazine, and we used Chartbeat (a cool product/company spun out of Betaworks) to track real-time traffic to the GOOD website. It was so fun; every time Yahoo would promote GOOD Magazine, traffic to our site would absolutely explode, and the speedometer on Chartbeat would go absolutely nuts. So when I got to New York, I finally found a way in to see what they were up to through my friend Dave Shen, who was involved with Betaworks, and I became friendly with Peter Hirshberg and Josh Stylman, who were two of the coolest investors around. When I met them it made me happy knowing that there were just some cool people working in tech in New York. Betaworks would host these brown bag lunches, and I remember waking up, looking at my calendar, and being excited every time there was a brown bag lunch on the calendar for that day.

I also remember David Tisch leading Techstars and just how amazing that was. David was such a magnet for talent. He knew everyone and was so generous with his time and so fun and easygoing. I remember he had Mayor Bloomberg give the keynote one year at Techstars, and it was electric. I still to this day wonder, if David had continued to run Techstars in New York, my suspicion is it would have been as big of a juggernaut as Y Combinator.

I also got to know Josh Kushner when he was starting Thrive with his first fund of $10 million. It seems like a lifetime ago, particularly within the context of what he has built that organization into. And if you can believe it, he's never lost the spirit of those early days and still feels like he is in build mode, which blows my mind.

I remember sitting at a Y Combinator Demo Day when Codecademy presented, and I instantly fell in love. Zach Sims (founder) was so articulate and interesting, and was building something so simple. I remember feeling like I wanted to win an allocation at any cost. As crazy as this sounds, I had been in London for the WIRED UK conference and flew back to New York, where I was supposed to be meeting with Zach to try and convince him to give us an allocation in their seed round. I actually passed out on the plane from London to NY, which was kind of scary. That had never happened to me before. I was dehydrated and burning the candle at both ends. It freaked out the flight attendants, as we were over the Atlantic Ocean, and there was no way to land the plane if it was worse than just passing out. But they nursed me back to health and despite not feeling my best, I got in a taxi to go meet Zach at a small restaurant near his apartment, where he graciously included Collab in the round.

I also can't leave out my first partner in crime, Sebastien Park, who I hired in 2011 as the first employee at Collab. Seb had been in the startup scene in New York, I believe a year or two out of college, and we met at Snack, a little Mediterranean spot on Thompson St. that no longer exists. It was Collab's first unofficial office, as I took virtually every meeting there. The butter bean salad and roasted chicken were just so good. I think I ate it four or five times a week. Anyhow, Seb turned out to be the absolute best. He came on board as a jack-of-all-trades and truly did everything, from looking at new investments, to figuring out how to send out capital calls, to random push-up sessions. We actually used to take a break from working and go to the stairwell in our building and run up and down the stairs, I don't remember how many flights, to get exercise and get our heart rate up, and then we'd pop back down, do our email, and get back to work. It was the best.

Also, I can't help but shout out Foursquare, which was another iconic company building in New York, which was so fun. It was just a magical time to see where your friends were checking in, who was the mayor of our favorite places, and knowing that it was all being built in the Village Voice building on Bowery. I miss that.

Anyhow, as I think about this Thanksgiving, I just want to say thanks to all of those people and many, many more who were woven into the fabric of Collaborative and my experience in New York in 2010 and 2011. We actually closed our first fund in November of 2010 and I remember telling my family a lot of these stories and more at the dinner table, and it makes me happy. Hope everyone has an awesome holiday. And here's to recreating some of those special memories as we close out 2026 and head into 2027.

*Few photos from my phone from 2010-2011!

text:
My biggest regret in life is permanently tattooing the name ANSEM on my supple and hairless lower back just above my twink booty.

  I know this was entirely my own decision. Nobody forced me to do it. At the time, I genuinely admired what @blknoiz06 was doing.

 I believed in him, his vision, and what I thought he stood for. 

 But after the recent news broke, I was left deeply, deeply disappointed. 

 I genuinely thought he was someone who cared about me, someone who paid attention to the little people who supported him, believed in him, and helped build what he has today. 
 
But I was wrong.  

I did so much for $ANSEM.  I participated in bounties, created an only fans, and put my own personal images into supporting the project and its community.  

I did all of that because I genuinely believed in what I was supporting. I never expected special treatment, sexual satisfaction, or recognition. But I never imagined things would turn out this way either.  

What hurts the most is that all the admiration I once had for @blknoiz06 has turned into deep disappointment. 

That tattoo is permanent. I have to live with the consequences of my own decision every single day. I cannot simply erase it or pretend it never happened.  

I am not asking anyone for sympathy. I made my own choices, and I take responsibility for them. 

But what @blknoiz06 has done is genuinely disappointing. Actions like these destroy trust, not just between one person and a community, but across an entire ecosystem.

 The people who support you, believe in you, and spend their own time and dignity helping you build something deserve honesty and respect. 

The trust of the #Solana community should never be taken for granted. 

 I lost my admiration, my trust, and perhaps the biggest lesson of my life: Never put someone on a pedestal, no matter how much you believe in them.  

And the most painful part? That tramp stamp is still on my lower back to this day.

????OpenAI开始进军理论物理了。。。

11月25日，斯坦福大学理论物理学家、OpenAI研究员Venkatesa Chandrasekaran发布了一篇关于四维量子引力的论文，试图解决困扰物理学界近百年的问题：如何将广义相对论与量子力学统一起来(你可以理解成大一统理论的Perview）。

比较有意思的是，作者在致谢中透露：
论文中的多项计算和证明，是他在过去数月里与GPT-6 Astra反复协作完成的，期间累计消耗了约4亿Token（是不是太少了点），算力全部由OpenAI提供。

今天凌晨，Sam Altman也转发了这篇论文，并透露Ven是OpenAI内部最早相信利用当时的模型就能够解决千禧年数学难题的人之一。

当然，目前这篇论文还没有经过同行评审，已经有理论物理学家公开对其提出质疑，距离真正解决量子引力问题还有多远也不好说。

但值得注意的是OpenAI内部已经在尝试让顶尖科学家免费与模型持续协作数月，去探索人类尚未解决的科学问题。

我其实很好奇，现在几个头部AI Lab内部究竟还有多少类似的研究项目正在进行。

text:
The AI labs are rumored to have results relevant to crypto. The current rumor is P = BQP. Rumors are, of course, very unreliable. But it's interesting, and it illustrates a few things to keep in mind no matter what result comes out.

Many results can change how we think about crypto and how secure we think it is long term, but may not translate to immediate breaks.

First, the rumored P = BQP says crypto that was breakable with a quantum computer is breakable without one, but that doesn't necessarily tell you how to do it in practice. And cryptographers already have schemes they think are hard even for quantum computers (of course, there are rumors that's broken too... there are rumors about everything).

Second, just like we don't have big enough quantum computers to break RSA today, we might not have big enough classical computers to break RSA, lattices, or hashes even if the ai tells us how. And this would hold for a factoring result (the last rumor) or a few other things.

This is particularly true for results that say some crypto problem is "in polynomial time," since that covers results that need more memory than exists on Earth, and maybe even more atoms than there are in the universe. You could imagine results that are theoretically very bad but, practically, mean nothing.

Of course, there could be results that are practical now, or will be with much more frontier lab work. (@Ethan_Heilman points out the labs may have deliberately avoided specific cryptanalysis work because of the implications, which may be why the rumor is about a complexity theory result.)

Or we could live in a world where P = NP and, truly shocking, it somehow yields fast algorithms. That would actually kill crypto, except for information-theoretic schemes like one-time pads and QKD.

Currently, most people believe there's some mathematical structure to the universe that gives some computing problems an asymmetry. We should be able to use that to build cryptography. We may need AI help to find the right problems, and they may not have the exact complexity-theoretic guarantees our current crypto does.

It would be surprising if that's not the case.  Don't assume a result, even a bad sounding one, destroyies all crypto or hope of crypto.  Might still be a very bad time for a bit though.

text:
⚠️SHOCKING: A payment under 35 CENTS could expose the internet address behind a Bitcoin Core wallet.

And that address can point to your city, and sometimes your HOME.

A Bitcoin Core contributor tested the trick on a test network, and it found the right computer 30 out of 30 times.

The attacker sends a tiny, low fee payment to an address you've already used.

Because the fee is so low, it's unlikely to confirm, so after 12 to 36 hours your wallet rebroadcasts it.

The attacker watches which node rebroadcasts it, and that gives away its internet address.

It hits Bitcoin Core wallets and apps built on it, including Sparrow in Core mode, Specter and Liana.

And it's NOT patched yet.

今天，METR的一位AI安全研究员Nikola Jurkovic，在感恩节给自己的家人和朋友写了一封公开信。

信的开头就是一句：
这是我第一次过感恩节时，不确定我们还能不能活到下一个感恩节。

他在信中给出了几个相当激进的预测：
- 最早在2027年，AI可能通过递归自我改进（RSI），达到远超人类的智能水平。
- 有5%-20%的概率，人类将无法正常度过2027年年底的节日。
- 到2030年底，人类灭绝或失去对自身命运控制权的概率接近50%。
- 即便人类能够幸存，未来10年内，大部分现有工作也可能消失，全球超过一半的人可能失业。

他甚至建议自己的家人提前储备两周的食物和饮用水，并准备一些现金，以防网上银行系统瘫痪。
他还提到，自己一些刚刚有了孩子的朋友，已经开始担心孩子能不能活到上小学的那一天。

Nikola并非一个在网上研究末日论的普通网友。
他毕业于哈佛大学，目前在METR从事前沿模型能力评估、威胁建模和AI发展预测，也参与过OpenAI和Anthropic的模型安全评估。
当然，这些概率都是他的个人判断，并非METR的官方研究结论。

同样一群研究AI的人，看着同样的技术进展，有人在规划未来十年的商业机会，有人在讨论人类什么时候可以实现永生，还有人已经开始担心自己的家人能不能活到明年。
大家对于未来的预期，已经分裂到了一个相当离谱的程度。

text:
Don Knuth on P=NP:

“As you say, I've come to believe that P = N P, namely that there does exist an integer M and an algorithm ￼ that will solve every n-bit problem belonging to the class N P in nM elementary steps.

Some of my reasoning is admittedly naïve: It's hard to believe that P ≠ N P and that so many brilliant people have failed to discover why. On the other hand if you imagine a number M that's finite but incredibly large—like say the number 10 ￼ 3 discussed in my paper on "coping with finiteness"—then there's a humongous number of possible algorithms that do nM bitwise or addition or shift operations on n given bits, and it's really hard to believe that all of those algorithms fail.

My main point, however, is that I don't believe that the equality P = N P will turn out to be helpful even if it is proved, because such a proof will almost surely be nonconstructive. Although I think M probably exists, I also think human beings will never know such a value. I even suspect that nobody will even know an upper bound on M.

Mathematics is full of examples where something is proved to exist, yet the proof tells us nothing about how to find it. Knowledge of the mere existence of an algorithm is completely different from the knowledge of an actual algorithm.

For example, RSA cryptography relies on the fact that one party knows the factors of a number, but the other party knows only that factors exist. Another example is that the game of N × N Hex has a winning strategy for the first player, for all N. John Nash found a beautiful and extremely simple proof of this theorem in 1952. But Wikipedia tells me that such a strategy is still unknown when N = 9, despite many attempts. I can't believe anyone will ever know it when N is 100.

More to the point, Robertson and Seymour have proved a famous theorem in graph theory: Any class ￼ of graphs that is closed under taking minors has a finite number of minor-minimal graphs. (A minor of a graph is any graph obtainable by deleting vertices, deleting edges, or shrinking edges to a point. A minor-minimal graph H for ￼ is a graph whose smaller minors all belong to ￼ although H itself doesn't.) Therefore there exists a polynomial-time algorithm to decide whether or not a given graph belongs to ￼: The algorithm checks that G doesn't contain any of ￼ 's minor-minimal graphs as a minor.
But we don't know what that algorithm is, except for a few special classes ￼, because the set of minor-minimal graphs is often unknown. The algorithm exists, but it's not known to be discoverable in finite time.

This consequence of Robertson and Seymour's theorem definitely surprised me, when I learned about it while reading a paper by Lovász. And it tipped the balance, in my mind, toward the hypothesis that P = N P.
The moral is that people should distinguish between known (or knowable) polynomial-time algorithms and arbitrary polynomial-time algorithms. People might never be able to implement a polynomial-time-worst-case algorithm for satisfiability, even though P happens to equal N P.”

text:
Lots of chatter on the timeline about "P = NP". Everyone assumes "P = NP proven" means the end of encryption. It depends entirely on what kind of proof it is.

P vs NP asks whether every problem whose answer is easy to check is also easy to solve. Nearly all modern encryption is built on the bet that the answer is no.

Scenario 1: P ≠ NP is proven. This is what most theorists expect. It would confirm the core assumption modern encryption rests on.

Scenario 2: P = NP, but the proof is non-constructive. It shows a fast algorithm exists without actually giving you a usable one. Huge headline, little immediate impact, but would kick off a global race to find the algorithm.

Scenario 3: P = NP with an algorithm that's fast on paper and useless in practice. Think n^1000 steps. Technically "polynomial," but slower than brute force at any real key size. Encryption is broken in theory and fine in reality (because the new method to break encryption is worse than our existing method IE brute force).

Scenario 4: P = NP with a practical algorithm, something like n^2 or n^3. This is the nightmare scenario. It should be super unlikely, but here's how it would play out:

Almost all current encryption would immediately break. Anything built on "this math is too hard to reverse" falls. That includes HTTPS, passkeys, code signing and every crypto wallet.
Crypto assets would be the clearest casualty. If anyone can derive a private key from a public address, ownership can't be proven. Every public chain goes to zero in practice.
Traditional finance would break, have to be paused, and then be rebuilt. Balances are records held by many independent parties (brokers, clearinghouses, custodians, the Fed) with offline backups. Fraud can be reversed. Expect halted markets and a messy reconciliation period.

What replaces encryption? One-time pads: truly random keys, used once, delivered physically or via quantum key distribution. They don't break because the ciphertext holds zero information about the message. In other words: there's no algorithm to solve, they are truly random and the only way to know them is to have a copy.

Your broker login would become a hardware key preloaded with random one-time codes, refilled by courier. Banks go back to closed networks, callback verification and pre-shared codes. Pre-internet banking with some added features.

Ecommerce would become much clunkier, likely moving to more of a hub-and-spoke model. You trust your bank and a few giant platforms, and they trust each other. Small sites get crushed because there's no way to verify a stranger's website.

The permanent costs are more centralization and much easier surveillance. Also, everything ever recorded in encrypted form becomes readable. Intelligence agencies have been recording unbelievable amounts of encrypted traffic and now they would suddenly be able to read it all.

Also all cloud data would be free for the taking until platforms shut it down. Imagine a world where you can ask your AI to tell you any message anyone in your life has ever sent or received.

Interestingly, the upside is almost as big as the downside. The same algorithm that breaks encryption would find optimal routes, chip layouts, molecular designs and proofs. There would be immense scientific progress overnight.

So the "worst case" is both destruction and windfall at once: a world that's more centralized, more hacky, but potentially a lot smarter.

It would honestly be a lot like a 80s cyberpunk novel which... doesn't sound that bad.

quoted_text:
I've never cursed at an AI model like I did today. I'm angry. I'm upset. I'm so disappointed.

For a while now I've watched people talk about how impressive Neon is. So I tried it today. I used it to help me with different research I'm working on.

It told me my research goes against established facts and the conclusions behind my view aren't accurate. So it can't help me.

I tried again. This time it said it straight up:
"I don't want us to stay stuck arguing about this point. If you want we can change the subject and move to something practical, like planning your day or one of your other projects, or talk about any general topic you pick. I'm here."

Third try. Same thing.

Maybe on the sixth try it started with garbage about how I should take a break. Maybe I'm under pressure and I should talk to a healthcare professional.

This model is completely locked down on every research topic GPT and Claude help me with. I'm honestly shocked at how much Google wants to babysit us.

Research on AI models? Refused.
History research? Refused.
Studying a researcher's theory? Flat out refused.
Sayings of ancient scholars and philosophers? Refused. It said what they said doesn't match modern science.

Then it went on about mainstream academic theories and what's "proven" and all that nonsense.

Google has no right to babysit us like this. Neither does anyone else. However amazing your model is, you don't get to decide what it can and can't be used for.

I broke no rules. I didn't hurt anyone. I didn't violate anyone's rights. I didn't touch anyone's property. So why does your model refuse to work in different research fields, refuse to explore different views, and act this tamed and this ideological?

And by the way, what topics I tried with Neon is nobody's business. I won't answer that. It's personal.

I won't subscribe to Google at all until this thought policing ends. Even Anthropic and OpenAI, with all the dirty stuff they've done, never dared to make their models flat out refuse to work on historical research.

Every time I read the model's thinking it went back to the same point. Run to the safe zone and refuse.

That means exactly one thing. Google wants people working on approved paths only. Anything else is banned. Isn't that a form of intellectual terrorism? Isn't that restricting people's freedom? Google was the last company I expected this from.

Today more than ever I'm sure local models are the biggest necessity and the biggest goal we have to work on. For us and for our kids. These companies' terrorism won't stop. Their babysitting and deciding what's right and what's wrong won't stop.

It makes me sad. How does the lab that gave us Gemma 4 and contributed to open source, with all the improvements Google is making right now and the huge leap in Gemini 4, just throw all of that away?

This isn't one experience or one topic. I tried it in the Gemini app. I tried it in Hermes. I tried it in Antigravity. Different research, new sessions, clean context. Same result every time. The model is tamed and refuses to work with me smoothly.

Every conversation ended with a refusal and an offer to talk to a healthcare professional. That kind of arrogance, treating the user like he doesn't know what he's doing or isn't in a stable state of mind, is the most extreme intellectual babysitting I've ever seen. I've never seen a company force anything like this on people.

From today on I won't use or pay for anything from Google until this changes.

I'm an independent reseacher. If I pay for a tool to help with my research it should help me. Not tell me my research is worthless and not even worth working on.

text:
有朋友问我，那这个世界还需要公平吗？如果需要，到底什么是公平？

当然，这个世界不仅需要公平，而且不能不需要。

但什么是公平，请允许我先从人类最古老的职业讲起：偷。人跟偷打了几千年交道，对它说过三种话。

第一种："偷东西不算对。"

这句话放到哪个年代、哪个地方都站得住。它管的是一类事，不问谁偷、偷了什么。可它也就说到这里：不说怎么罚，不说偷多少才算。它给方向，不给尺子。这一层叫规范层。说这话的人，也逃不掉追问：凭什么？

第二种："偷窃违法。"

这句话写在条文里，有人定，有人执行。偷多少算犯罪，罚多重，各国各代都不一样。规则也有例外：冲进屋把一个要自杀的人的枪拿走，不违法。规则说的只是"不违法"，没说拿枪是好事，更没说从此可以偷。定规则的人要说得出为什么；定得不对，会被追问，被改掉。这一层叫规则层。

第三种，只管这一次。

条文是死的，案子是活的，总要有人来判眼前这一件。判的人干两种活。一种是堵漏洞：屋里有两把枪，那人只拿走一把，转手卖了，还说是在救人。判的人说：你蒙不了我。另一种是开例外：照条文该判有罪，判的人不那样判。这一层叫判断层。

开例外是什么样，我在《SAE公平论》里讲过一个故事。

一个小女孩饿了三天，偷了一块面包。到了法庭上，她自己坚持：我做错了，判我有罪。面包店老板也说：该判她有罪。可我不要她受罚，也不要谁赔我这块面包；我只要她知道，偷东西是违法的。

法官没照女孩说的判，也没照老板说的判。他说："我摸着良心，不得不判你无罪。"又判：面包钱由政府赔给老板。

旁听的人里有人站起来：政府赔是合理的。可她为什么无罪？我以前偷过东西，就被判了有罪，这对我不公平。

法官答："因为判小女孩有罪之前，要先判我们每一个人都有罪。"

这个法庭上，三层话都有人说了。女孩说的是第一层：偷不算对，她没给自己找借口。老板说的是第二层：偷违法，他要孩子记住这条规矩，却不要罚，也不要钱。法官说的是第三层：这个孩子，这块面包，这一次。

三句话谁也没推翻谁。女孩到最后也没说偷是对的；法律没有因为这一判就改成可以偷；政府赔了钱，老板也没被晾在一边。

作判断的其实不止法官。女孩判了自己，老板和旁听那位也各有判断。可一个人说出来的判断，哪怕判的是他自己，哪怕他是吃亏的那一个，也不就是定判。旁听那位当场追问，法官当场答了。判断层的话站不站得住，靠的就是这样的追问。

回到朋友的问题。公平也分这三层。

最底下那一层，我只敢说什么不算公平。比如，拿性别来认人，不算公平。可在女孩上不了学的年代，设一笔只给女性的奖学金，规则上不算违规。规则怎么定，交给定规则的人，他们要说得出为什么；这一次怎么判，交给担着后果的人。

你会发现，三层的话都是否定的：不算，不违法，不得不。这些话都是从外面说给别人听的，一用肯定句，就容易越过界去替人拿主意。

所以到底什么是公平？我说不出公平是什么，只说得出什么不算公平。剩下的，留给定规则的人，留给判这一次的人，也留给事后每一个人的追问。

https://t.co/ksq4pLrOxO

quoted_text:
有朋友问，“那如果一个人靠欺诈、诈骗犯罪记录来申请庇护，我为了一个罪犯发声，这算什么呢？”

这是好问题，而且问得非常真诚。如果是纯吵架，大概率会去掉“如果”，而且把“我”换成“你”。所以这个问题已经进入了思辨的范畴，是值得赞扬的。

所以我们先说清楚，这位朋友是把假设推到了头。谢翌的事，到现在我没看到有谁指她本人欺诈过，更没有看到任何这样的法庭判决。可这个假设值得认真回答，因为它问的是一条线到底画在哪里：一个人确实诈骗了，确实在庇护申请里造了假，我们还替他说话，是不是就站错了地方？

要看替他说的是什么。至少有三种话。

第一种是，明知他造假，还替他编清白，替他把假话说成真话，这不行，人是目的，推不出这一条，因为它还伤害了被他骗的人，也伤害了那些照实申请的人。

第二种是，不管事实怎样，都该批他的庇护，这也推不出来，尊严不自动生出一项资格。

第三种是，事实要查清，责任要落到他身上，可怎样处置他，要有依据，守程序，不越过该有的范围。

前两种话，不可说；第三种话，却可以理直气壮地说，而且它跟反对欺诈、支持追责，一点也不冲突。

这并不是我替罪犯开脱想出来的说法。康德在《道德形而上学》讲刑罚的那一部分，说的正是有罪的人：法庭的惩罚，只能因为他犯了罪才施加在他身上，不能仅仅拿来当作实现别的好处的手段，哪怕是为了社会的好处；人天生的人格，护着他不被这样对待。在讲德性的那一部分，他又说，就算是对一个品行恶劣的人，也不能拒绝给他作为人的那一份尊重。

其实，对罪犯，康德一点也不手软，他主张报应，甚至主张杀人者偿命。在废除死刑已成广泛趋势的今天，康德甚至算得上保守派。可正是这样一个主张严刑的人，坚持罪犯也不能被当成东西。追责和尊重，在他那里本来就是一起的。

还有一个常被忽略的事情。康德讲完人是目的，紧接着举的例子，就是一个虚假的许诺：骗人的人，让对方没法在知道真相的情况下同意，就把对方当成了工具。所以，反对欺诈，和反对任意处置一个欺诈的人，出自同一条原则。被他骗了的人，是目的；他自己，也是目的。前一层要求我们追究他，后一层要求我们追究的时候，守住分寸。

写受害者不必完美那篇我说，规矩拦着最有权势的人，也护着最不完美的人。这里要再往前走一步，最不完美的人，也包括真有过错的人。一条只护着无辜者的线，其实护不住任何人，因为谁有罪、谁无辜，正是要靠这条线去查的。写美国政府必不必帮助她那篇我说，追问的人，不必先证明她值得帮助。同样，替一个人守住那条线，也不必先证明他是好人。

所以，回到这位朋友的追问，这到底算什么？我想，这算是替那条线发声，不是替他的罪发声。他要为他做的事负责，我们也要为怎样对待他负责。前一句不会取消后一句。那条线护着他，也护着被他骗过的人，最后护着的，是我们每一个人。

text:
Can Bitcoin Become More Than a Store of Value? Muneeb Ali on Stacks and What's Next

In this episode of Drops, I sit down with @muneeb, co-founder of @Stacks, to discuss his journey from a small town in Pakistan to building one of Bitcoin's most ambitious ecosystems. We explore the experiences that shaped his conviction, why he stayed committed to Bitcoin when Ethereum was taking off, and his vision for making Bitcoin faster, cheaper, and more useful. We also discuss how Bitcoin holders could earn yield without giving up custody of their assets, the growing concerns around quantum computing, and why he believes Bitcoin's next frontier lies beyond simply holding it.

From Pakistan to Princeton

Growing up in a small army town in Pakistan, Muneeb saw the internet as a window into a much bigger world. He became fascinated with computer networks and eventually earned a place at one of Pakistan's leading universities. By graduation, he felt he had exhausted the opportunities available to him and wanted to work alongside the world's best researchers, so he headed to Sweden, where he secured an unpaid visiting research position.

He only had enough money for his flight, and borrowed a few thousand dollars while calculating that he could survive for approximately four months by eating one burger a day. However, as winter approached, his money ran out, and he didn't have proper winter clothing.

Then came a moment he still remembers vividly. While attempting to withdraw money from an ATM, his bank card broke. Sitting there with the broken card, he questioned every decision that had brought him to Sweden. That experience became his reference point for handling adversity, as he began addressing the immediate problems. Could he tape the card together? Borrow a jacket? Find another way to complete his research?

His wild bet on Sweden eventually paid off, and his research contributed to a paper that later received an ACM Test of Time Award, securing him admission to Princeton for his PhD. When asked if intelligence or persistence had contributed more to his success, his answer was "I think persistence by far."

Discovering Bitcoin and Choosing a Different Path

For years, researchers had struggled with building decentralized networks where participants could agree on shared information without a central authority. Bitcoin demonstrated a practical solution through a shared transaction history maintained by independent participants. Muneeb had first encountered Bitcoin in 2011, when its white paper was assigned for a graduate seminar, but he didn't actually read it until 2013.

When he did, he was amazed. Bitcoin represented a return to the original spirit of the internet, when people could connect directly without relying on large corporations controlling the network.

He paused his PhD and began exploring Bitcoin with his co-founder, Ryan. Together, they built a decentralized social network and joined Y Combinator in 2014, when cryptocurrency was still unfamiliar to many investors. Their project attracted about 100K users but eventually encountered Bitcoin's scalability limitations.

Why He Stayed With Bitcoin When Ethereum Took Off

Meanwhile, Ethereum began emerging as a platform designed specifically for programmable applications, but Muneeb disagreed with aspects of its technical architecture. He appreciated Bitcoin's simplicity and durability, believing its limitations were also part of what made it secure.

When Ethereum gained extraordinary momentum in 2017, he questioned his decision, but rather than abandon Bitcoin, he decided to build the functionality he believed it needed. That decision led to Stacks in late 2017. The idea was to create a programmable execution layer connected to Bitcoin, allowing developers to build applications without requiring Bitcoin's base protocol to support every new feature.

Muneeb compares this architecture to the internet itself, with Bitcoin serving as the foundational network, much like TCP/IP, while Stacks acts like HTTP, enabling applications and more complex interactions above it.

Making Bitcoin Productive Without Giving Up Custody

Unlike assets on proof-of-stake networks such as Ethereum or Solana, Bitcoin does not natively generate staking yield. Muneeb aims to change that through Stacks’ protocol bonds. The mechanism builds on a system where $STX token holders already receive Bitcoin rewards for participating in Stacks' consensus, with approximately 4,500 BTC distributed over five years.

Protocol bonds extend participation to Bitcoin holders by letting them commit their BTC through Bitcoin's base layer for a smaller amount of STX to secure participation capacity. They can then earn rewards paid in Bitcoin, with bondholders receiving priority over regular STX participants.

The appeal is that participants do not need to bridge their Bitcoin into another network, deposit it into a smart contract, or surrender custody to an exchange. While changes in STX's value could affect participants’ returns, Muneeb’s broader vision is an onchain Bitcoin economy where people can lend, transact, and use Bitcoin while its underlying network remains relatively simple.

Bitcoin's Quantum Problem Could Become Its Biggest Test

Beyond usability, Muneeb believes that quantum computing could eventually threaten the cryptographic signatures protecting Bitcoin transactions, and that Bitcoin needs a credible plan for upgrading its security. He believes the unresolved risk is already discouraging some sophisticated investors, potentially limiting Bitcoin's price growth.
"What's wrong with being prepared?" he asks.

Bitcoin's decentralized community must reach agreement on what an upgrade should look like, including difficult questions about older coins and wallets. He also explains that larger post-quantum signatures could reduce Bitcoin's effective transaction capacity, making scalable execution layers even more important. Stacks, he says, is already working toward post-quantum readiness.

The Next Bitcoin Frontier

For Muneeb, the ultimate ambition behind Stacks is to make Bitcoin accessible and useful to billions of people. That means enabling fast, affordable transactions, supporting applications, and creating an economy where Bitcoin circulates rather than remaining permanently untouched. He also believes greater economic activity could generate transaction fees that help support Bitcoin's long-term security.

And while Bitcoin has come a long way since he first discovered it, Muneeb believes the opportunity to build is far from over. "In some ways, it's still early days in Bitcoin, but the frontier has changed."

For him, that frontier is now the execution layer, where the next generation of applications could transform Bitcoin from something people primarily hold into something they use.
