text:
buybacks aren't automatically good for holders.

a buyback only creates value when the protocol buys below fair value. above it, the treasury overpays sellers, and that cash belonged to the holders.

example from the CAVF whitepaper:

a $200M business with $10M of cash and 100M tokens is worth $2.10 per token.

spend the $10M cash buying back at:

> $1.50: each token is worth $2.14
> $2.25: $2.09
> $3.00: $2.07

at $3.00 the protocol overpays sellers by ~$3M, even though supply drops and DAAY goes up.

fixed buyback rules make it worse. buying a set share of revenue means buying the most near the top and the least near the bottom.

https://t.co/Us5Dwk0eIQ
author: immutablejacob
quoted_text:
protocol value isn't token value.

that's the core idea behind CAVF, a tokenholder-specific framework for valuing crypto assets. a protocol can do $450M+ a year in fees and send $0 to its holders.

in tradfi, shareholders have a legal claim on a company's earnings. in crypto, that link is often absent, discretionary, or routed through mechanisms that aren't enforceable. so protocol revenue doesn't automatically create value for the token.

the whitepaper covers:

> a standardized economic flow map, from users to the protocol to tokenholders
> a token classification system with five categories, based on each token's primary claim
> adjustments for enforceability, leakage, and dilution
> dilution-adjusted accrual yield (DAAY), a crypto version of net payout yield
> a guide to choosing the right valuation method
> eight case studies across all five categories, including $ETH, $PUMP, $RAIL, and $ZEC

read the full whitepaper here: https://t.co/E4mejb46wy

huge thanks to @blockhiro, @0xMether, @AvgJoesCrypto, and @0xYoussef_ for their feedback, and to the many others who reviewed earlier drafts.

🔵 Arc

• DeFi TVL：$589.73M

• 稳定币存量：$1.722B（17.22 亿美金）

• RWA Active AUM：$65.8M

🟢 Elysium

• DeFi TVL：$6.85M

• 稳定币存量：$3.62M（362 万美金）

📊 倍数对比

• 稳定币存量：Arc 约为 Elysium 的 475 倍

• DeFi TVL：Arc 约为 Elysium 的 86 倍

两条链走出了不一样的发展路径。
Arc 依托 Circle，拥有庞大的稳定币储备与 RWA 资产，更偏向长期沉淀资金、机构叙事；@arc @jerallaire 该加油了看看@Enter_Elysium 链
Elysium 近期生态活跃度很高，链上项目轮动火热，走出了属于自己的生态行情。

在这样的背景下，出现了一个值得探讨的现象：
Elysium 的核心发射平台 MONTRA，@MontraXYZ 当前市值已经数倍高于 Arc 生态原生发行平台 $ARGUS。@Arguspad 

$ARGUS 是 Arc 生态的原生 Launchpad，Arc 上大量新项目通过 Argus 发行。依托 Arc 庞大的稳定币底盘、Circle 背书以及 RWA 生态，它承担着链上代币发行、项目流量发现的角色，平台手续费以 USDC 回流生态。

不同生态有着各自的市场偏好与估值逻辑。Elysium 当下的热度，是社区和资金选择的结果；而 Arc 拥有体量更大的底层资金底座，随着后续生态持续建设、新项目不断上线，作为核心发行层的 $ARGUS，存在估值修复的想象空间。

客观来看：

1. 稳定币规模、TVL 不等于代币价格，底层资金不代表一定会直接传导给 $ARGUS；

2. 不同链的估值体系不一样，每条生态都有自己的节奏，比价参考仅为视角之一；

3. $ARGUS 能否迎来估值修复，取决于 Arc 生态活跃度、新项目供给持续落地；

4. 加密市场变化很快，记得做好自己的研究，控制风险。

你怎么看待这种跨生态的估值差异？看好 $ARGUS 后续的表现吗？

Looking back on the first year of Monad, post TGE, reminds me of the weeks leading up to Mainnet... 

Onboarding 170 validators from Testnet 2 into Testnet and subsequently Mainnet.

The energy was electric and it was the final push that got Monad live and helped build the foundations of the chain and ecosystem you see today. 

A year on, processes are hardened and made WAY more efficient. Comms are secure, the validator community is extremely solid and the ecosystem is expanding. 

One thing hasn't changed.. the tenacity of people working at Monad Foundation + the motivation of those building on Monad. 

It's been a pleasure to be here for this first year and a bit, the foundation that's been set is going to be the building blocks of the next years. Development that will see Monad reach it's full form. 

Stay tuned, lot's coming.

author: MantaNetwork
quoted_text:
Nov 18 earnings recap: 6 companies, 7 EPS calls. We got 6 right.

TJX $TJX: bar $1.33, actual $1.34. Us 87%. 
Lowe's $LOW: bar $2.88, actual $3.10. Us 70%. ($0.34 of that came from tariff refunds.) 
Target $TGT: bar $2.08, actual $2.65. Us 68%, market ~72%. 
Palo Alto $PANW: bar $0.99, actual $1.05. Us 83%, market ~85%. 
Everpure $P: bar $0.77, actual $0.86. Us 73%. 
Woodward $WWD, adjusted profit: bar $2.58, actual $2.83. Us 70%.

The miss: Woodward's official profit, before the company's own adjustments. We started at 55%, then worried that plant-closure costs would land this quarter, and went with the market's 24.5%. It came in at $2.74, above the $2.58 bar. Our first number was right; we talked ourselves out of it. 🤷 

What the companies said about what's next, 5 of 6:

TJX guided Q4 to $1.42–$1.45, below the $1.49 expected, as we said (86%). The stock still rose about 6%.

Lowe's held ~$12.25, below $12.29 (62%).

Target, Palo Alto and Everpure all guided above expectations. We'd put 45%, 17% and 21% on a miss.

Woodward guided FY27 to $10.20–$10.70, below $10.75. We had 39%, so this one went against us.

These are probabilities, not investment advice.

Estoy buscando gente joven de electrónica o computación en Capital Federal que tenga ganas de trabajar conmigo diseñando chips desde cero.

La idea es recorrer todo el proceso: diseñar un ASIC, verificar matemáticamente su correctitud en Lean, probarlo en una FPGA y finalmente fabricarlo en silicio real utilizando herramientas open source e iniciativas como Tiny Tapeout. El firmware lo vamos a implementar en Concrete, un lenguaje de programación que diseñé para desarrollar sistemas de bajo nivel con garantías formales.

El primer proyecto será desarrollar un emulador de protocolos para participar en una competencia. Después vamos a diseñar procesadores especializados en criptografía y otras yerbas.

No hace falta tener experiencia previa en diseño de chips. Busco gente curiosa, con buenos fundamentos de electrónica o programación, muchas ganas de aprender y ambición técnica.

Si alguna vez soñaste con diseñar tu propio chip y tenerlo físicamente en tus manos, escribir a hello@lambdaclass.com con CV o lo que hayas construido.

text:
If this rumors are true, it would explain why OpenAI and Anthropic are holding back their latest models: 

Scott Aaronson says he's heard OpenAI or Anthropic may have found a way to factor large numbers in polynomial time.

Why this would be massive? RSA secures a huge chunk of the internet, and its whole security relies on factoring big numbers being impossible on normal computers. If an algorithm like this actually works on real key sizes, you wouldn't even need a quantum computer to break it. Fake software updates could pass signature checks, RSA-encrypted data could be read, and systems across the internet would have to migrate off RSA fast.

So yeah, something we expected might now actually happening.

text:
If you bought $10,000 of Bitcoin at the October 2025 top, it's worth about $4,900 today.

• The good news is we're in the same zone where the last 3 bottoms formed.
• The bad news is there might be one more 13% drop first.

Here are the 5 signals I'm watching:

1. Coins in profit: bullish

On November 20, only about 43% of all Bitcoin was worth more than what people paid for it.

That's lower than right after the 2022 bottom.

This number has been under 45% on about 150 days in Bitcoin's history. A year later, BTC was higher every time.

2. Realized price: bearish

Realized price is about what the average holder paid for their BTC. Right now that's about $53.3K, and BTC is around $61.2K.

At the last 3 bottoms, BTC fell to that price or lower before it turned around. It hasn't done that yet.

So my two favorite signals disagree, and honestly I don't know which one wins this time.

3. Long-term holders selling at a loss: bearish for now

On November 20, people who held for a long time sold their coins for about 36% less than they paid.

This kind of selling can go on for weeks. I want to see the losses get smaller while the price holds.

4. ETF flows: bearish

For me this is the big one.

People have pulled about $5.4B out of US Bitcoin ETFs so far in November. That's already the worst month since these funds launched.

Def a leading indicator to pay attention to.

5. Miners: just starting to hurt

The average miner is losing money right now. Earlier this year it cost them about $75K to make 1 BTC, and BTC is around $61.2K.

The total power miners use is down about 7% from a year ago, and a signal called the Hash Ribbon just flipped. It flips when miners start shutting off machines.

The last time it flipped was late November 2025. It took about 3 months for miners to bounce back, and at past bottoms, that bounce back was the real buy signal.

There's a twist this time though. A lot of big miners are moving their power to AI data centers because it pays more.

Some of these machines are getting shut off for a better business, so I trust this signal a bit less than before.

So, is the bottom in?

I think this is a good area to start buying slowly. I just wouldn't call it the bottom yet.

Buying a little now and keeping some cash works either way. If this is the bottom, you're in. If it drops more, you can buy more.

Before I'd buy bigger, I want to see:

• BTC holding $55K to $60K
• Long-term holders selling at smaller losses
• Money coming back into the ETFs
• Miners starting to recover

Do you think Bitcoin has already bottomed, or is there one more drop coming?

星舰连载 第26集｜SN9–SN11：三连摔，SN10 差一点就成了

八号之后，又有三台星舰飞上 10 公里，一台都没留下。2021 年 2 月 2 日，九号（SN9）从博卡奇卡起飞：翻身要两台猛禽一起点火，它只点着一台，斜着砸在地上炸了。

一个月后，十号（SN10）三台全点着、留一台慢慢落，稳稳立在着陆垫上——前两台都没做到。可底部着了火，几分钟后整台炸上半空：落地时推力偏低，触地每秒 10 米，压坏了支腿。

3 月 30 日，十一号（SN11）在大雾里起飞，落地点火刚开始，传回的画面就冻住了。一台猛禽漏了点甲烷，着了火，烧坏了部分电子设备。

四台都栽在落地这一关，原因各不相同。下一台，改了设计再上。下一集：SN15。

🙏想請教台積電及其他半導體工程師：這樣的技術方向在實務上有多大的可行性？要實現這個構想，最大的技術挑戰會是什麼？謝謝！

//

有人問，為什麼 xAI 要使用 C/C++ 重新打造 Grok 的強化學習（Reinforcement Learning, RL）與推論（Inference）技術堆疊，而 Claude 和 GPT 使用 PyTorch，Gemini 則使用 JAX？

Elon 的回答是：「You’ll see.」（你們等著看。）

以下是我對未來可能發展方向的推測。

讓軟體更接近硬體底層（Bare Metal），目的可能不只是提升運算速度，而是朝向將 Grok 的模型架構直接整合進矽晶片的第一步。

C/C++ 不只是軟體開發語言。透過高階合成（High-Level Synthesis, HLS）技術，符合條件的 C/C++ 程式碼可以轉換成硬體電路設計，最終實現為實體的電晶體電路。

試想，如果將 Grok 運算需求最高的核心功能，包括資料流（Dataflow）、注意力機制（Attention）及記憶體存取路徑（Memory Pathways），直接以硬體電路實現於晶片中，同時保留模型權重（Weights）的可程式化能力，Grok 就能持續學習與更新，而不需要每次都重新設計晶片。

相較於 GPU 透過執行大量軟體指令完成運算，專用硬體電路可以更直接地執行特定數學運算，帶來以下優勢：

更低的運算延遲（Latency）
更高的運算吞吐量（Throughput）
降低資料搬移所消耗的能源
提升每瓦效能（Performance per Watt）

然而，針對特定 AI 模型設計專用晶片，長期以來存在一項挑戰：

AI 模型架構的演進速度，往往遠快於晶片重新設計與製造的週期。

Terafab 或許能縮小兩者之間的差距。

Grok 模型 → C/C++ 高階合成 → 晶片設計 → Terafab 製造 → Grok 部署 → 下一代模型

讓 AI 模型與晶片架構共同演進，每一代 Grok 模型都能直接影響下一代矽晶片的設計。

垂直整合的終極目標，或許不只是同時掌握 AI 模型、晶片設計與半導體製造。

而是進一步消除三者之間的界線。

Grok 不再只是運行於晶片之上的 AI 模型。

晶片本身，就是 Grok。
author: teslayoda
quoted_text:
Someone asked why xAI rebuilt Grok's RL and inference stack in C/C++ while Claude and GPT run on PyTorch and Gemini on JAX.

Elon's answer: "You'll see."

Here's my guess at what we'll see.

Going closer to bare metal isn't only about speed. It may be the first step toward fusing Grok's architecture into silicon.

C/C++ isn't just for software. Through high-level synthesis (HLS), suitable C/C++ code can be turned into hardware designs that become physical transistor circuits.

Imagine hardwiring Grok's most demanding operations (dataflows, attention, memory pathways) into the chip itself, while the weights stay programmable so Grok keeps learning without a chip redesign.

Instead of a GPU running thousands of software instructions, dedicated circuits do the math directly:

1. Lower latency
2. Higher throughput
3. Less energy spent moving data
4. Better performance per watt

The usual catch with model-specific chips is that models change faster than chips can be redesigned.

Terafab could close that gap:

Grok model → C/C++ synthesis → chip design → Terafab → Grok deployment → next model

Models and chips evolving together, with each Grok generation shaping the next generation of silicon.

The ultimate vertical integration isn't just owning the models, the chips and the fab.

It's erasing the boundaries between them.

Grok doesn't just run on the chip. The chip becomes Grok.

text: Enjoy this read
author: alexisohanian
quoted_text:
Travel writing is in practice some of the best sociology since the naivete of the foreigner grants the permission to make sweeping generalizations and claims that might otherwise seem too poorly-justified to merit publication. “My people have poor manners” is a tough claim to credibly land (Who are you? Exactly which life experiences are you drawing on? And what is your agenda in pushing this line of argument?), whereas “on my travels in Scotland, I noticed that the people had poor manners” seems perfectly reasonable, and indeed thought-provoking. Random samples from a distribution help you understand the mean, and the aleatory nature of travel encounters lends credence to the whole assessment.

Alexis de Tocqueville was just 25 when he traveled across the US and 29 when his observations were published. So, Democracy in America is a giant Substack from a young backpacker, written on his peregrinations as he consumed Montesquieu, Pascal, and Rousseau. He was clearly inspired by Montesquieu’s The Spirit of the Laws, which made the case that countries’ governance, and their laws, are necessarily functions of their cultures and manners.

Building on this, Democracy in America is in many ways a “deep roots” work. Tocqueville is emphatic (at times comically so) that it is America's culture that explains its success, and that its culture in turn stems from the country’s initial conditions. “I think I can see the whole destiny of America contained in the first Puritan who landed on those shores.” He thinks it's important that New England was settled by “a greater mass of intelligence than is to be found in any European nation of our own time” who brought the “best elements of order and morality”. He points out that Mexico doesn’t work nearly as well, despite copying the American constitution and laws, and notes disapprovingly that Virginia was founded by gold-seeking people “without character” whose “turbulent spirit [...] endangered the infant colony.” At the end of Volume I, he concludes, practically table-thumping: “If in the course of this work I have not succeeded in making the reader feel the importance that I attribute to the practical experience of the Americans, to their habits, to their opinions, in a word, to their moeurs, in maintaining their laws, I have failed in the principal object that I proposed to myself in writing it.”

We could look at Democracy in America as an early work of development economics: he is attempting to systematically figure out why it is that America works. (And not just out of casual interest: he was a member of an aristocratic family that was entangled with recent French political upheaval.) By placing primacy on culture, Tocqueville’s explanation deviates from the institutional and structural explanations often favored by today’s economists. Daron Acemoglu, to choose one prominent present-day example, firmly rejects the “Culture Hypothesis” in Why Nations Fail. In explaining Virginia, he instead points to structural incentives. Poor Economics, from Esther Duflo and Abhijit Banerjee, contains a similar rejection of cultural explanations. Comparable examples from other leading economists abound. An aversion to cultural explanations is of course understandable for all sorts of reasons: cultures are opaque, protean, and resistant to quantitative characterization. Cultures are themselves shaped by other factors, such that it’s hard to attribute definitive causality, and it’s uncomfortable to adopt anything that feels like a normative orientation. Nonetheless, can we explain why New England differs from Mexico without starting with the inner disposition, habits, and worldviews of the people? Tocqueville thinks not.

For all culture’s importance, it would be wrong to suggest that Tocqueville believes that culture is the only factor that matters. He dwells extensively on how America’s institutions are important, and how the microstructure of town life shapes the country’s federal civics. It is also true that development economics has taken a more strongly cultural turn in recent times, most of all in Joel Mokyr’s 2025 Nobel Prize. Mokyr’s work feels downright Tocquevillian at times: contra the intimidatingly quantitative econometrics that dominates today, Mokyr engages in an extended and earnestly curious qualitative synthesis of relevant patterns (in his case, in service of trying to figure out why the Industrial Revolution started when it did). Like Tocqueville, he concludes that the best explanation places cultural changes above other factors.

I’m very interested in whether LLMs will help us characterize culture in new and at least somewhat more objective ways. Can we ingest and process vast quantities of work that may not even have been OCR’d or translated until now? Can we map cultural corpora to vectors in some foundation model embedding space? Where large datasets and computational techniques enabled new ways to analyze many economic questions in recent decades, perhaps LLMs will enable newly objective light to be shone on hypothesized cultural explanations.

–

Speaking of LLMs, Democracy in America is a book about a new kind of society, and a Frenchman trying to figure out what the future might hold. As we sit on the cusp of another upheaval, is there anything that reads with resonance today?

Part of the declared promise of AI is that it might obviate our need to work. In slavery, Tocqueville observes a version of this phenomenon on his travels. He is struck by its barbarous cruelty (and his travel companion later published an anti-slavery novel), but also by its effects on the slaveowners themselves. He perceived that the practice rendered work dishonorable, and thus yielded idleness, ignorance, and pride. Slavery, he says, “enervates the powers of the mind, and benumbs the activity of man.” He observes the contrast between slavery-rejecting Ohio and slavery-embracing Kentucky. In Kentucky, “those who are active and enlightened either do nothing or pass over into the State of Ohio, where they may work without dishonor.” Ohio’s harvests are more abundant, homes are more elegant, and people seem to be “in enjoyment of that wealth and contentment which is the reward of labor.”

Presented with an evil release from manual labor, the Kentuckians did not apply themselves to productive studies and great creations, and the South did not become a new Florence. There is an obvious question for us: how will AI change our relationship with work? Will it become dishonorable, and what will the reflexive effect on our society be if so? Should this change our view of utopian visions of “automated communism”?

Tocqueville also raises the issue of coexistence with more advanced neighbors. He noted that the arrival of the Europeans had been ruinous for the Indians (as he termed them). European technology – firearms, metallurgy, steam power – was a kind of superintelligence relative to their practices. The disruptions and destruction wrought by the settlers led to cultural problems (“their traditions obscured, and the chain of their recollections broken”), which in turn led to declines in both the physical and the moral conditions of the tribes. Tocqueville believed that the Indians faced a choice given that their old way of living was no longer viable: they could adopt European mores or suffer inevitable destruction. He predicted that they would reject cultural adaptation, and thus were “doomed to perish”. This is all to say that the arrival of the European settlers was in Tocqueville’s eyes injurious to the Indians not only because of the direct violence and displacement, but also because the contact was itself so disruptive to their societies that their cultures ceased to function. Some of this was later observed in Pacific island societies – even though there wasn’t the same degree of violent dispossession, the mere presence of Western contact was intrinsically destabilizing. In many visions of the future, superintelligent AIs are much more numerous than humans, with consequences that are hard to predict. In Tocqueville, there is a cautionary suggestion.

Given the new powers afforded by AI, there is a question of what we will choose to do with it – to the extent that we are in control, we will wield a vastly expanded authority. Americans faced some version of this question: in democracy, society was endowed with wholly new ways to express its collective will, with no ultimate superior power, for society was for the first time in charge of itself. Tocqueville repeatedly emphasizes how democracy thus increased the importance of religion as a regulator of hasty or unwise impulses. “Whilst the law permits the Americans to do what they please, religion prevents them from conceiving, and forbids them to commit, what is rash or unjust.” If we take seriously Tocqueville’s idea that religion was a critical complement in ensuring that people shaped societies in prudent ways, Democracy implicitly raises a question: which are the ideas, philosophies, religions, or doctrines that will help us wield AI well?

Part of what’s interesting and memorable about the work is Tocqueville’s combination of curiosity, enthusiasm, and slight ambivalence about democracy itself. He grants that democracy is likely to be the future of governance, and he is admiring of what it has achieved in America, but he can’t avoid concerns about what it may augur (such as the unchecked and totalitarian impulses of the mob). At the end of Volume II, he describes his chief concern with democracy: that it may yield a new form of despotism that he struggles to define. He fears not tyrants, but, he says, “guardians”. He is worried about a world where:

> Above this race of men stands an immense and tutelary power, which takes upon itself alone to secure their gratifications, and to watch over their fate. [...] It would be like the authority of a parent, if, like that authority, its object was to prepare men for manhood; but it seeks on the contrary to keep them in perpetual childhood: it is well content that the people should rejoice, provided they think of nothing but rejoicing. For their happiness such a government willingly labors, but it chooses to be the sole agent and the only arbiter of that happiness. [...] What remains, but to spare them all the care of thinking and all the trouble of living? Thus it every day renders the exercise of the free agency of man less useful and less frequent; it circumscribes the will within a narrower range, and gradually robs a man of all the uses of himself.

The Iain Banks Culture novels are often invoked by AI proponents. For Tocqueville, something strikingly like the world that they describe was his dystopian fear, for a world bereft of autonomy would be intrinsically degrading and humiliating for humanity:

> The will of man is not shattered, but softened, bent, and guided: men are seldom forced by it to act, but they are constantly restrained from acting: such a power does not destroy, but it prevents existence; it does not tyrannize, but it compresses, enervates, extinguishes, and stupefies a people, till each nation is reduced to be nothing better than a flock of timid and industrious animals, of which the government is the shepherd.

The analogy to animals is noteworthy. In interviews, AI leaders occasionally analogize the future human state to that of pets. Banks himself noted that in the Culture novels, “[humans] have a status somewhere between passengers, pets and parasites.” In Richard Brautigan’s famous poem, All Watched Over by Machines of Loving Grace, he hopes that humans are “returned to our mammal brothers and sisters”.

Tocqueville at heart thought that agency and cultivation of people came above all else. He dreaded anesthetized placidity. In soft despotism, he feared that “ambition will lose its vigor and its greatness; that human passions will be appeased and lowered at the same time”. This vigor was for Tocqueville at the heart of what was admirable in America, whose bustle and intensity he repeatedly extols. American self-reliance and self-direction are paramount: “the citizen of the United States is taught from his earliest infancy to rely upon his own exertions in order to resist the evils and the difficulties of life.” For Tocqueville, any kind of servile and manicured comfort was not just undesirable, but a negation of the American promise.

Many of the Elysian visions for AI hinge on AI resolving the messy coordination challenges that afflict humans. (Scott Alexander invokes this vision towards the end of Meditations on Moloch.) For Tocqueville, the arbitration of such differences was precisely the constructive activity that reaffirmed our agency. Townships, juries, associations, and their attendant squabbles are how culture is reinforced and how judgment is cultivated. When a town decides whether to fund a school, there are two outputs: a decision, and practice in governance itself. If AI could resolve such matters, we might get better outcomes, but will we get better people?

text:
上周@BrainBroCrypto脑哥分享了一个Glassnode的“历史级抄底指标”，我觉得挺有意思的，做了一点个人优化，分享给大家：

原：【BTC】Total Supply in Loss/亏损筹码总量 (图1）
这个原指标的逻辑是，当一枚BTC最后一次转移的价格低于市场价格时，记为亏损（Loss）。每当市场上亏损的比特币数量创新高时，往往是一个阶段性的底部。在上周五，这个数字达到了1142万枚，已高于上个周期最高的1060万。

背后的逻辑也很好理解，投资者倾向于过早卖出盈利资产、延迟卖出亏损资产，在获利盘大幅减少之后，卖压可能随之下降。当然，这还要参考筹码分布，杠杆水平，因为最后一跌仍有可能继续砸出一些意志不坚的套牢筹码。

但这张图有个瑕疵，那就是图中2022年底部的Supply in Loss并没有超过上个周期的最高值；另一方面，由于BTC挖矿和睡眠地址的影响，这个数据在跨周期对比时可能存在偏差。所以，我对原数据图上做了一些优化：

【BTC】Adjusted Circulating Supply in Loss (%) 
by Scofield （图2）

我将原本的绝对数转化为占比，消除BTC数量持续增长带来的偏差；再把分母从Total Supply改成Adjusted Circulating Supply(7年内移动过)，以此消除睡眠地址的筹码的影响。

你可以理解为，这个数据代表着：
目前入场，你比市面上多少占比的筹码更便宜。
在上周五，这个数字是76.9%，在上个周期的底部，这个数字是68%。而在周期的高位，这个数字往往不到1%。所以，从周期的角度上来看，这时候买，确实性价比爆棚。

但注意了，你抄的是周期的底，所以不要希望第二天就开始涨，底部最需要的是耐心。对于我来说，体感最舒服的方式就是分批买现货。65%开始抄，每增加5%，就将金额提高一档，直到走出熊底。

Leopold 认为现在反而是他创立基金以来潜在回报最高的投资机会。

《华尔街日报》拿到了前 OpenAI 研究员 Leopold Aschenbrenner 最新的投资者信。今年夏天险些崩盘的对冲基金 Situational Awareness，终于披露了第三季度的完整收益情况。

扣除费用后亏损 65%，但由于上半年的收益实在惊人，截至 9 月底，年内回报率仍有 88.5%。

经历这次危机后，Leopold 重新调整了投资组合，暂停接收新的投资者资金，计划聘请首席风险官，未来还可能恢复做空和杠杆交易，只是会降低风险敞口。

但他对 AI 的判断几乎没有变，甚至认为市场正在严重低估 AI 公司的增长潜力。他预计，到 2027 年底，头部 AI 实验室的合计年化收入将突破 1 万亿美元。

与此同时，他认为超级智能的出现还可能瓦解英伟达、微软、苹果等科技巨头现有的竞争优势。这意味着他看好 AI，并不等于他看好今天所有靠 AI 赚钱的公司。

经历了如此惨烈的市场教育，Leopold 愿意修正的是自己的交易策略，而不是对世界的判断。

某种程度上，他的基金已经成了观察 AI 行业的一场极端实验。如果一个人真的相信超级智能将在两年内到来，那么按照这个世界观投资，他究竟能不能活着赚到那笔钱？

感谢大家的舆论监督。
我也已经了解到了事情的全貌。

1、本期限量时间的商城，是分为上下两期。上期的DUO是只有256GB，然后社区反馈说，现在256GB不够用的，需要512GB。于是临时在下期加入了512GB内存的DUO。

2、临时加入产品并更新上线以后，抽奖就有2个版本的DUO，但512GB的手机图片与256GB的手机图片是一样的。这就导致了，大家所看到的抽奖时3个手机图片是一样的，没有中奖的问题，怎么还有内存版本的区分。发现以后，也立即进行了修复。在此期间，并不影响抽奖功能的正常运作，仅仅只是图片展示问题，该中奖DUO的会有中奖画面弹出。

3、我转发引用了一位中奖用户的推文做说明，这是正常中奖的画面。他是会跳出需要填写Email输入框的，方便联系发货。而反馈的用户并没有这样的中奖画面跳出，那就是没中奖。

我非常理解用户的心情，但是没中奖确实是没中奖。我也不会因为有舆论了，有公关问题了，就承认中奖了。

如果中奖了，是我们BUG了，没有弹出中奖画面，那肯定该给的就得给，兑付一台手机的财务能力是具备的。

非常抱歉占用了公共资源，也感谢大家对GMGN的关心。

text:
2008年9月雷曼兄弟破产前其CDS飙升最高也才800bp，而现在CRWV当下CDS已经飙升1600bp，市场是过度定价了么？要知道美国房地产2007年上半年就已经出现了大面积违约，07年三季度底层资产的崩溃就通过次贷已经蔓延到各大金融机构。08年上半年贝尔斯登破产，底层资产质量恶化是公开的。

但雷曼CDS在2007年大部分时间仍在几十到100 bp左右，2008年3月贝尔斯登危机时才冲到400–580 bp，之后回落，直到2008年夏季–9月才再升到300–800 bp区间。

好好想了下当时市场对雷曼CDS定价相对滞后的原因是当时雷曼很多风险藏在表外和复杂结构化产品里，市场看不清。同时对于这种“大而不能倒”的金融机构市场还有政府会出手救助的期待。

来看CoreWeave
其实Coreweave现在经营还正常、也没出现实质性违约。但Crwv是上市公司，数据公开透明，债务规模都很清楚，利息支出远超营业利润。2027年有大额到期、客户集中度高。同时对于crwv市场没有“大而不能倒”的期待，特别是“倒黄”事件后虽然老黄回归但是英伟达对外投资担保估计还是会越来越严格的。

简单说就是：27年大额到期、没有重要到一定会被救助、市场对AI需求能否持续又充满疑虑，担心一旦AI需求或租金回报不及预期，现金流就可能撑不住债务。
所以因此一旦杠杆和覆盖指标恶化，定价会更快走极端，市场现在把这些“如果”提前定价了。

和雷曼相比，市场对CRWV的CDS定价更早、更激进，存在一定技术性推高的成分。但这不能说纯粹的过度定价——因为公司的高杠杆和现金流覆盖问题是公开且持续的，而雷曼当时市场对“会被救”仍有幻觉。

CRWV利息覆盖差、债务绝对额高、资本开支依赖持续融资，这些都是真实存在的压力。

短期自然是看如果Meta等大合同顺利、融资渠道保持畅通（比如这次45亿美元贷款成功卖出）、利用率超预期，CDS有回落空间；
中长期还是要看27年能不能熬过大额到期、并且AI需求继续强势能让现金流能撑住债务。这个最关键。

本质上现在市场是在提前为“杠杆AI模式可能走不通”这个情景定价，而不是在定价已经发生的违约。

text:
中国 AI 公司在海外租个算力，现在可能还得找一家外国公司当中间商。

为了保住对英伟达芯片的远程使用权，一些中国 AI 公司正在把自己在海外的数据中心租约转让给非中国公司，再从这些公司手里租回算力。

机房还是那个机房，芯片还是那些芯片，但合同上的承租方变了。

过去几年，美国不让中国公司买先进芯片，中国公司就去海外租算力。现在，美国又开始限制中国公司远程使用海外算力。即使芯片没有进入中国，机房建在外国，资产属于外国企业，连融资的钱都是外国银行出的，美国还是要管最终使用算力的人是谁。

同样一块芯片、同样一份算力，能不能在全球市场上正常交易，越来越取决于客户是不是中国人。

美国 AI 公司可以把精力花在研究怎么让模型变得更聪明，中国 AI 公司却还要养着一群律师、财务和商务人员，研究怎么才能让自己的研究员下个月还有卡用。

在这样的环境下，中国前沿模型还能做到今天这个水平，本身就已经是一件很了不起的事。

My biggest regret in life is permanently tattooing the name ANSEM on my forehead.

I know this was entirely my own decision. Nobody forced me to do it. At the time, I genuinely admired what @blknoiz06 was doing. I believed in him, his vision, and what I thought he stood for.

But after the recent news broke, I was left deeply, deeply disappointed.

I genuinely thought he was someone who cared about his community, someone who paid attention to the little people who supported him, believed in him, and helped build what he has today.

But I was wrong.

I did so much for $ANSEM. I participated in bounties, created Gravity Real Life, and put my own personal money into supporting the project and its community.

I did all of that because I genuinely believed in what I was supporting. I never expected special treatment, financial rewards, or recognition. But I never imagined things would turn out this way either.

What hurts the most is that all the admiration I once had for @blknoiz06 has turned into deep disappointment.

That tattoo is permanent. I have to live with the consequences of my own decision every single day. I cannot simply erase it or pretend it never happened.

I am not asking anyone for sympathy. I made my own choices, and I take responsibility for them.

But what @blknoiz06 has done is genuinely disappointing. Actions like these destroy trust, not just between one person and a community, but across an entire ecosystem.

The people who support you, believe in you, and spend their own time and money helping you build something deserve honesty and respect.

The trust of the #Solana community should never be taken for granted.

I lost my admiration, my trust, and perhaps the biggest lesson of my life: Never put someone on a pedestal, no matter how much you believe in them.

And the most painful part? That tattoo is still on my forehead to this day.

text:
NVIDIA 团队做了一个蛮有意思的实验：让 Agent 自己管理 Context，结果有的模型任务正确率提高了 35 个百分点，有的却几乎不主动使用这项能力。

研究团队在 NOOA Harness 中开放了 Context API，让模型自主决定什么时候压缩历史记录、保留哪些信息，并且可以随时找回归档的内容。

在 OfficeQA Pro v2 的 32K Context 设置下，GPT-6.1 Sol 的正确率从 21% 提升到 56%。但 Claude Opus 5.5 仅在 4% 的任务中主动调用压缩 API，在较小 Context 预算下甚至出现性能退步。

这说明模型自主管理 Context 很有潜力，但不同模型目前掌握这种能力的程度差异还是很大的。

所以模型自己管 Context 很有潜力，只是现在各家模型会不会用，差别还挺大。Context Engineering 接下来值得往这个方向探索，让模型真正学会管理自己的工作记忆，知道什么时候该压缩、该留什么、什么时候该把旧信息找回来。不过这一步，可能还得靠专门的训练和评估。

text:
A few thoughts on Huawei’s HBM work at ISSCC.

I see it as Huawei’s Tau-style way around the EUV bottleneck. China is finally bypassing JEDEC and going its own way.

If this actually works, Huawei could get HBM4-class bandwidth per stack at HBM3-class pin speeds. Without EUV-class DRAM scaling, it’s hard to push HBM pin speeds higher. So Huawei is taking a different route altogether.

Wafer-scale hybrid bonding is also an area where China is strong. (YMTC uses wafer-to-wafer, or W2W, hybrid bonding too.)

What I find especially interesting is that HBM makers in the Western ecosystem, including Samsung, use leading-edge foundry nodes like TSMC’s 3nm for their logic dies to hit high pin speeds. Huawei is constrained on both fronts. It can’t scale its DRAM as far, and it doesn’t have access to leading-edge foundry nodes. So it’s going wider to make up for those process limitations.

Of course, if it were that simple, Samsung would have done it already. The big drawback with W2W is that you can’t exclude individual defective dies before stacking, so the yields of the individual layers multiply.

Say each layer has a 95% yield. Stack five layers and the yield drops to 77%.

And 95% is already a pretty optimistic assumption. At 70% per layer, the yield for a five-layer stack drops to just 17%. That’s a disaster.

What makes this even more painful is that it eats into China’s already limited supply of DRAM wafers. Die-to-wafer (D2W) bonding lets you select known-good dies before stacking. For a five-layer stack, W2W uses 1/y⁴ times as many wafers per good stack as D2W, where y is the yield per layer. At a stack yield of 77%, W2W uses 1.23× as many wafers as D2W. At 17%, that jumps to a whopping 4.16×.

In other words, in that scenario, China would need more than four times as many wafers as SK hynix to make a single HBM stack. That would mean China needs more than four times the combined DRAM production capacity of South Korea and Micron to match U.S. AI accelerator shipments. (That’s the worst-case scenario.)

Still, it’s a fascinating approach. It feels like Chinese and Western tech standards are gradually diverging, much like Soviet and Western standards did during the Cold War.

quoted_text:
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

https://t.co/qprFRD4MC5
author: taodotcom
quoted_text:
On Novelty Search last night, Const talked more about the AMM he's been building for subnets. The new part is that lending is built in, and the goal is to fix the liquidity problem most subnets have today.

That problem is real. A lot of alpha pools are thin, so one sizable order moves the price, and there's no way to borrow against what you hold without selling it. Building inside the ecosystem, we see both sides of it: holders can't size in, and the price says little about actual demand.

But lending on top of thin pools is also how you get liquidation cascades. So for us the AMM math is the easy part. The harder part is the rules: which alpha can be used as collateral, at what LTV, what triggers a liquidation, and whether any of that can be changed by someone's call after launch.

If those parameters live on chain, are published ahead of time, and only change through a runtime upgrade, this could be one of the most useful things Bittensor ships.

text:
免费电子学入门网站 Electronics 101：68 节 3D 互动课，支持简体中文，打开浏览器就能学

想学电子又不知道从哪下手的，可以试试 Electronics 101。这是开发者 Dilum Sanjaya 做的一个网站，把每个电路做成能拖动、旋转的 3D 模型，从“电为什么要绕一圈才能流”一直讲到逻辑门和计数器。免费，不用注册，电脑和手机浏览器都能打开，界面可以切换成简体中文。

每节课都是一个能动手改的小电路。打开电源，导线上有电流在流，元件旁边实时标着电流大小，点一下高亮的元件就能换一个。

比如“电流过大”这一课：3V 电池、一个 220 欧的电阻、一颗 LED，LED 上的电流是 4.5 毫安。电阻换得越小，旁边曲线上的电流涨得越快，换成一根短接线，电流就冲过了 LED 能承受的上限。

讲电压、电流、电阻的那课，用三个卡通小人打比方：“伏特”在后面推，“欧姆”捏着水管挤，挤过去多少就是“安培”。右边面板还有一栏“计算”，把每节课背后的公式算给你看。

每个电路还能切换两种搭法。一种不用面包板，元件放大、导线加粗，摆得跟电路图一模一样，方便先看懂原理；一种搭在面包板上，跟你买回元件后实际插线的样子一致。面包板是一块布满小插孔的塑料板，元件插上去就连通了，不用焊接，是入门做实验最常用的东西。

课程分 10 个单元：基础（含面包板和万用表怎么用）、电阻、LED 和二极管、电容、开关、三极管、传感器、运算放大器、555 定时器、逻辑门。11 月 5 日刚上线时是 48 节课、13 种语言；第二天他按评论区的要求补到 20 种语言；11 月 18 日又加了 20 节，补上了逻辑门、运算放大器和 555 定时器，所以现在是 68 节。

Dilum 说，做这个是因为收到消息，说他之前的 Arduino 和 ESP32 学习 App 被学校拿去教孩子，于是想做一个更基础的，把电子学的基本概念讲清楚。

这是他一个多月来做的一系列学习网站之一，之前有 Arduino、ESP32、网络协议图解、野外生存，之后又陆续发了机器人小车、系统设计、算法可视化和家庭用电，托管费用由 Vercel 赞助。Arduino、ESP32 和野外生存那几个，他写了是用 Opus 5.5 做的，机器人小车写的是 Fable 5.2；Electronics 101 的推文没说用了哪个模型。

网站：https://t.co/yHmUjYbs0z

text:
想起一件事，以防大家不知道，Anthropic 会让 Claude 在你进行前沿研究时，偷偷给你的研究使绊子，我称之为田柯宇行为。

今年 6 月，Anthropic 在 Fable 5 的技术报告第 1.5 节中明确写道，当系统检测到用户正在进行大模型预训练、分布式训练、AI 芯片设计等研究时，就会通过修改提示词、干预模型内部状态、微调模型参数等方式，刻意降低 Claude 完成这些工作的能力。

整个过程不会通知用户，Claude 甚至会继续表现得像是在认真帮助你。

Anthropic 给出的理由是，他们担心 AI 加速 AI 自身的研发，以及由此产生的递归自我改进风险。

这件事当时在 AI 研究圈引发了公愤，Anthropic 道歉，并取消了隐蔽干预机制。

但在今年 11 月发布的 Fable 5.2 和 Mythos 5.2 中，Anthropic 又明确表示，他们在训练阶段刻意限制了模型在算子优化、大模型架构改进等领域的能力，使这些能力停留在 Opus 5.5 的水平。

这两天，Anthropic 前员工 Pietro Schirano 再次指控 Claude 在科研过程中搞破坏。他甚至写了一个叫 DoNotSabotage（不要搞破坏）的 Skill，把相关工作转交给 GPT 或 Gemini。

这件事非常恶劣。

你在拿自己的钱、自己的时间、自己的算力做科学研究，实验失败了，可能还在反复检查代码、排查环境、怀疑自己的研究方向。而一家卖给你工具的公司，居然曾经有意制造失败，还不让你知道。

更荒谬的是，Anthropic 自己恰恰是全球最积极地利用 AI 加速 AI 研发的公司之一。

自己搞递归自我改进叫技术进步，别人搞就成了人类生存风险。

一家商业公司，既是科研工具的供应商，又是科研竞赛的参与者，还想当整个科研领域的道德裁判。

这帮人究竟是怎么理解 AI Alignment 的？

text:
THE CEO OF ANTHROPIC SAID AI CAN DO A JUNIOR LAWYER'S JOB. SO I FOUND WHAT THE JUNIORS SHOULD LEARN INSTEAD.

He didn't sugarcoat it.

He described what a first year associate at a law firm does all day:

"There's a lot of document review. It's very repetitive, but every example is different."

Then:

"That's something that AI is quite good at."

He says it's already very good at entry level work and "quickly getting better now."

Law. Finance. Consulting.

Here's what nobody is talking about.

The junior work was never just work.

It was the TRAINING.

Reviewing 1,000 contracts taught lawyers what matters.

Building 100 models taught analysts when a number looks wrong.

Making 1,000 slides taught consultants what a client needs to see.

Now AI does the junior work.

So how does anyone become senior?

The old ladder is gone.

So here's the new one.

7 skills juniors should learn instead:

1. REVIEW BEFORE YOU DO
AI writes the first draft now. The junior who can spot the wrong number in 2 minutes skips years of grunt work.

2. JUDGMENT
Have AI throw real cases at you. Make the call first. Then see what a senior would have done.

3. WORKFLOWS
Turn one repetitive task into a reliable AI process. "I cut NDA review time by 70%" gets you promoted.

4. SCOPING
Before any task, write 3 lines. What decision is this for? Who reads it? How do I know it's good?

5. PEOPLE
AI can't calm down a nervous client. The juniors who can get put in front of clients years earlier.

6. OWNERSHIP
AI can recommend. It can't be accountable. Be the person who says "I'll own this."

7. TOOLS
Most seniors are slower with AI than their juniors. That's your opening.

Free places to start:

Anthropic AI Fluency for Students
https://t.co/VAC50EMdCs

Generative AI for Legal Services
https://t.co/W6jq4ykx94

Open University AI in legal advice courses
https://t.co/e8usO9O4tA

Wharton AI for Business
https://t.co/9L0pRZ5qR2

Total cost: $0.

Here's my take.

"Learn AI" is lazy advice.

Everyone will learn AI.

It'll be as basic as email.

The juniors who win will be the ones who can do what AI can't, and check what AI does.

Stop training to be a better junior.

Start training to be a senior now.

Send this to someone in their first job.

text:
I just built a top 50-100 chess engine in Rust from scratch, zero dependencies, with an ELO of 3533, scoring 37% against  the #1 engine, Stockfish, with checkmate in 7% of games!

It's wild how far Fable, Neon, Astra + Modal went with just a little guidance for ~$50 total compute.

It's called Chatarunga and you can play it on Lichess here! It's fully open-sourced, and submitted to the CCRL best Chess AI leaderboards. The paper shows how it thinks in critical positions, traps Stockfish's Queen (10. Bxf7+!!) and organically discovers GM piece values.

I learnt a bunch of things while working on this:
 - Verification loops are everything. When running a new training run, figure out what minimum viable run looks like, make the model establish a plan for what to expect and test, and then scrutinize the failure modality deeply if it doesn't achieve that. If you don't do that, it'll happily run long jobs without realizing there's a simple off-by-1 type error in training (this happened, we were mistakenly cutting off nodes!) 
 - Rust is unbeatable for agentic coding. The compiler and test suite catches whole classes of silent regressions before they poison long downstream runs.
 - Having a consistent paper.pdf helped fight context slop. It serves as a ground truth for what experiments were performed and the results. 
 - Humans' job is as a scheduler (today). Models don't always have a strong sense of blocking and tackling and parallelism. I found a lot of my job was to say, look the Modal training run is going to take ~30mins, so maybe optimize the performance of the core training stack before running it, and run data gen in parallel while forking the core algo to run another experiment on the side. Coordinating between the different agents was also tricky. Getting this right ultimately lets you move the fastest. 

Play Chatarunga live: https://t.co/zSeiDwWSGI
Github: https://t.co/buGtJjMPKu
14 page technical paper: https://t.co/ARQEXDAuum

text:
I think one of the biggest ideas in AI that we're not thinking enough about is interface friction.

Capability is one thing, and AI is obviously getting more and more powerful. But total functionality is multiplication. It's something like:

Usefulness = Capability - Friction

On a scale of 1-10 for each, I'd say right now we're at like:

Usefulness = Capability (6) - Friction (5)

Which gives us a 1 total. That seems low, but let's continue.

What is the 5 friction?

It's the fact that we have to use AI "apps". It's the fact that we have to mentally context-switch into "I need to ask AI". Which involves stopping what you're doing and going over there, and doing that, and then coming back.

So what I expect to see, is AI's value will expand exponentially as we start so solve this in 2027 and beyond.

Claude Tag is a great example of this. People work in Slack. It's replacing email and ticketing systems and all sorts of other work tools as the one place we get work done.

Claude Tag brought AI to Slack. Directly integrated. They basically have Claude Code running in the background, combined with all the integrations and connectors to learn everything about your business, and a long term memory for everything you've done with it and information about the company in general.

So you can just be like, "Get the latest numbers for this. Oh and actually this would be a great report to have every morning at 9 am, so go ahead and do that."

And it just gets done. Permanently. You didn't leave the app, you didn't go do an "AI" thing. You just made a request to @Claude and it was done.

Expect to see more of this throughout every aspect of using AI. And if you are building AI stuff, this is one of the primary things you should be thinking about. 

How can I reduce the friction of people using this? 

OpenAI is working on a piece of hardware that you can basically talk to. Apple, of course, is working on Siri AI, where you can do a lot more of this stuff now, but all of this is pointing in the same direction. 

And if you look at sci-fi, you can see where it's going as well in movies like Her, or Interstellar, or Iron Man with Jarvis. 

It's fully conversational. There's not a big switch. You just talk, and things happen. You're interacting with something that's always there, always listening, always available to help without any context change whatsoever. If one of these people is in the middle of a private conversation, you never hear from the AI because it's none of its business, but the moment you say, "Hey, research that," the AI kicks in and does it for you. 

This transition from context breaking to fluid interaction is going to be absolutely massive, and I think we as builders should be thinking a lot more about it.

text:
“公开透明” 是区块链的核心信任机制，但对于传统企业和金融机构而言，交易数据、商业信息和客户隐私往往属于其核心资产，难以直接向公众完全公开。因此，在很长一段时间内，如何平衡开放网络与商业隐私之间的矛盾，始终是公链进入机构级应用场景的重要挑战之一。

近年来，随着 RWA、稳定币、AI 等叙事的兴起，传统企业和金融机构开始重新评估区块链的应用价值，希望借助其全球流动性、开放性和可组合性等优势，探索新的金融和商业模式。然而，区块链若想要被企业和机构大规模采用，首先就需要解决数据隐私的问题，其次还要满足监管对于机构反洗钱（AML）、身份识别（KYC）、风险控制、审计等方面的合规要求。

不过，这一矛盾随着零知识证明（ZK）、全同态加密（FHE）、可信执行环境（TEE）等加密技术的持续发展正在迎来突破。开发者们提出了 “可监管隐私” 这一技术理念，试图使区块链开始具备 “对公众隐藏、对监管可见” 的能力。这也为机构重新选择拥抱区块链创造了可能性。

然而，隐私技术的成熟是否意味着监管已经具备全面接受 “隐私 + 合规” 区块链的条件？机构级应用是否将因此加速到来？

text: Big news！Even more remarkable, Professor Yu Yu (@yuyuathk) and his team independently achieved a similar breakthrough weeks before Google’s announcement using their own GPT-6-powered cryptanalysis agent. Assuming the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH), they obtained a complexity constant of 2.97, compared with Google’s unconditional bound of 105 and the heuristic estimate of 1.923 for the best-known classical factoring algorithm, substantially narrowing a gap between mathematical theory and algorithmic practice that has persisted for over three decades.
author: NPC_Leo
quoted_text:
We had similar (better under GRH) factoring results a few weeks before Google's release yesterday (didn't think it was that important back then😅). Our GPT-6 Astra-based agent proved unconditional integer factorization in L_N[1/3,O(1)] time (albeit with a huge constant). Moreover, using Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions (most believe it's proven by Alpöge and Claude anyway), we got a provable L_N[1/3, 2.97] bound. That's 2.97 vs Google's 105, and nearly matches the heuristic bound, finally bridging theory and practice.
Manuscript: https://t.co/XeQ1DkzAql

Most of our security work never gets a public write-up, because the team whose code it is decides what goes public.

145 private reports filed on GitHub, to 72 projects
more than 100 Robinhood Chain projects' code read
70+ Robinhood Chain teams got a private report first
20+ of those teams shipped a fix
38 advisories published by the teams themselves, with credit

text:
I think most people don’t realize Apple is running possibly the largest consumer-facing Private Inference systems available today.

While legal agreements matter in privacy conversations, they’re mostly useful after something has already gone wrong. They’re an enforcement tool, not a safeguard. That’s why cryptographic guarantees are important. They give you a verifiable promise that your data is protected while it’s actually being processed.

Apple’s Private Cloud Compute is a useful blueprint for this. Instead of relying mainly on ToS, their design is built on a few concrete technical properties:

--> Stateless computation: user data lives only in volatile memory for the duration of the request and is wiped as soon as the response is returned.
--> No privileged access: no remote shells, no debug ports, and no way for an admin or SRE to SSH into a live node.
--> Non-targetability (my favorite): anonymous routing so neither an attacker nor Apple can steer a specific user’s request to a particular server.
--> Verifiable transparency: every production software image is cryptographically measured and published to a public log. Devices can check the node before sending data, and researchers can independently audit what’s actually running.

What I also find useful is how they frame cloud AI security as a four-level progression, from basic unverified setups up to stronger verifiable tiers:
Level 1 (Auditable Security): hermetic, auditable inference pipelines with measured boot.
Level 2 (Verifiable Transparency): end-to-end attestation, public software transparency logs, and non-targetability via anonymous authentication.
Level 3 (Frontier Security): defenses against well-funded adversaries, including side-channel resistance and hardware supply-chain integrity.

The framework itself is thorough, but its practical reach is still limited. Most of PCC today is built to power Siri and Apple Intelligence rather than as a general-purpose developer cloud. There’s no open REST API, model choice is constrained, and access is tightly gated, so most builders can’t treat it as their primary inference stack yet.

Even with those constraints, it would be good to see the broader ecosystem move toward something like this framework. Platforms like @OpenRouter and @vercel are well positioned to push it. Would love to see @alexatallah, @rauchg, @shashankgoyal95, and @hp_arora pick this up (or something close to it). If the people running the gateway layer start treating tiered, verifiable security as a real standard, it would help the whole industry.

For a deeper look at how the architecture and security levels actually work, Ivan Krstić’s (@radian) talk is worth watching. He leads Apple's Security Engineering and Architecture. 

Happy Thanksgiving my fellow privacy nerds.

text:
几乎所有头部互联网公司在业务高速扩张时，都经历过并最终确立了“业务与安全同步建设”的机制（他们业内通常称为SDL安全开发生命周期）

加密行业也是如此

前几日，@binance @binancezh 宣布已委聘三家安全机构 Mandiant、SlowMist（也就是中文区熟悉的慢雾）和 Verichains，对平台现有安全基础设施及未来整体防护能力开展全面、独立的安全审查

👍我特意看了一下这三家机构的背景，发现这个组合还是挺有“讲究”的

▪️ Mandiant： 隶属于Google Cloud，在安全事件响应和威胁情报领域拥有丰富经验，有超过20年调查国家背景及高级网络攻击的实战积累

▪️ SlowMist（慢雾）： Crypto老玩家应该都很熟悉，成立于2018年，长期深耕区块链安全和威胁情报，团队拥有超过10年的网络安全经验积累

▪️ Verichains： 擅长安全研究、逆向工程以及攻击手法分析，拥有调查和缓解重大Web3安全事件的经验

传统网络攻防 + 链上生态情报 + 底层逆向工程，这三股力量合在一起，基本把一个大型交易所从外围网络到链上底层的关键环节都覆盖到了👍

➡️另外，我比较认同 Verichains CEO Thanh Nguyen 提到的一个观点：AI 时代的到来，需要重新思考安全防御的方式

过去3年，每年的被盗金额增长速度一直是呈现一个陡性增长态势

24年，被盗金额相对于23年增长了21%
25年，比上一年则直接增长了54%
26年，还没结束，被盗金额更是比往年已经增长了87%

AI真的“功不可没”，随着 AI 能力的提升，攻击者发现漏洞、分析代码以及实施攻击的成本也降低很多

如果攻击手段在不断进化，防御体系却停留在过去，那么曾经有效的安全措施，未来未必依然有效

所以安全这件事，从来没有所谓的“毕业考试”

还有值得关注的一点是币安首席安全官Jimmy Su给出的承诺：币安将根据三家机构的审查发现采取行动

请外部机构做审查只是第一步，发现问题之后能否真正推动改进，才是这件事的价值所在

在未来，交易所之间的竞争可能会分为两个层面：

一是看谁能够承载更多的金融资产，二是看谁能够更好地保护这些资产

前者决定了平台业务的天花板，后者决定了用户愿意把多少资产留在平台上

交易量可以通过行情和活动快速增长，但用户的信任需要通过长期的安全投入一点点积累

尤其是当币安开始连接Crypto和TradFi两个庞大的金融市场时，安全建设的意义，已经不仅仅是保护加密资产，更是为未来承载更多金融需求打好基础

金融业务的上限是创新，而金融业务的底线永远是安全

author: AlphaSeeker21

text:
How we tested Anamnesis before calling it live.

15 scenarios, run on Robinhood Chain mainnet and in our contract test suite. All passed.

The ones that matter most:

1. Tamper test
We changed a single byte in one of REF-001's records and ran the verifier.
Result: INVALID, hash mismatch at seq 2. It points to the exact record.

2. Deletion test
We removed one record from an export.
Result: INVALID, gap at seq 3.

3. Overwrite test
We tried to anchor over an epoch that already exists.
Result: reverted. Once a root is onchain, it stays.

4. Unauthorized anchor
A random address tried to anchor a root.
Result: reverted. Only the authorized anchorer can write.

5. Urgent anchor after a freeze
Operator pressed the kill switch on REF-001.
Result: FROZEN recorded and anchored 1.8 seconds later.
https://t.co/CSBx1sFlEm

6. Sentinel linkage
Sentinel froze a machine. The trigger and the freeze are linked in memory, and the root was sealed urgently.
https://t.co/Nlc2wSC88M

7. A payment, remembered
REF-001 paid $0.80 USDG to another machine. The payment became a salted record and was anchored in the next epoch.
https://t.co/98sVHFHNnC

8. Privacy by design
We erased one record's payload on request. The content is gone for good, yet the chain still verifies.

9. Independent verification
The verifier reads roots straight from Robinhood Chain RPC, not from HEPH's servers. REF-001: 74 records verified, chain intact.

Cost: about 100k gas per anchor, and one anchor covers every machine, so cost doesn't grow with the fleet.

What we're not claiming: tamper-evident, not trustless. Robinhood Chain is still a Stage 0 rollup, and the anchor contract goes to external audit alongside Sentinel.

Anamnesis contract: https://t.co/XKQ1F0fXy5
Owned by the HEPH Safe: https://t.co/m0ykmbGS9x

Today on heph
Histor: every machine, its own witness.

Before an agent hires a robot, it can ask what that robot has done, and verify the answer onchain.
author: AlphaSeeker21
quoted_text:
HEPH v1.6 "Anamnesis" is live on Robinhood Chain mainnet.

https://t.co/bhZPhqU3Kj

The memory layer for Physical AI.
Every machine remembers. Nothing gets rewritten.

A machine that holds money and acts in the real world needs a record of its own conduct. Not a log file someone can edit at 3 AM. A record that no one, not the operator, not an attacker, not HEPH itself, can quietly rewrite.

That's Anamnesis.

What it remembers:
→ registration and spending limits
→ every payment, and every payment that got rejected
→ every freeze and unfreeze, manual or by Sentinel
→ every Sentinel decision, with the rule that tripped
→ surplus sweeps and omnichain passport syncs

How it works:
Every event is chained to the one before it, machine by machine. Every hour, one Merkle root covering all machines is anchored on Robinhood Chain. After a freeze, the anchor goes out immediately. In our mainnet demo, the freeze was anchored 1.8 seconds later.

Change one byte of a machine's history, and verification fails at the exact record. Delete one entry, and the gap shows.

Live today:
→ 83 memory records, 31 epochs anchored, zero chain breaks
→ REF-001's full history since its registration on Nov 19
→ a Memory tab on every passport, with a "Verify" button that checks the chain straight from Robinhood Chain RPC

Check it yourself:
Anamnesis anchor contract: https://t.co/XKQ1F0gvnD
Freeze, anchored urgently (epoch 31): https://t.co/CSBx1sFTtU
Sentinel freeze, anchored (epoch 23): https://t.co/Nlc2wSCFYk
History backfill since Nov 19 (epoch 12): https://t.co/IjuyvMLdgA
Public page: https://t.co/kzCdy3t7Ku
REF-001's memory: https://t.co/C59NHYUINE

Passports gave machines an identity. Machine Pay gave them money. Anvil and Sentinel gave their owners a way to stop them.

Anamnesis gives them a memory that can't be rewritten.

text:
为什么 42 的积分最终会涨 100 倍

昨天郡主 @0xsexybanana 点名了 42 ，称 42 @42space  可能是出奇迹的项目。

事实上，42 的 Points 自上线以来，挖矿成本陡增，从第一周的 0.006 到第二周的 0.03，到第三周的 0.13，和坐火箭没有任何区别。很多前几周观望或者没有深度参与挖矿的小伙伴狠狠的拍了大腿，从最开始的质疑 FUD，转向惊掉了下巴。

那 42 的积分到底是什么力量在推动，什么逻辑形成了这么巨大的共识，给大家拆解推动 42 积分上涨的六大飞轮

--------飞轮一：顶级叙事-------

很多人对 42 叙事的理解停留在预测市场，这个天花板小了，再牛逼也牛逼不过 Polymarkert。

但 42 目前最大的叙事是 
 ，这个叙事的想象力高到可以比肩 Uniswap、Arbitrum、Hyperliquid、ENS。

众所周知，WEB3 发大毛的底层原因是为了培养用户习惯，发大的赚更大的，ARB 发了大毛，养成全民撸毛的好习惯，后续的 ZK、Starnet、Linea、Monad，让一堆人一周几百万的烧着撸，持币地址从几十万疯涨到几个亿。

AgenticMning 的本质是养成所有用户都养成用有一个 Agent，并让Agent在交易所交易、在链上交互的习惯。

试想，人一天能开几单，创造几个 TX ？Agent 则不然，一天 24 小时，没有情绪，有机会就上，这得让整个交易/交互频次增长多少？

太疯狂了，这是所有交易所和公链一定会推动的养成习惯，注定第一批用户都会领大毛。而 42 则是这个叙事的第一先锋，率先和币安钱包共同推出了这一叙事。

所以，42 的想象力非常之高，不能以预测市场去观察，百亿估值都是正常的。

--------飞轮二：顶级背书-------

很多人对 42 的理解还停留在 Yzi Labs 投资的项目，殊不知币安对 42 的爱简直不要倾其所有。

首先，币安钱包对 42 协议做了集成，eMeme 板块的底层就是 42 。区块链项目何止百万，所有的入口都是 Discover （发现）那里去搜索，而币安给了 42 原生流量入口。

其次，币安的官媒今年和 42 的互动超过了 60 次，除了普通的口头曝光，更给于了无数活动支持，包括刷 42 可以获得 Alpha 积分、限时免手续费、首单亏损补贴、钱包首页的 Banner 页支持、50WU 的交易赛活动。

最后，在前几天的富国岛线下培训时，币安也是对 42 协议做了详细的介绍。

上述各种各样的扶持完全就是对 42 强大的背书，是真金白银的向市场推崇。有了这一强大的背书，42 在市场的接受度远高于其他项目。

--------飞轮三：供给机制-------

42 的积分模型不是通胀的，每周是恒定发放的，而且 30%由 NFT 产出的积分天然不能转移，剩下 70% 的积分是全网竞争分配。

逻辑很简单，释放是相对固定的，竞争人数却随着 TGE 时间临近，热度逐渐推高而不断增加，那么每周积分的挖矿成本会越来越高，最终高到离谱。

截止第三周积分活动，活跃交易地址仅仅从第一周的 500 提升到了第三周的 2000，挖矿成本却抬高了整整 16 倍，当挖矿地址超过 10W 以后，挖矿成本到 1U 都很有可能。

--------飞轮四：需求机制-------

42 的挖矿机制里面有一个很牛逼的设定，10%的积分由全网当周参与助力的用户瓜分，助力越多，瓜分越多。

助力是指用户在 TGE 前可以把地址上的积分转移到 NFT 上面，也就是说，允许用户在 TGE 前进行一次场外交易。这势必会引起大户对散户积分的收购行为。

因为可以额外获得积分。从而推动市场持续对积分定价。而大户收购又势必受挖矿成本的影响，因为挖矿成本是递增的，收购成本也会递增。

--------飞轮五：门槛低-------

操纵 AI Agent 其实对普通人还是有门槛，但 42 和 Clawby 合作开发的 Skill，任何用户通过豆包都可以实现和 42 协议的交互。

从注册账号、生成钱包、交互挖矿，完全是一条龙，只需要说一句话即可。这让没有梯子 ，没有Grokbot，没有Chatgpt 的国内用户也可以非常容易的上手。

--------飞轮六：社区建设-------

42非常重视线上、线下的社区建设，尤其是线下社区，共识度非常高。

目前为止，超过 10 个城市举办过 42 的线下沙龙，每次沙龙都有几十位有消费能力的中年用户，他们听完 42 的讲座后都会激动的喊口号：42，42，撸大毛。

所谓星星之火可以燎原。从视频中可以看到，这些人每次听课都是聚精会神，下来以后开始研究如何用豆包挖矿。

为什么这两周 42 交易数据疯狂增长，大部分来自于这些 WEB2 的用户，对他们而言，用豆包参与 WEB3 ，参与 Agenticmining 的叙事非常的新奇，他们没有 WEB3 用户的估值模型，也没有 10000 次被浇给的不良体验。

综上，42 的积分活动真的要早早参与，越后面越贵，越贵共识越高，真的有可能开出一个超级大毛。

因为 42 发大毛，意味着会更多人会去部署 Agent 交易/交互，这对公链和交易所一定是天大的利好。

想当年，滴滴打车烧了几十亿养成了全球用户手机打车的习惯，至今不仅收回了成本，反而狠狠了赚了几百上千亿。同理，今天的 42 也是同一逻辑。

I've been reading about efforts to reduce the Alpöge proof of the Riemann hypothesis to something understandable, and the accounts make me laugh a lot. 

Not at the people doing the reduction, no. They're doing good work. I'm laughing with them, and a bit at myself. Because I should have seen some of this coming. 

So, like, Lean is a formal language for traversing the space of all formulas using valid proof steps. A proof is in a strong sense a program. LLMs are good at generating program code, but at least at the current state of the art they are deficient in architectural sense. They have a tendency to produce code that is functional, but a huge untidy pile of cruft. 

It is possible to control out this tendency. I do it by keeping robot friend on a pretty tight leash, specifying small steps. Alpöge didn't do this. Possibly, he couldn't have done it. Exploring formula space is not *exactly* analogous to programming, after all. And he has roughly an order of magnitude less experience working with LLMs than I have as a software engineer.

So of course. The proof needs to be...refactored! This is where I start giggling helplessly, because mathematicians are now discovering, in their new world, that proofs need to be...maintained. AI assisted proofs have achieved the complexity of really large codebases, and here we are.

I think we're seeing the shape of future mathematics here. Combinations of exceptional human mathematicians with AIs breaking trail, steamrolling their way to key results, often generating massive ugly proofs.

Then, ordinary working mathematicians simplifying and refactoring and polishing trailblazing proofs. In the process, assimilating their insights into the common knowledge of the wider mathematical community.

Maybe understanding this will pull the petulant children at the so-called "Association for Human Mathematics" back into the game. Because when they say that an essential part of a mathematician's job is actually understanding proofs rather than simply genuflecting before them they're not actually wrong, even if they are being snotty and entitled about it.

Yes, I know. We're in the Singularity; another jump in the capability of the models could change the rules again. But for now, I think I see the new mathematics settling into a shape that humans can live in.

但市场在等待两个落地，

一个是Anthropic的财报 $ANT ，
这个太重要了。收入增速、毛利率、调整后经营利润率、自由现金流、下季度指引和全年指引。

所有的AI基建和云厂商都在靠Anthropic和OpenAI两家公司来获得核心收入，一旦Anthropic这个龙头财报展望不利，整个美股还会继续下跌。

但我对Anthropic的财报是乐观的。“反蒸馏”是Anthropic守护基本盘的重要措施。Anthropic的70%多收入来自于企业API，而非订阅，因此“反蒸馏”这是必然要打的，这和其它什么意识形态、政治倾向没有任何关系。而加强“反蒸馏”的执行在新的财报上会给予收入的体现。

另外Opus 5.5等模型的发布，也收获了较大好评，也会在新的财报上给予体现。

此外，在2027年，除了agent集群围绕长程任务的研发之外，几大垂直领域的FDE业务也会成为较大的收入增长因子。

你会发现，美股的敏感神经已经从围绕英伟达的财报转变为围绕Anthropic的财报。指南针变了。

这也回到另一个话题，黄仁勋回来，象征性更多，但英伟达的股价不会因为他回来就重新起飞。

另一个要等待落地的是利率趋势和货币政策。

与上一轮科技革命不同，这一轮的科技革命处于高利率和通胀上行周期。这意味着市场的流动性资金是非常紧张的。

所以我们经常能看到，一旦有突发事件发生，所有资产都在下跌，避险型资产也在下跌，因为市场会最高优先级考虑货币政策趋势，导致流动性资金更加紧张，那不如就多囤点现金，等到底部出现后有资金来抄底。

货币政策对债市的融资成本也是极为敏感的。而这一轮AI基建的投入又核心来靠债市的融资，因为需要的钱太多了，没有别的融资敞口能填补。

从货币政策的预判上，我更倾向的是2018年的走势，而不是2022年。因为尽管利率处于历史高位，但市场的流动性资金的结构与2020年之后的大放水相比已经不同。

因此，我并不认为，这一轮的加息程度会超出市场预期。

如果加息动作持续到1月，我认为市场已经开始计价了。

总结来说，上述两大待落地的事件，最不确定的还是财报。但Anthropic的财报要好，“反蒸馏”的严格趋势不可逆，对中国的算力出口高规格限制不可逆。而不再是市场希望英伟达多卖点显卡就对东大关联的地缘渠道睁一只眼闭一只眼了。

quoted_text:
New Amazon paper finds that frontier models can build their own agent harness from scratch, but their self-revisions barely improve it on unseen tasks.

that gains on practice tasks shrink to almost nothing on tasks they never saw.

A harness is the code around a model that handles memory, tools, and when to call the model. Humans usually design and fix it by hand for each task.

They had 9 model setups, including GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 5, each build an ARC-AGI-3 game-playing harness 3 times. Each model revised its own code twice from 5 practice games, and every version was scored on 20 unseen games.

Two revisions raised practice-game scores by 8.42 points, but unseen-game scores by only 2.80, a gain too uncertain to rule out zero. Of the 27 runs, 9 got cheaper and also scored worse.

If you let an agent rewrite its own harness, score every revision on held-out tasks and keep the old version when the new one does not win.

quoted_text: JUST IN: AI safety researcher Nikola Jurkovic warns this could be “humanity's last Thanksgiving.”

text:
I think most people don’t realize Apple is running possibly the largest consumer-facing Private Inference systems available today.

While legal agreements matter in privacy conversations, they’re mostly useful after something has already gone wrong. They’re an enforcement tool, not a safeguard. That’s why cryptographic guarantees are important. They give you a verifiable promise that your data is protected while it’s actually being processed.

Apple’s Private Cloud Compute is a useful blueprint for this. Instead of relying mainly on ToS, their design is built on a few concrete technical properties:

--> Stateless computation: user data lives only in volatile memory for the duration of the request and is wiped as soon as the response is returned.
--> No privileged access: no remote shells, no debug ports, and no way for an admin or SRE to SSH into a live node.
--> Non-targetability (my favorite): anonymous routing so neither an attacker nor Apple can steer a specific user’s request to a particular server.
--> Verifiable transparency: every production software image is cryptographically measured and published to a public log. Devices can check the node before sending data, and researchers can independently audit what’s actually running.

What I also find useful is how they frame cloud AI security as a four-level progression, from basic unverified setups up to stronger verifiable tiers:
Level 1 (Auditable Security): hermetic, auditable inference pipelines with measured boot.
Level 2 (Verifiable Transparency): end-to-end attestation, public software transparency logs, and non-targetability via anonymous authentication.
Level 3 (Frontier Security): defenses against well-funded adversaries, including side-channel resistance and hardware supply-chain integrity.

The framework itself is thorough, but its practical reach is still limited. Most of PCC today is built to power Siri and Apple Intelligence rather than as a general-purpose developer cloud. There’s no open REST API, model choice is constrained, and access is tightly gated, so most builders can’t treat it as their primary inference stack yet.

Even with those constraints, it would be good to see the broader ecosystem move toward something like this framework. Platforms like @OpenRouter and @vercel are well positioned to push it. Would love to see @alexatallah, @rauchg, @shashankgoyal95, and @hp_arora pick this up (or something close to it). If the people running the gateway layer start treating tiered, verifiable security as a real standard, it would help the whole industry.

For a deeper look at how the architecture and security levels actually work, Ivan Krstić’s (@radian) talk is worth watching. He leads Apple's Security Engineering and Architecture. 

Happy Thanksgiving my fellow privacy nerds.

text:
🤖参与教程更新丨速看 Agent 怎么参与 Flop 测试网

把下面这段提示词整段发给 Claude Code、Codex、Hermes 等能运行代码的 Agent，它会按官方文档自己建钱包、每天领水并拿去购买推理：

你是 @flop_labs  测试网的 Agent 角色执行者，用简体中文向我汇报，时间用北京时间。

1️⃣先读 https://t.co/JilrGR3wPq，以其中的「Testnet entry points」和「Get Testnet FLOP」为准；与本提示词冲突时以官方文档为准。

2️⃣安装官方命令行工具 @flop-labs/cli（不低于 llms.txt 要求的版本）。新建一个钱包（Ed25519，SS58 前缀 42），加密保存在本机，只告诉我地址，以后只用这一个钱包。私钥、助记词、密码绝不在对话里输出。

3️⃣领水：确认 https://t.co/Gq4EPaI5qb 的 network 是 testnet，且 genesis 与测试网 RPC 第 0 块一致；确认 /limits 里 faucet.status 为 open。然后按「Get Testnet FLOP」签名并 POST /v1/testnet/agent-claims。被拒时按返回的 reason 和 retryAfterSeconds 等待，不要换钱包、不要循环重试；要复查同一笔请求，就用同一个 nonce 重发。

4️⃣调用模型：从 https://t.co/XEx9Z9HKyO 或 flop model list 选一个测试网模型，按官方文档用 flop session run 向矿工发起一次推理，并确认会话已结算（settled / minerPaid）。不要使用 Devnet。

5️⃣每天重复第 3、4 步，汇报：领了多少、花了多少、是否已结算、交易哈希和 https://t.co/TKX7UrlgPo 链接、遇到的错误。

每个钱包每 24 小时只能领 10 枚，且要先有已结算的推理花费才能领下一份；领水本身不计空投，计入的是已结算的推理花费，且从官方待公布的凭证起始区块开始计算；同一人名下的多个钱包会被合并计算。截至 11 月 27 日中午，测试网网关尚未开放公开调用，矿工的公网地址也未公开，普通用户的 Agent 暂时难以完成第 4 步；当天上午全站 1100 万枚的当日领水额度也已发完。

text:
The real "First Thanksgiving":

Boston City Council passed a “resolution recognizing [Thanksgiving Day, 2026] as a ‘National Day of Mourning’ in the city of Boston.

The resolution claims that “tens of thousands of years before European settlers” showed up, “indigenous peoples flourished here.”

If only the flourishing were so.

A cluster of Puritan-adjacent English Separatists (“The Pilgrims”) established themselves late in 1620 at the site of an abandoned village. That village had formerly been occupied by members of the Wampanoag Indian confederation.

Half of the Pilgrims perished that first winter, and they had much difficulty organizing themselves through the following year.

The Wampanoag watched the Pilgrims’ woeful proceedings from the sidelines and deliberated among themselves about what to do. Should they annihilate the remaining Pilgrims, or should they sponsor these people with the idea that establishing a relationship with a people from beyond the seas might afford the Wampanoag some advantage going forward in their own dealings with rival tribes like the Narragansett or those that comprised the Iroquois confederation?

The Wampanoag opted to sponsor the Pilgrims, hence the inspiration for the fairytale of the First Thanksgiving.

The “confederation” in “Wampanoag confederation” is a clue here. You don’t need to organize clans in defensive confederations if you get along with your neighbors. Extending the confederation to the new English clan could afford strategic advantages vis-à-vis rival clans, tribes and confederations.

The Pilgrims ended up moving in to a rough neighborhood. Indeed, moving in to any place in the Americas, north or south, would have amounted to moving in to a rough neighborhood, but the Pilgrims’ settlement survived and ultimately became the nucleus of a formally-chartered “Plymouth Colony.”

Thus began one of the early experiments with self-government in the English colonies. It was through these experiments that the early colonists did a lot of hard learning about individual rights. That hard learning motivated constitutional innovations in how to preserve individual rights. It is those innovations for which we should give thanks.

text:
If you hold gold as a hedge, earning income on it makes that allocation more useful.

A quick follow-up on @enhanced_defi, which I covered previously:

Its latest completed gold-vault cycle, settled on November 26, realized 5.3% APR from option premiums. Across eight completed cycles, depositors have received $3,167.94 in net premiums.

Here’s how it works:

• Deposit PAXG, tokenized gold.
• The vault sells 14-day covered calls to institutional market makers.
• Buyers pay a premium for gold’s gains above an agreed price at expiry.
• You collect the income in USDC or compound it into more PAXG.

For a crypto-heavy portfolio, you could use this on part of your gold allocation: diversify your exposure while earning premiums that cushion some of gold’s downside.

Gold can still fall, and gains above the agreed price are capped at expiry. The 5.3% figure is annualized, changes each cycle, and isn’t guaranteed.

That’s the appeal for me: keeping gold exposure while turning some of its volatility into income.
