author: jonbma
quoted_text:
I think 2026 has been one of the most challenging years to navigate equities over the past four years.

Let's walk through how this year started and all of the things one needed to do in order to actually participate in the bull market...

To start off, I think 2026 was fundamentally different from 2023, 2024, and 2025 because of sector rotation and long/short pair trades across different sectors. 

Over the past 3 years, everyone lost money together across all industries when the markets went down and everyone made money when everything went up. The trend was quite literally your friend and if you followed it short, you won, if you followed it long, you won. 

2026 was different.

First, in January you had to basically get two trades right to really benefit: long oil and long metals. We saw gold and silver breakout of a 15 year base and we saw a Venezuela operation that made oil the most important commodity trade of the year. However, you then had to sell commodities into a blow off top by the end of January. If you didn't, you had a 40% drawdown waiting for you. 

As we got into the end of February, we saw the administration take us into a war. No one knew how long it really would last for as it was pitched as a short, special operation. It ended up taking the S&P down to 6200 and growth stocks were down 30-40%. Once again, you had to really be long oil or short the $QQQ to seriously benefit off of this.

So, let's say you bought the dip coming out of March and into April when the first ceasefire was announced. We essentially got the most aggressive, leveraged rally we had seen in a decade from March to June...but only in semis. 

If you didn't own the semis, you really didn't benefit. You also couldn't just own anything in $SMH, you had to own very high-beta semiconductor stocks that were the definition of picks and shovels, essentially the bottleneck bros trade. Owning $NVDA was not going to carry your year even though it was the most important semiconductor company. Now, you could have also participated in some other sectors, like space with names like $RKLB $RDW $ASTS, but you had to be aggressively in something within the most high-beta growth sectors for the market to feel comfortable giving you a premium. 

If you owned anything in software, you had to suffer 50-60% declines across some of the most incredible companies in the space like $PLTR, $SHOP, and $MSFT because the narrative became that Anthropic would kill software. $IGV got cut by 30%. 

Well, then comes July. Now, we finally figured out why software was getting hit as hard as it did. Leopold had made one trade very popular -- long semis, short software. Other hedgefunds had copied it. The problem was, the trade had become so popular and so leveraged that other market participants realized a collapse of the trade could literally wipe out entire funds and the overall sectors. As much money as was made on the upside for the AI trade, the downside had now begun. Leopold's fund blew up but survived, Citadel came in and bought everything at a steep discount, and AI names basically fell 50-60%. 

In August, we got a bounce. If the entire downside of the trade was based on a hedgefund getting over levered, then that meant the AI trade was back on since the main event had already taken place. However, things felt different. The excitement around memory had faded. The neoclouds were not seeing the same momentum as they were before. AI names were still doing well, but something obviously fell off. If you did not sell the June highs and chose to hold on, you were basically getting ready to roundtrip the entire gains as we progressed through the year. The space names literally fell 70% as $SPCX marked the top for the market and for the space names. 

The reason this is so important is because I believe many people bought most of these AI names in May/June, not early in the year. I am a victim of that as well. The rally was so aggressive that if you didn't have any meaningful semi exposure, you probably ended up buying something that was more rooted in hype even if the fundamentals were strong. I mean some of these names were flat for 25 years and had just seen a massive move up, so obviously there were a ton of people buying into names that likely were too high to begin with. 

Towards the end of August, the software trade finally started coming back, along with the hyperscalers. $META began showing off Muse, $MSFT guided to FCF positive, $AMZN had their best operating margins ever. Apple $AAPL was strong all year as a defensive play. The narrative about Claude destroying software went away. 

September was flat. Nothing crazy to see.

Then came October. We hit ATHs again, not every name in the AI trade got to their June highs, but many names came back. $NBIS was back to $250, $NVDA hit $240, it felt like the bull market was back in action. 

Unfortunately, $CRWV was the reason everything changed. By the middle of October, their bonds began to plummet and yields began to spike. Their unsecured debit was yielding 15%...everyone was confused for why a neocloud with $130B+ in backlog was seeing their debt get sold this aggressively. At the same time, Jensen went to Europe for business and back in the states, you couldn't go a day without some type of datacenter delay, credit headline, backstop issues...basically, the entire market started wondering if the financing of this buildout was possible. The 10 year hit 5.4%, the S&P stayed at all time highs, and AI stocks started to weaken but they didn't give out yet. You could've sold and protected some gains here across the entire market, but if you didn't, November was going to be what really wrecked you.

We enter November with the midterms. Everyone, including myself, though it was going to be a clearing event. Instead, it ended up being an event that showed the market that democrats had such a majority of support because of the concerns around the Iran war (which still hadn't ended) and datacenter backlash, that now what needed to be priced in was the slowdown of the buildout and a potential 2027 peak to capex growth.

This changed everything, and the market really started to feel it. By the middle of November, Jensen was ousted as CEO after reports about affairs with a Chinese spy and the market basically round tripped across the entire AI trade. The only safety during this time was consumer staples like $MCD $TGT $COST, basically companies that didn't have anything to do with AI. We got some horrible inflation reports so the chances for a hike went further up and that continued to put pressure on growth stocks. By last Friday, the S&P hit $689 as the Nasdaq fell 5.5% in a day and we wiped out $7.4T of marketcap within a week. 

We still don't know if that was the bottom or if we created a double bottom with Wednesday's price action and maybe we are out of the woods, but most AI names ended up either going negative YTD or meaningfully came down from their peak. 

All of this to say, it's been a hard year. I think everyone should have some empathy for everyone this year. If you were heavy on margin, chances are you got wiped out as we saw the KOSPI in South Korea round trip a +100% move on their entire index. If you didn't take profits at the top and just kept buying, even when the fundamentals made sense for a company like $MU when it was already down 30% from the highs, you had to experience another 25% decline. If you went short into the first ceasefire, you got hit hard. If you went long commodities at the end of Jan, you got hit hard. If you even picked SaaS names like $NOW at $80 and saw it go to $150 and didn't sell, you got hit hard because of one earnings. $META was a big winner for so many people as the company got through lawsuits and went from $520 to $780, but then they diluted and the stock crashed. Obviously, if you had a meaningful $NVDA position, you had to see that entire position go to 8x forward earnings because of what happened with Jensen. Crypto...didn't even really get to have a meaningful moment outside of the 60K to 85K pump on $BTC which gave some momentum to names like $MSTR $COIN and $HOOD but then Bitcoin also fell back below 60K and crypto ended up falling with tech stocks. 

I am not sure if 2027 is going to be this challenging or because we went through this year, maybe next year is going to be similar to one direction across all sectors.

What I do know is volatility is likely not going to end as this market has more and more narratives being part of the story daily with the Fed, AI's impact across the economy, geopolitics, and more. My fundamental belief is being long in exceptional companies that can compound earnings over the long term will likely outperform most strategies and there should be risk mitigation through trying to avoid the really excited moments or really ugly moments by never getting too happy or too sad. There's always opportunities to trim and opportunities to buy the dip, but being net long in the most important technology revolution we have ever seen is probably a better idea than not. 

Finally, I really think we should try to have more empathy for one another because the equity markets are supposed to be hard. We all follow them everyday because we are junkies that are obsessed with this game, but this game isn't easy, and 2026 showed how hard the game can be with all the things we had to navigate. Hoping 2027 is a little easier but even if it isn't, excited to still try to navigate and have a chance at playing the game.

text:
This is Neverland.lean — a Riemann Hypothesis proof we built on purpose to be fake.

It compiles in Lean. The kernel accepts it. Axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound — the standard three, nothing more.

The same file also proves the Riemann Hypothesis is false.

Our zeta function is a constant. Our "nontrivial zeros" are defined as zeros that are already on the critical line. The hard identity is the same term written twice. Every trick is annotated against the finding it mirrors in the real artifact.

Lean isn't broken. "It compiles" certifies that a statement follows from its definitions. It cannot certify that the definitions are honest.

Run it yourself — one file, twelve seconds: https://t.co/rr2xtB1Bzs

Educational. Not a paper. A demonstration.

#RiemannHypothesis #Mathematics #Lean

text:
最近看到不少人認為，交易所推出 TCG 卡機，就是在吸引更多人參與賭博，甚至質疑平台會在背後暗改抽卡機率。

但早期參與鏈上 TCG 的玩家都知道，現在導入 VRF 隨機數驗證機制的卡機，只要卡池配置、抽取邏輯與驗證機制足夠透明，就能大幅降低黑箱操作的可能性。

再來，如果說抽卡是賭博，那麼 Meme、預測市場、合約交易，甚至是項目打新，哪一個不存在投機與博弈的成分？

Web3 的本質，很大程度上就是風險與收益的博弈，否則大家為什麼來到幣圈尋找財富機會？

所以每次看到有人將 TCG 簡單地定義為賭博，我都覺得有些啼笑皆非。

大家往往只想聽自己想聽的、看自己想看的，卻忽略了事物的本質。

事實上，TCG 的可塑性遠比大家想像的還要高。

・它可以是資產，透過質押獲取收益。
・它可以是收藏品，具有實體交付與長期收藏的價值。
・它可以是交易標的，透過二級市場進行流通。
・它可以結合卡牌升級、合成與煉金機制，讓價值較低的卡牌有機會再次挑戰更高的稀有度。
・未來甚至可以延伸至 CardFi、抵押借貸、指數交易及更多金融衍生產品。

除此之外，它也可以是一個具有娛樂性的入口。

就好比日本的柏青哥（Pachinko），多數玩家都知道長期遊玩並不容易獲利，但為什麼這個產業依然能夠存在數十年？

因為對部分玩家而言，消費的目的並不完全是為了賺錢，而是追求娛樂、感官刺激與遊戲體驗，當然，這也伴隨著成癮與金錢損失的風險。

TCG × iGaming 的發展同樣如此。

從開包動畫、稀有卡牌揭曉時的驚喜，到卡牌升級、合成與收藏圖鑑，這些都是能夠延伸的娛樂體驗。

而 TCG 與傳統 iGaming 最大的差異之一，在於玩家取得的卡牌可以對應真實存在的實體資產，並具備獨立於平台之外的收藏與交易市場。

這也是為什麼我一直看好 RWA × TCG 這條賽道。

它同時具備娛樂、收藏、交易與金融四種屬性，也有機會成為連接 Web2 與 Web3 的重要入口。

我並不否認抽卡具有博弈性，也不認為所有 TCG 平台都值得信任。

但抽卡只是 TCG 生態中的一種玩法，而不是 TCG 的全部。

真正值得討論的，應該是機率是否透明、資產是否真實、價格是否合理、玩家權益是否受到保障，以及平台能否建立一個可持續發展的生態。

如果你只看見 TCG 的博弈屬性，卻看不見它背後的娛樂價值、收藏文化、資產流動性與金融可組合性，那麼你可能也低估了 RWA × TCG 在 Web3 的發展潛力。

text:
A few thoughts on Huawei’s HBM work at ISSCC.

I see it as Huawei’s Tau-style way around the EUV bottleneck. China is finally bypassing JEDEC and going its own way.

If this actually works, Huawei could get HBM4-class bandwidth per stack at HBM3-class pin speeds. Without EUV-class DRAM scaling, it’s hard to push HBM pin speeds higher. So Huawei is taking a different route altogether.

Wafer-scale hybrid bonding is also an area where China is strong. (YMTC uses wafer-to-wafer, or W2W, hybrid bonding too.)

What I find especially interesting is that HBM makers in the Western ecosystem, including Samsung, use leading-edge foundry nodes like TSMC’s 3nm for their logic dies to hit high pin speeds. Huawei is constrained on both fronts. It can’t scale its DRAM as far, and it doesn’t have access to leading-edge foundry nodes. So it’s going wider to make up for those process limitations.

Of course, if it were that simple, Samsung would have done it already. The big drawback with W2W is that you can’t exclude individual defective dies before stacking, so the yields of the individual layers multiply.

Say each layer has a 95% yield. Stack five layers and the yield drops to 77%.

And 95% is already a pretty optimistic assumption. At 70% per layer, the yield for a five-layer stack drops to just 17%. That’s a disaster.

What makes this even more painful is that it eats into China’s already limited supply of DRAM wafers. Die-to-wafer (D2W) bonding lets you select known-good dies before stacking. For a five-layer stack, W2W uses 1/y⁴ times as many wafers per good stack as D2W, where y is the yield per layer. At a stack yield of 77%, W2W uses 1.23× as many wafers as D2W. At 17%, that jumps to a whopping 4.16×.

In other words, in that scenario, China would need more than four times as many wafers as SK hynix to make a single HBM stack. That would mean China needs more than four times the combined DRAM production capacity of South Korea and Micron to match U.S. AI accelerator shipments. (That’s the worst-case scenario.)

Still, it’s a fascinating approach. It feels like Chinese and Western tech standards are gradually diverging, much like Soviet and Western standards did during the Cold War.

text:
A mentor once told me that the worst businesses to compete in are those where your competition doesn’t care if they lose money. Think restaurants or sports teams.

Plenty of people own restaurants as vanity investments. They want a cool place to impress friends. Sports teams are similar. The revenue rarely justifies the valuation, but how baller is it to own a sports team?

I wonder whether venture is heading in a similar direction.

Think about all the centimillionaires minted from Anthropic’s IPO. How many will turn around and start their own funds? There’s potentially a wave of price-insensitive capital entering venture.

So how should venture funds respond?

I think the answer is the same as it’s always been: be contrarian. The word gets thrown around so much that it’s almost lost its meaning. But being contrarian is about finding great businesses where others aren’t looking. That might mean investing in companies that aren’t cool to talk about at an SF dinner.

text:
Japan's biggest power producer is in talks with Anthropic and Meta to put data centres right next to its power plants around Tokyo.

JERA's chair says Amazon, Microsoft and Google are in the conversation too.

So many data centre projects around Tokyo have applied to connect to the grid that the wait for a new grid hookup is now up to 10 years. A data centre inside a power station takes its electricity straight from the plant and skips that queue.

The first one is already lined up. JERA's Chiba Thermal Power Station is getting a $15 billion, 400 MW data centre with Dell and Rhaelm, due to start in 2028, and tenants are being picked now. Yokohama is also a candidate, and JERA runs more than 20 thermal plants.

Power plants also sit in industrial areas, so there are fewer neighbours to object.

In my opinion we'll see a lot more of these power plant deals in Japan over the next few years, and that means more compute online sooner than the grid alone would allow

text: I am slowly analyzing the set of notes which I managed to generate with Fable and Astra, based on the original Lean code which proves the Riemann Hypothesis and I get this eerie feeling that mathematics which is grown from the LLMs at such an unprecedented scale is escaping our comprehension. When I focus on one part of the proof, I cannot grasp another and probably it will take many shorter papers, checked by many people independently to build a good story, which hides many details, to build a very rudimentary understanding of this proof. And yet, this is a vastly shortened version of the proof compared to the original Alpöge's version. And the ingredients are all rooted in well-established mathematics. Imagine now what will happen if LLMs soon start proving theorems with newly made methods and completely foreign definitions. This might happen very soon in algebra, cellular automata theory, complexity theory or set theory. We might end up with proofs which will take humans decades to actually comprehend, or worse, no group of humans will ever be able to digest those proofs fully. Mathematics at scale is just something else entirely. Not sure how to think about this but we probably need a massive shift in our understanding and comprehension of the word mathematics here. It's like watching the game called Factorio being played by an agent (which I actually did recently myself) and just seeing it build a fully working pipeline that delivers a rocket that flies to space. You can only appreciate the end result but you must accept that internal understanding of the "factory" is gone, we lost it and never will recover. Slightly optimistic about RH digestion but in general not so optimistic about the deep understanding of global arguments in future proofs.
author: nasqret
quoted_text: I have prepared a 1,200-page human-readable deformalization of Luke Sernau's condensed Lean proof of the generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions, itself a rewriting of Levent Alpöge's proof. It is the result of combined work with several AI agents, which first decompiled the proof into so-called structured proofs (in the sense of Leslie Lamport) and then wrote the final text. The draft is already readable. Its notation is rather pedantic, because it follows the formal proof closely, and it gathers the whole argument into a single document. I hope it will help mathematicians around the world gain deeper insight into the proof and keep simplifying and beautifying the argument. My contribution is only the design of the skills and the orchestration of the agents.

Two things we all accept about sending crypto.

You paste a 42-character string you can't read into a box you can't undo. And the moment you pay someone, they can see your whole wallet.

@Americanfort_io is fixing both, and $AF launches December 1. Here's what it is in plain terms.

The address problem. One wrong character and the money is gone. Scammers also send you tiny amounts from a lookalike address so it sits in your history, hoping you copy it next time. That's address poisoning, and it works because nobody actually reads 42 characters.

The history problem. Names that point to one public address make this worse. Type someone's name and you can see every transaction they've ever made. Pay someone once and they know your balance, what else you hold and who else you deal with.

FortressNames fix both. One name works across 13 chains. Every person who pays you gets their own private address for that name, one only the two of you can compute. Outsiders can't link your name to your wallets or see who pays you, and there's no static address for a scammer to copy.

What does $AF do? Every active FortressName locks $AF for as long as someone holds the name. American Fortress handles that at checkout, so you never have to hold or touch the token to use a name. More names in use means more $AF locked.

The facts: fixed supply of 10 billion. ERC-20 on Ethereum, bridged to Arbitrum and 0G. 16 patents: 2 granted, 1 allowed, 13 pending. Partners include 0G, Arbitrum, Brinks and Sumsub.

The honest part: $AF launches before the production wallet, which is planned for Q1 2027. Today you can reserve a name and run the desktop wallet beta on macOS and Windows.

We had similar (better under GRH) factoring results a few weeks before Google's release yesterday (didn't think it was that important back then😅). Our GPT-6 Astra-based agent proved unconditional integer factorization in L_N[1/3,O(1)] time (albeit with a huge constant). Moreover, using Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions (most believe it's proven by Alpöge and Claude anyway), we got a provable L_N[1/3, 2.97] bound. That's 2.97 vs Google's 105, and nearly matches the heuristic bound, finally bridging theory and practice.

text:
ZEC 一天砸掉 11.5%，不是被黑，是被"提前拆迁"。

先给框架：Zcash 的屏蔽池现在分两代——

①老池 Sapling：基于配对密码学（pairing），池里约 40 万枚 ZEC，占总量约 2%，按现价约 2.7 亿美元；

②新池 Ironwood：不走配对，官方明确不受影响；透明层资金也不受影响。

发生了什么（11/26，The Block / CoinDesk）：Zcash 联创 Sean Bowe 所在的 Zakura 团队发长文，建议网络升级后禁止再往 Sapling 存币、只留取出，催持有人迁往 Ironwood。升级日期还没定。

为什么市场反应这么大：触发点是两个"没坐实"的消息——Anthropic 数学家宣布用 Lean 验证了黎曼猜想证明（没过同行评审），外加 AI 大数分解突破的传闻（The Block 注明未经证实）。配对密码学万一被数学突破，老池理论上能被伪造证明、无声增币。

三点注意：

①团队自己原话：实际攻破"高度投机"，按他们估算，攻击效率再提高 10 亿倍，算力成本还要 1 万亿到 3000 万亿美元；

②目前没人给出从这两个消息到攻破 Sapling 的真实路径；

③走不走持币人投票、多久上线，都没有答案。

我的判断：这是预防性换锁，不是失窃。真正值得记的是机制层面——同类配对密码学还护着以太坊的 BLS 签名和一大批 ZK 系统，ZEC 只是第一个公开做"密码学原语代际迁移"的。老池迁不迁得动，盯后续链上迁移数据。

数据：ZEC 约 $682，24h -11.5%；BTC 约 $60,512（北京 11/27 早 8 点，CoinGecko）。@Zcash

DYOR，不构成投资建议。#Zcash #ZEC

👀 I suspect Elon did this to optimize RSI.

C is, essentially, human-readable assembly language - which makes it the perfect place for human and computer intelligence to "meet in the middle."

Also, I suspect there is so much more, and better, C/C++ source code to train on. Plus, all "synthetic" code/content generated by AI/SI, if it does works properly - which is something that can be objectively tested & measured - becomes essentially as good as human-generated code and can be fed into the next round of training for RSI.

In this way, C code is very precise and more like a mathematical proof than any English-language text.
